en: The Third Section, titled "The Supreme Self," within the *Śrī Bhāgavata-sandarbha* known as the *Ṣaṭ-sandarbha*.
In order to please the two saintly ones, Śrīla Rūpa and Sanātana, this is now analyzed by the southern Bhaṭṭa. i.

Having examined the first manuscript of that work— which was displaced, missing, and fragmentary— and having made a systematic arrangement, Jīvaka writes it down. [ii] Now, the Supreme Self (Paramātman) is explained.
In this regard, he describes that [Self] by means of two verses, preceded by a definition of the living beings within the world:
"The Knower of the Field [perceives] these manifestations of the mind..."
For the soul fashioned by Māyā, these [states] are eternal;
they are sometimes manifested and sometimes concealed.
Indeed, the pure one perceives them, even though he is the agent of impurity.
The Knower of the Field, the Self, the Person, the Ancient One, manifest self-luminous, unborn, the Supreme Lord,
Nārāyaṇa, the Blessed Vāsudeva.
Being perceived within Himself by His own *māyā*—

He who, though pure and beyond *māyā*, [perceives] these manifestations, which are the functions (*vṛtti*) of the mind or internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), fashioned by *māyā* and belonging to the entire field (*sarvakṣetra*) that is about to be described.
He perceives, that is, he sees specifically; seeing, he becomes absorbed therein,
and he is indeed that which is called the individual soul (jīva).
The meaning is that he is called the "knower of the field" (*kṣetrajña*) because of his being the knower of the field characterized by his own two bodies.
As it has been said:
"By which [nature] the individual soul (*jīva*) is deluded..."
"Even the Supreme Being considers the self to consist of the three qualities (guṇas), and thus undergoes the misfortune caused by them. [BhP 1.7.5] Thus it is said.

Regarding the nature of that mind which is fashioned by *māyā*, he says: "of that which is fashioned as the adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), through identity with the individual soul.
And thus, the meaning is: "of that which is metaphorically designated as such [i.e., as the individual soul]. From that...
And of what kind [is he]?
He is one who performs impure actions that are turned away from the Blessed One; such is he.
Of what kind are the manifestations? They are eternal, having been present from time immemorial.
In response to the inquiry as to when and of what nature these [powers] are, he says: "They manifest in the waking and dreaming states and are withdrawn in deep sleep.
As for that ancient Puruṣa who is the cause of the universe—
"The first incarnation is the Supreme Person," and so forth, as is well known from the second chapter onwards;
He is directly self-luminous and self-manifesting, unlike the individual soul which depends on something else; He is unborn, devoid of birth and other such states.
He is the Lord even of others, such as Brahmā and the rest;
He is one for whom the multitude of individual souls (nāra) constitutes His abode (ayana) by virtue of being subject to His control.
The Blessed One is [called] Vāsudeva because he possesses the qualities of sovereignty and so forth;
he is the refuge of all beings.
By his own *māyā*, that is, by the power of his own essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*), within himself...
Being observed in its own nature— that is, being established therein—
this is a construction where the object and the agent are identical (*karma-kartṛ-prayoga*).
Although He has entered into Māyā and its products by way of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), by the power of His own nature, He remains [established] in His very own nature.
But the meaning is that he is not attached to it.
Because, by virtue of being Vāsudeva, he is the knower of all fields (kṣetrajña), he is "the other";
he is distinct from the individual soul (jīva) who is deluded by māyā, being free from māyā and pure.

The knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is the self (ātman), that is, the supreme self (paramātman). Thus, even in this way, the primary state of being the knower of the field belongs to the supreme self alone. As it has been said:
"A man knows everything, yet he who knows that [Self] does not know the qualities; I praise the omniscient and infinite One.
Thus it is said in the *Śrī-Gītā-Upaniṣad*.
This body, O son of Kuntī, is called the field (kṣetra).
Those who know this call him who understands it the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
And know me also as the knower of the field in all fields, O Bhārata.
"The knowledge of the field and the knower of the field— that, in my view, is true knowledge" (Gītā 13.1).
Here, indeed, by the words "know Me also as the knower of the field," one should know Me as the knower of the field within all fields.

However, it does not convey the sense that [the Lord] resides only in His own field like the individual soul (jīva); nor does it indicate, through grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the soul, that the undifferentiated conscious reality alone is the object of knowledge. For otherwise, the phrase "in all fields" would become redundant.

This is because, in the passage beginning with "I shall declare that which is to be known" (Gītā 13.12) and continuing with "It has hands and feet everywhere; it has eyes, heads, and faces everywhere" (Gītā 13.13), it is precisely the qualified [Brahman] that is about to be described.
Furthermore, because knowledge is likewise to be taught by means of the passage beginning with "humility" (amānitvam) and so forth;
and moreover, because in the verse "And also the Knower of the Field," there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), just as in the expression "Thou art That" (tat tvam asi).

If non-distinctive knowledge were intended to be expressed, one would have referred to it simply as "the knowledge of the Kṣetrajña and the Īśvara," rather than "the knowledge of the Kṣetra and the Kṣetrajña.
However, the meaning of the phrase "of the Kṣetra and the Kṣetrajña" is as follows: [it refers to the knowledge of the distinction between them].
The knowledge of both the field and the knower of the field is considered by Me alone to be My own knowledge;
the meaning is that this knowledge has the oneness [of the object] as its sole purport, according to the maxim "but the reference is for another purpose.
This is because the object of knowledge is indicated as being one, and because such is the fitness [of the context].
And knowledge is not considered by me here to consist merely in the distinction between the field and the knower of the field— as held by the atheistic Sāṅkhya—
because, by this [statement], God is taken into account.
Furthermore, unlike the Vivarta-vāda (theory of illusory manifestation), even for Īśvara, there is no state of being a person perceived merely through delusion;
this applies to the scriptures such as the Vedas and the Gītā, which are characterized by his speech.

Because [the scripture] would lack authority, it would result in the adoption of Buddhist doctrines; and since that is the case, for those who maintain the theory of illusory manifestation (vivartavādin), an explanation of it would be as untenable as it is for the Buddhists.

Furthermore, even though he is a true person (*satya-puruṣa*), the notion that knowledge devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa-jñāna*) alone is the means to liberation is not to be adopted from his other scriptures;
for in the preceding chapter, beginning with "those who are ever-steadfast" (*satata-yuktā ye*), such knowledge devoid of distinctions was shown to be something to be abandoned.
Because that is what is intended to be expressed;

and in that very context, with the words beginning "But those who... all actions" (12.6), [the Lord] refers to those whose devotion is directed toward no other, and by the statement "I am their deliverer from the ocean of death and saṃsāra" (12.7), [He indicates] that.
Even the requirement for knowledge is not honored;
this was stated by the Blessed One himself in the eleventh book: "That which is [attained] through ritual acts, through austerity," and so forth (BhP 11.20.32).
And in the Mokṣadharma:
"Whatever perfection of means exists for the four goals of human life, a man who takes refuge in Nārāyaṇa attains those [goals] even without them. Thus it is said.
But here, in order to make that very same subject—which was praised in the preceding chapter—not in vain, it is pointed out with particular detail:
"Thus the field, as well as knowledge and the object of knowledge, have been briefly described;
my devotee, having understood this, attains to My state" (Gītā 13.18).
By this [concluding] verse, the work has been made easy to understand by being permeated with devotion;
for this very reason, here the individual *kṣetrajña* (the field-knower) is designated as the devotee (*bhakta*), whereas the universal *kṣetrajña* is designated as the object of knowledge (*jñeya*).

Because the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is taught together with the field-knower (*kṣetrajña*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), it is recalled that immediately thereafter, each of those—the state of being the individual soul (*jīvatva*) and the state of being the Lord (*īśvaratva*)—is shown not to be perishable (*akṣara*). For it is said:
"The person (*puruṣa*), situated in nature (*prakṛti*), indeed experiences the qualities born of nature (*prakṛti*)."
By stating, "The cause of its birth in good and evil wombs is attachment to the qualities" (Gītā 13.21),

having thus indicated that the individual soul resides within primordial nature (prakṛti), it is clearly made known that its true nature is that of the Imperishable (akṣara), by demonstrating that it is not of the nature of primordial matter in itself.
"The witness, the permitter, the supporter, the enjoyer, the Great Lord,

and also called the Supreme Self— this is the Supreme Person within this body" (Gītā 13.22). Thus, by the very fact that the Person named the Supreme Self is designated as being superior to the individual soul (jīva), [the superiority of the former is established] *kaimutya* (by a fortiori).
That has been shown:
"There are these two persons in the world, the perishable and the imperishable; the perishable consists of all beings, while the one who stands at the peak is called the imperishable" (Gītā 15.16).
"But the Supreme Person is another, declared as the Supreme Self (paramātman), who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them as the imperishable Lord" (Gītā 15.17).
In this passage, the imperishability (akṣaratva) of the individual soul (jīva) is indeed explicitly stated.
In that regard, he is the witness (*upadraṣṭṛ*), the supreme observer (*parama-sākṣin*);
the permitter (*anumantṛ*), who impels [the self] according to each respective action;
the sustainer (*bhartṛ*), the nourisher (*poṣaka*); and the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*).
He is the protector, Maheśvara, the supreme ruler over all,
the Supreme Self, and the inner controller of all; thus it should be explained.
Regarding the two subsequent verses,
however, the meaning is understood from the *Amarakośa*: "That which pervades time by virtue of its unchanging, uniform nature is called *kūṭastha*."

"That one is indeed the pure jīva, while the other is the Supreme Person (uttama-puruṣa)"—this is established from the subsequent verse. Thus, here too, both the field (kṣetra), the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), and all knowers of the field have been described.

Furthermore, by the word "other" (anya) in the two subsequent verses, it is shown that although the two imperishables (akṣara) exist as distinct entities, they do not possess those respective forms [of the individual soul].

It has been shown that since renunciation must occur, there is never an abiding in a state devoid of distinctions; therefore, even what was said— that "one is born for the sake of my own nature"— has as its intended meaning the attainment of equality with me (*sārṣṭi*).

Thus, although there is equality between the two in terms of being imperishable (akṣara), because the individual soul (jīva) possesses inferior power and is permeated by primordial nature (prakṛti), the intention is that the Lord alone is to be known as the object of worship for the sake of attaining liberation from that nature.
Therefore, the passage beginning with "this body" and so forth should be analyzed as follows:
the meaning is that this is one's own direct perception (*aparokṣa*).
Here, the singular number is used for both "body" and "field" (*kṣetra*) to denote the individual instance.
It is understood that [this occurs] by way of completion and precisely by way of prioritizing birth;
this is because of the restatement using the plural form "in all fields" (*sarva-kṣetreṣu*).

Regarding the phrase "he who knows this," the meaning is that the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) knows these manifestations of the mind—beginning with "the body, the vital breaths, the senses, and the mental faculties"—in accordance with the direction stated in [BhP 6.4.25]: "The person knows everything, as well as the qualities and the one who knows them. This is according to the manner described therein.
"Know Me also as the Knower of the Field"—
this has been stated: "Pervading this entire world with but one part, I stand as the universe" (Gītā 10.42).
Where no other alternative is possible, one should resort to the difficulty of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā);
nevertheless, if grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with that [indicated meaning] is intended.
In that case, it would have been sufficient to say merely "know me as the Knower of the Field" (kṣetrajña), or simply "know him as me";
there would not have been the additional phrase "in all fields, O Bhārata. However, [it was indeed said].
Just as in the passage beginning, "The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) [knows] these manifestations of the mind," two Knowers of the Field must indeed be mentioned;
and thus the Brahma-sūtra states: "For two Selves have entered the cave, because that is seen" (Brahma-sūtra 1.2.11).
[1.2.11] And that very distinction has been summarized by the passage beginning with "For the person situated in nature" (puruṣaḥ prakṛtistho hi).
Therefore, since the meaning of the opening statement depends upon its conclusion, this alone is the consistent meaning.

As stated by the authors of the Brahma-sūtras: "If it be argued that [the effect] does not exist because of its designation as non-existent, we say no, because of the difference in attributes, as indicated by the remainder of the sentence" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.17).
Now, regarding the phrase "knowledge of the field and the knower of the field," that which pertains to the field consists of the cognitive faculties and consciousness—

And the knowledge that has departed will be shown; for whatever individual field-knowledge was previously displayed in each respective field-knower, because it is a reflection of a portion of My knowledge within those fields, and because it enters into the field-knowers as a minute fraction of a part, that is considered to be My own knowledge.
Therefore, it has been rightly said that the primary state of being the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) belongs to the Supreme Self alone;
herein also occurs the manifestation of the Blessed Lord in His form as the Supreme Self.

And that which was born by me should remain under the control of that [Supreme Self] without being liberated; according to this direction stated [in BhP 10.87.30], because the individual souls (jīvas) manifest from whichever specific portion they are embraced by a particular power (śakti), it should be understood that they do so through that very same [portion].
Thus it is said in that very same place,
beginning with "I, having pervaded," and so forth;
and also in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"We bow to that Imperishable One, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, in even a ten-thousandth part of a fraction of whom this power of the universe resides" (ViP 1.9.53). Thus,
the complete and pure power is shown by the passage beginning with "Kalā, kāṣṭhā, nimeṣa," and likewise by the venerable...
In the Nārada-Pañcarātra,
Nārada said:
"O Lord, I desire to know the pure creation (śuddha-sarga) in its true essence."
And that which exists as the transcendent state beyond these two creations.
In this regard, it should be understood that what was previously mentioned—the Prādhānika and the Śākta—refers to these two types of creation.
The Blessed Lord said: "He who is the all-pervading God, the eternal Supreme Brahman..."
In this world, the universal consciousness is characterized by supreme bliss.
But he is non-different from Vāsudeva, possessing the splendor of hundreds of fires, suns, and moons;
and the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva is likewise of that same nature, the Supreme Lord.
O twice-born one, the Lord, whose nature is light, indeed agitates his own radiance when joined with that energy, and he repeatedly enters the Imperishable.
That Acyuta, possessing infallible splendor, indeed expands his own form by taking refuge in Vāsudeva, remaining established in himself like a cloud containing water.
Having agitated his own self, whose form was radiant with truth,
he then brought it forth like the water of a sea wave.
Consisting of consciousness and having light as its essence, he produces by himself from himself that which is called the Puruṣa— an infinite and great expansion of light.
And that Supreme Lord is indeed the refuge of all living beings,
and He is their inner controller, just as the sky is for the stars.
Just as fire, O twice-born one, spontaneously impels a mass of sparks,
even so does the Supreme Lord.
"For the sake of liberation from bonds bound by prior latent impressions (vāsanā), know that the unborn Lord (aja-prabhu) is the totality, while those [deities] are His partial portions. Therefore,
it is for this very reason that Śrī-Pradyumna is present in Brahmā and others, Śrī-Viṣṇu in Manu and others, and [Śrī-Nārāyaṇa] in Rudra and others.

The state of being the inner controller (*antaryāmitva*) of Śrī Saṅkarṣaṇa is heard in scripture; that should be understood as his very same [state], who has descended assuming various portions (*aṃśa*), acting as the inner controller of this or that [being] through this or that portion.
For this very reason, [it applies] to Rudra as well.

Both his nature as Saṅkarṣaṇa and his nature as Puruṣa are traditionally taught; for instance, in passages such as "O Bhava, you resort to that Prakṛti known by the name Saṅkarṣaṇa" (BhP 5.17.16) and "In the beginning there was Śatadhṛti" (BhP 11.4.5). This very one—
You alone exist in five forms: as the self of the elements, the self of the senses, the self of primordial matter (pradhāna), the individual self (ātman), and the supreme self (paramātman).

Thus it was explained at the beginning [of the Viṣṇupurāṇa 5.18.50]. Therefore, it is established that the Person who is the inner ruler of all is indeed Brahman, and that he is designated as the Supreme Self (paramātman) and so forth in the opening passages as the Supreme Self.
And this has been explained by the Master (Śrīdhara Svāmī) in his commentary on the hymn to Varuṇa: "Obeisance to you, the Blessed One, the Brahman, the Supreme Self" (BhP 10.28.6).

"To the Supreme Self, the controller of all living beings. The status of this Supreme Self as a "Person" (puruṣa) is merely figurative, due to its having *māyā* as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). This has been stated in the Vaiṣṇava [Purāṇa] itself:
There is no end to that which has no origin,
and no growth for that which is devoid of transformation;
nor does it depend upon anything else, being an object free from conceptual construction.
I bow to Him, the Supreme Person, the primordial one worthy of praise;
who, though truly one and pure, appears as if impure through various divisions of forms, while experiencing the qualities of that very [Prakṛti] in manifold ways.
"I bow to that eternal and imperishable Puruṣa, who is endowed with knowledge and is the creator of the manifestation of all beings.
Thus, immediately after that Supreme Lord mentioned in the preceding sequence:
In many ways, such as in the form of Brahmā and others; appearing as if impure and as if attached to the acts of creation and so forth;
[this refers to] the divisions of forms, such as Dakṣa and others.
The Lord is the one who manifests and expands the power of all sentient beings through various forms such as Manu and others.
In this context, "the enjoyer of qualities" means the enjoyer of the bliss of the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*).
That which is subtle, unknowable, unmanifest, immovable, and eternal, devoid of the senses, the objects of the senses, and all elemental beings;

"For he is indeed called the inner self (antarātman) of beings and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña); he is conceived as the Puruṣa who is truly distinct from the three guṇas. Thus it is stated in the Mokṣadharma, in the Nārāyaṇīya episode.
The Vedas also describe this very one as pure:
"The one God is hidden in all beings."
Pervading all, the inner self of all beings,
the supervisor of karma, the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious one, absolute and devoid of qualities. [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11]
The one unborn [Self] lies beside the single unborn [Prakṛti], which is red, white, and black,
and which produces many offspring of similar form; yet, being unborn, he remains indifferent and eventually abandons her.
Another unborn one enjoys her whose pleasures have already been experienced.
Thus begins [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5]. Therefore, the two verses beginning with "The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) [is distinct] from these" have been correctly explained.
// 5.11 // The Illustrious Brāhmaṇa to Rahūgaṇa // 1 // [2] Now, regarding his manifestation, it should be understood that devotion alone is the requisite qualification, as before;
furthermore, the manifestation is threefold.
As it is stated in the Nāradīya Tantra:
"The wise know that Viṣṇu has three forms designated as Puruṣas:
one is the creator of Mahat, and the second is situated within the threads [of the cosmic egg]."
The third is that which abides in all beings; by knowing these, one is liberated.

Here, the first [type] is as follows: because of such statements as "Just as tiny sparks fly forth from a fire" and "He thought," it refers to the Seer who has attained oneness with both the Great Universal Soul (mahā-samaṣṭi-jīva) and primordial nature (prakṛti).
He is indeed one; He alone is Saṅkarṣaṇa and Mahāviṣṇu. As it is said in the Brahma-saṃhitā:
In that *liṅga*, the Lord Śambhu, eternal and consisting of light,
appeared; and within that *liṅga*, Mahāviṣṇu, the Lord of the world, manifested—
beginning with the passage "The Puruṣa with a thousand heads" (BrahmaS 5.11).
From that eternal Lord Nārāyaṇa, the waters manifested;
from them arose the ocean-receptacle of causes, consisting of Saṅkarṣaṇa.
Within that, the Great One himself, the thousand-rayed, entered into yogic sleep.
And within the network of the pores of his hair, the seed of Saṅkarṣaṇa produced golden eggs enveloped by the great elements.

The phrase "and so forth" refers to the *liṅga* (indicative mark) in [BrahmaS 5.13]. According to the passage in [ViP 1.9.53], "In a ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth part of whom this power of the universe resides," it is the *liṅga* of that Great Blessed One, Śrī Govinda, because he is the progenitor of the Puruṣa.
That which is indeed the non-distinction (aviśeṣa) within the subtle body (liṅga) is Śambhu himself;
the meaning is that he is the primary locus of the word "Śambhu."
Then, having created that [egg], the second person entered into it; thus he is described as the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) of the collective individual souls (*samaṣṭi-jīva*).
Due to the many divisions of those [souls] whose nature is the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), there is a manifold division [of the inner controller].
In that very same context, it is sometimes stated that Pradyumna is the inner controller of the subtle and Aniruddha is the inner controller of the gross;
by this, Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others residing in Mahā-Vaiṣṇava-loka (Mahā-Vaikunṭha) are shown to be the possessors of those [energies],
while those who are the mind and so forth—
One should discern that the presiding deities, such as Vāsudeva and others, are indeed portions (aṃśa) of Him;
this also applies to the third person—
the two birds, companions and friends, dwelling together.
They both embrace the same tree; one of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating. (Ṛg-veda 1.163.20, Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1)
Thus has been described the inner controller (antaryāmī) within each individual;
due to their many divisions, he is manifold. Among these, the manifestation of the first is as stated: "The first incarnation is the Puruṣa of the Supreme" (BhP 2.6.41).
And the commentary [states]: "The Person who impels primordial nature (prakṛti) is the Supreme Abundance;
he whose playful embodiment was described in the verse beginning with 'Thousand-headed' is that first incarnation."
Thus ends this [section].

In this and other instances, what is called "being an incarnation" (avatāratva) should be understood as the manifestation of a single portion of His vibhūti (divine opulence). 2.6. Śrī Brahmā [said] to Nārada: 2. [3]
As for the second [verse], it is as follows:
"In time, that unborn one, through a human lifespan and by means of yoga already set in motion, developed awakened understanding."
He himself beheld that which had been shining within his own heart, which he had not seen before.
A single person is lying upon a couch formed by the body of Śeṣa, which is as white as a lotus stalk;
this one residing within the waters of the cosmic egg is indeed Pradyumna, the thousand-headed one.
"Puruṣāyuṣā" means by a hundred years of human life. "Yoga" refers to bhakti-yoga.
This [term] also applies later in the phrase "avyakta-mūla," where "avyakta" [is used].
The meaning is: "that whose root and lower part are the Pradhāna.
Regarding the phrase *bhuvanāṅghripendram*: the fourteen worlds are the "feet" (aṅghripas), and he is their "lord" (*indra*) by virtue of being their controller.
The meaning is "the present. // 3.8 //
The venerable Maitreya said to Vidura:
3. [4] As for the manifestation of the third [state]:
some [perceive it] within the space of their own hearts.
Through meditative concentration, they remember the Person, the size of a span,
dwelling within, four-armed, bearing the lotus, the discus, the conch, and the mace. [BhP 2.2.8]

A "span" (prādeśa) is the distance between the extended index finger and the thumb; that is the measure [of the heart] with respect to the heart, according to the principle that [scriptural injunctions] have human beings as their qualified subjects.
2.2 // Śrī Śuka //4// [5] Thus, although the Puruṣa is of many kinds, he establishes his oneness by means of an illustration:
"Just as the wind [is one], though [it enters] into moving and stationary beings..."
He would rule, established in His own essential nature;
thus the Supreme Lord Vāsudeva, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), has entered this as the Self. [BhP 5.11.14]
In its own essential nature and in the form of vital breath (prāṇa), it rules—that is, it governs—this entire universe. And the Śruti says:
"Just as the one wind has entered the world..."
He became the counterpart of every form;
likewise, the single inner self of all beings becomes the counterpart of every form both within and without.
Thus it is said in the Kaṭhaka [KaṭhU 2.2.10].
5.11. The venerable Brāhmaṇa [said] to Rahūgaṇa. 5.
[6] Likewise,

For there is indeed only one supreme Self for all embodied beings; it is perceived as if manifold by the deluded, just like light or the sky. (BhP 10.54.44) "Of embodied beings" means of living souls (*jīvas*).
The Self is the Supreme Self. 10.54.
Śrī Baladeva [embraced] Śrī Rukmiṇī. 6.
Thus, indeed, the one supreme Self alone is situated within the self among all beings. 7.
"Just as the moon [is reflected] in various vessels of water, and as all beings are of one essence"—

he says that within all beings and living entities there is but one Supreme Self, yet He does not become smeared here and there like those individual souls, for He remains established in His own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
The elements and even the living bodies are of one essence by virtue of that causal form. // 11.18 //
The Blessed Lord said to Uddhava: [8] Having thus established the manifold nature of the one Puruṣa, His portions (aṃśas) are now further explained.

That which is evolving is designated as having the nature of an adjunct (*upādhi*),
just as in the beginning [of the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 3.26.8]: "They know the cause in the state of being the agent of cause and effect to be *prakṛti*," and so forth, regarding the Supreme Self.
But he says that when it functions through predominance, it is indeed without qualification:
"The agent characterized by sattva is unattached;
the one characterized by rajas is known to be blinded by passion."
One who is characterized by tamas is deprived of right mindfulness, devoid of the [higher] qualities, and takes refuge in me [only through delusion].
This is clear. 11.25. Śrī Bhagavān. 35. [36]

Now, as for the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), since it consists of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvedana-rūpa*), it ultimately culminates in that very same conscious form (*cid-rūpa*); thus he says: "In the state of being an enjoyer of pleasures and pains, the person (*puruṣa*) is beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*)" (BhP 3.26.8). The word "cause" (*kāraṇam*) is to be construed with the preceding verse. 3.26.
Śrī Kapiladeva.
[36] [37] Now, it should be explained that [the soul] has the Supreme Self as its sole remainder (*eka-śeṣatva*); "one" means other than the Supreme Self.
"Remainder" (śeṣa) means a part. That [part] and that [other part] constitute a "single remainder" (eka-śeṣa).

The single remainder of the Supreme Self is the "Supreme-Self-single-remainder" (paramātmaika-śeṣa). His state is his reality; that very thing is his nature (tattvam eva svabhāvaḥ), which is his primordial substance (prakṛti). He who possesses that is [the one described].
Its nature is that of being subservient solely to the Supreme Self;
and the meaning is that it remains so at all times, even in the state of liberation.
And this nature of his is due to his very own intrinsic essence, not through any limitation or the like;
it arises by means of his own natural, inconceivable power and his own natural rays.

The meaning of the term "by itself" (*svataḥ*) is that because [the Self] occupies the position of an atom (*paramāṇu*), while the states conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-avasthā*) possess only partial dependence upon *prakṛti*.
Furthermore, its nature as power (*śakti-rūpatva*) is that of a marginal power (*taṭastha-śakti*).
Because it is of that nature,
and likewise, even though it occupies the place of its rays, it is eternally dependent upon them and is non-different from them in its absence.
It is understood that [the cause] is the source for the creation of this world and so forth, because it serves as the means for that creation;
furthermore, even though its nature is substantial, it is recognized as being similar to *pradhāna*. Thus it has been said:
And its status as power (*śaktitva*) is due to its being a specific primordial nature (*prakṛti-viśeṣa*):
"The supreme power of Viṣṇu is proclaimed, and likewise another called the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*)."
Ignorance, known by the name of karma, is said to be the third power.
Thus, in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (6.7.61),
it is said: "Earth, water, fire, and air"— and immediately following [the Gītā 7.4], "Nature is divided eightfold at the outset."
But know, O mighty-armed one, that this is my lower nature; there is another, higher nature of mine, which is the life-force.
By which this world is sustained.

Thus it is said in the *Śrī Gītopaniṣad*. Furthermore, in the statement from the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa* beginning with "The power of Vi�ṣṇu is declared to be supreme," since the three [powers] alone are specifically designated as powers (*śaktitva*), the "supreme" (*parā*) refers to the fact that the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) possesses the nature of a power through its connection with ignorance (*avidyā*) and karma.
That [is not so]; rather, it follows that [the soul exists] by its very own nature. And thus it is sung: "A portion of My very self.
For this very reason, it is said: "This is the lower; but other than this... and so forth.

In the passage beginning with "The Knower of the Field [knows] these manifestations of the mind," the term *kṣetrajña* (Knower of the Field) is applied even to the Pure [Self], because the word *kṣetra* (Field) is used merely as a figurative designation.
Thus, even though it is a power (*śakti*), its distinctness arises from its being "standing on the bank" (*taṭastha*);

and its state of being "standing on the bank" results from its transcendence of the power of *māyā*. This is because the Supreme Self is untainted by defects such as the subjugation by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because it does not enter into either of the two extremes;
and even though that [agency] possesses the power for that [action], there is no staining of the Supreme Self, just as when a ray of light situated in one place is obscured by a shadow.
The sun is likewise beyond being eclipsed;
and its state of being "situated on the bank" (taṭastha) has been stated in the Śrī-Nārada-Pañcarātra:
"That which is the form of consciousness situated on the bank..."
"Emerging from self-awareness,
colored by the passion for qualities—
that is called the *jīva*," and so forth.

Therefore, even in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, he is mentioned as being in the intermediate state; and the difference between them is stated in the Śruti: "The Illusionist creates this universe from this [Self], and another, bound by illusion, is confined within it" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.9).
"Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit," and so forth.
For this very reason, it is said in the *Vaiṣṇava* [Purāṇa]: "When the knowledge that produces the sense of duality has gone to absolute destruction..."
Who could bring about the non-existent difference between the self and Brahman?
Even regarding that specific difference characterized by being a deity, a human, and so forth, which [one might think] produces it—

The meaning is this: when ignorance has been destroyed, who will make that inherent difference between the self—the individual soul (jīva)—and the Supreme Brahman non-existent? On the contrary, everyone will make it exist, for it is already existent.

In the subsequent reading, because *nāsanta* is that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), its meaning is restricted solely to "difficult to create"; thus, even in the case of *mokṣadā*, there is no deviation from being a part of that [creation], precisely because it is an inherent power (*svābhāvika-śakti*).

Therefore, in liberation— which is characterized by abiding in one's own true nature preceded by release from ignorance— there occurs for that which has merged [into Brahman] an attainment of similarity with it,
according to such scriptural passages as, "The stainless one attains the highest equality."
Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature;
they are not born even in heaven, nor at the time of dissolution.
And from the Śrī-Gītā Upaniṣads it is said, "They tremble.
Therefore, in passages such as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9), it teaches precisely the identity with Brahman.
It is like the statement, "The attainment of its own nature [occurs] through logical possibility.

Thus, since its status as a power (śakti) is established, because of the mutual interpenetration of the power and the possessor of power, there is the absence of power when there is the absence of the possessor of power, and because there is no distinction in their being consciousness (cittva).
In some cases, there is a description of non-difference; and because even a single entity is seen to possess a diversity of powers, a description of difference is not inconsistent.
The followers of Śrī Rāmānuja, however, [maintain this] even regarding the locus and the controller.
They maintain that the designation of non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is like the designation of "cow" and so forth for both the individual and the genus;
as it is stated in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "O Lord, he who has come here to you..."
"The host of deities is near;
you alone are the creator of the world, since you are omnipresent. Thus [he said].
And in the Śrī-Gītā it is said: "You pervade everything; therefore, You are everything.
In that regard, the scripture teaches non-duality for those who desire knowledge, but teaches duality for those who desire devotion. However, in some places...
That it is a reflection of the Supreme Self is heard in scripture, as for example:
"Just as a person might see his own single self appearing as two-fold in a mirror or in the eye, even so [is the distinction] between us two."

Even that is stated solely for the purpose of nourishing the vision of non-duality for those who desire knowledge, and not by way of actual ontological reflection. This is the doctrine of non-duality (*advayavāda*).

Furthermore, even according to the Guru’s view, because of the contradiction with the principle stated in *Vaiśeṣika Sūtra* 3.2.19, "Also, in the case of the teacher's opinion, there is no apprehension as in the case of water," and because of the acceptance of a mere similarity to a reflection— however one might interpret it— according to the principle in *Vaiśeṣika Sūtra* 3.2.20, "It is thus, because of the participation in increase and decrease, because of its internal existence, and because of the consistency of both."

Thus, the eternality of His nature as a plenary portion (aṃśa) of the Supreme Self is also demonstrated by the Śrī Gītā Upaniṣads: "In the world of living beings, a portion of My very self has become the eternal living soul.
Such, indeed, is His state as a portion.
Regarding that, he says [the following] concerning the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*):
"For this is a portion of the self of the Supreme Self belonging to all sentient beings without exception."
"The first incarnation is that wherein this multitude of beings is manifested.
And the commentary states: "The Self of all beings—that is, of all living creatures—because He is the part (*aṃśa*) of the individual selves (*vyaṣṭi*), He is their portion."

The soul (jīva). The statement regarding his being an incarnation is intended to mean that he is an manifestation of Nārāyaṇa; such is this [verse]. 3.6 Śrī Śuka. 37 [38] Now, concerning the individual (vyaṣṭi):
O Great-minded One, for this very soul, which is but a single portion of Me,
bondage exists through beginningless ignorance.
"And by knowledge, so is the other.
The "other" refers to liberation (*mokṣa*).
In this context, the individual soul (*vyaṣṭi*) occupies the position of a ray or an atom.
In that regard, it should be understood that a certain one who possesses all forms of conceit is the collective totality (samaṣṭi). // 11.11 //
The Blessed Lord: //38// [39] In this regard, they manifest His state as a part (aṃśa) precisely by virtue of His power (śakti):
"Even within the city created by Himself, these [souls] possess a concealment that is neither external nor internal."

"They call you the Person (puruṣa) created from a portion (aṃśa) of Him who possesses all potencies. Thus [it is said]. "Unconcealed by the internal and external" means that it is untouched by causes and effects—external causes and effects being the "external," and internal ones being the "internal"—by those [factors] it remains unconcealed. It is "created from a portion."
The meaning is "a portion.

By means of the qualification "akhila-śakti-dhṛtaḥ" (the bearer of all potencies), which refers to the possessor of all powers, it is made understood that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a portion of You specifically as one characterized by the *jīva*-potency, and not [a portion] of Your pure [nature]. Thus, [the portion] of the individual soul—its...
By the statement "participation [in the creation] occurs precisely through the nature of power (śakti)," they clarify that this is indeed what constitutes being a part.

Furthermore, his state of being a bystander (taṭasthatva) is evident in such passages as "he who, by means of the Unborn, enters into the latent impressions (anuśaya) of those who abandon," because he does not enter into either of the two categories [of the created or the uncreated]. 10.87.
The Śrutis [speak of] the Blessed Lord.
[40] Now, with regard to one who desires knowledge, he states the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara):
"I am you, and I am not another than you."
"You alone are I; behold this, O friend!
The wise do not perceive even the slightest gap between us at any time."
This is clear. 4.28. The illustrious Supreme Self [spoke to] Purañjana. 40.
[41] Therein, according to the manner previously described, first of all, there is the mutual interpenetration of all the principles (tattvas).

The intention is that unity is perceived through the speaker's intent; thus, the Lord Śrī Bhagavān intends that the very desire to express the entry of the power called the individual soul (jīva) into the Supreme Self, who possesses that power, is the reason for their identity in this view of unity—
namely, "due to mutual entry."
The enumeration of the principles in their sequential order, as intended by the speaker, was addressed to that bull among men.

And the commentary [states]: "Because they enter into one another, according to the speaker's intention, the former is a smaller number and the latter is a larger number; their state is 'succession' (*paurvāparya*).
By means of that, 'enumeration' (*prasaṅkhyāna*) is counting. Thus ends [the explanation of] verse 11.22.
The Blessed Lord said: 41. [42] Now, He teaches their identity even through the absence of difference, owing to the lack of distinction in their nature as consciousness:
"In this regard, there is not even an atom's worth of disparity between the individual soul and the Lord."
"Thus, other conceptualizations are useless," [BhP 11.22.11].
And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: "How then is there a position of twenty-five? To this he replies: 'The Person' (*puruṣa*); [this indicates] the distinctness."
There is no dissimilarity between the two, because both have the nature of consciousness;
therefore, this notion that there is an absolute difference between them is futile.

Here, by means of both similarity and non-difference, the relationship of power and the possessor of power between those two is demonstrated; by that, their non-distinction is also established. // 11.21 //
The Blessed Lord //42// [43] Now, He teaches the distinction between those two for one who desires devotion: when [the yogi perceives] the Self as devoid [of qualities]...
Seeing himself endowed with his own true nature, yet accompanied by the elements, the senses, the qualities, and the latent impressions, one attains self-sovereignty.

The self, the individual soul, is endowed with me—the possessor of power—who serves as the substratum for that power of the individual soul; [it attains] self-sovereignty, such as equality in power and so forth. (3.9)
[He is] Brahmā, lying within the womb.
[44] Regarding that, he states the reason for the distinction:
For a person joined with beginningless ignorance, self-knowledge is not possible by itself; therefore, it must come from another.
"One who knows reality should be a giver of knowledge" (BhP 11.22.10).
And the commentary states: "It does not arise from oneself, but rather arises from another."
The intention behind the negation of the twenty-sixth principle (*tattva*) is that there might be another supreme Lord who is omniscient by his own nature;
however, this [negation] indeed makes known the Lord’s state of being the giver of knowledge (*jñānadatva*), which is the distinction between the knower and the knowledge itself.

This is the state of being. Furthermore, the words of Uddhava appear later: "Thus, knowledge indeed comes from You; for the loss of that knowledge of living beings occurs here through Your power" (BhP 11.22.28).
In this context, if His status as the Supreme Lord were merely imagined by the ignorance of the individual soul (*jīva*), then He would be like a wooden post (*sthāṇu*).

Since even the knowledge granted to him would not be effective as it is for an ordinary person, the glorious Lord Himself has thus taught its existence to the deluded— by means of that very person’s identification with the ultimate Lord— that the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is indeed real.

This is clear. Furthermore, in this very context, for those who maintain the doctrine of difference (*bheda-vādinaḥ*), it is distinguished as follows: "Whatever face we grasp here, we do so because of the possibility of reasoning" (referring to *BhP* 11.22.3), and "But the difference born of supreme discrimination (*parama-vivekaja*) is indeed difference"; likewise, "For those who speak while upholding my Māyā, what indeed is difficult to accomplish? (*BhP* 11.22.4).
One thinks:
"Is it not the case that the fourfold means of knowledge consist of scripture, perception, tradition, and inference?"
"Because there is no finality regarding the means of valid cognition, he becomes detached from conceptual constructions (vikalpa).

(BhP 11.19.17) Here, only difference (*bheda*) is negated, because the word *vikalpa* has the sense of "doubt" (*saṃśaya*). The meaning is that, having abandoned doubt, he establishes his firm conviction in the reality itself.
Therefore, because actions are subject to transformation, the Vipaschit should perceive everything up to the realm of Virinchi as inauspicious and perishable, even if it has not yet been seen.

Furthermore, in this verse and even in the subsequent verse beginning with "api dṛṣṭavat," the perception of perishability is stated by taking Viriñca alone as the limit, and not even Vaikuṇṭha and the like. // 11.19 //
The Blessed Lord: [44] Furthermore, because the definition of the individual soul (jīva) taught elsewhere by the venerable Jāmātṛ-muni is to be relied upon, He defines it with three verses: [45]—
When the mind is free from the impurities of desire, greed, and so forth, which arise from the conceits of "I" and "mine," it is pure.
"Neither painful nor pleasant, equanimous"—
at that time, the person perceives himself as solitary, beyond material nature.
[He perceives] the uninterrupted, self-luminous, and indivisible atomic essence by means of that which is joined with knowledge and detachment.
With a self endowed with devotion,
he perceives the indifferent Lord and Prakṛti, whose power has been destroyed.
The application [of the terms] is indeed clear:
by the verse beginning with "I am yours," that Self is shown to be eternally pure; and by the word "the Self" (ātmānam), it is shown to be the referent of the word "I" (aham-artha).
Otherwise, there would be an absence of the cognition of selfhood (*ātmatva*).
By the word "merely" (*kevalam*), it is indicated that [the self] possesses a nature consisting of a single form;
by the phrase "beyond primordial matter" (*prakṛteḥ param*), [it is indicated that it is distinct from] transformation (*vikāra*).
By the phrase "endowed with devotion," it is shown that [the soul's] manifestation is dependent upon the grace of the Supreme Self;
by the phrase "uninterrupted," it is shown that because of its eternity, the soul exists solely for the sake of the Supreme Self;
and by the phrase "self-luminous,"...

By the word "this" (*anena*), [it is shown that the Self] is not merely of the nature of cognition, as in the view that "it is self-luminous to itself. By the word "atomic" (*aṇimānam*), [it is shown that the Self] is indeed atomic and distinct in every body.
By the word "unfragmented" (*akhaṇḍitam*), [it is shown that the Self is] not divided—

Because it possesses the powers of knowledge and so forth, it is characterized by its own inherent attributes of being a knower, an agent, and an enjoyer; this has been made manifest. Thus says the venerable Kapiladeva.
Furthermore, this also does not contradict the previously stated definition.
The Self is eternal, immutable, pure, one, the knower of the field, the substratum,
changeless, self-luminous, and the cause.
"Pervasive, unattached, and unobstructed"—
by these twelve supreme characteristics of the self, the wise man [should know it].
One should abandon the unreal notion of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth, which arises from delusion;
[the Self is] immutable, being devoid of decay.
He is one, and not of the nature of the aggregate consisting of the body, senses, and so forth; he is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), possessing attributes such as being a knower,
and is the substratum of the senses and other faculties.
Precisely because of its intrinsic nature as a knower, it is changeless;
it is self-seeing, manifesting itself to itself.

The *hetu* is the cause for the beginning of creation and so forth. This was stated by the venerable Sūta: "The individual soul (*jīva*), being the agent of ignorance and karma, is the cause of this creation and so forth" (BhP 12.7.18). The term *vyāpaka* means one whose nature is pervasion.
It is unattached and unobstructed because its nature is self-luminous.

One should abandon the unreal existence of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth, which arises from delusion; thus, the phrase "the meaning of 'I'" refers to the abandonment of only that which is rooted in delusion and has the body etc. as its locus, but not of that which constitutes one's true nature.
It is manifested.
Thus, some maintain that the *jīva* is of the nature of subtle light because it is a portion (*aṃśa*) of That;
for it is indeed so.
It is manifested as a portion of the Kaustubha gem.
And so it is stated in the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa* of the *Skanda-purāṇa*, in the section defining the individual soul (*jīva-nirūpaṇa*):
Neither its form nor its color, nor its measure, is seen anywhere;
it cannot even be described, for it is subtle and possesses infinite bodies.
If the tip of a hair is divided into a hundred parts, and each of those parts is further divided into a hundred, the deity is subtler than that; he is conceived as being infinite.
"Yogins see [the Self], which has the color of the sun and a subtle luster like a drop of water on a lotus leaf, with the eye of knowledge, as if it were a star. Thus [it is said].
//7.9// Śrī Prahlāda [taught this] to the young asuras.
[46] [47] Thus, in this way, those very powers called *jīvas* are indeed infinite and are *taṭastha* (intermediate) potencies; therein lies their classification.
There are two [groups]: one class has been oriented toward the Blessed One from time immemorial, while the other has been averse to the Blessed One from time immemorial;
this is due to their respective natures and the presence or absence of knowledge regarding Him.
And because of the absence of [ordinary] knowledge:
here, the first [type] consists of Garuḍa and others, who are eternal members of the Lord's retinue, sustained by the play of internal power.

As it is stated in the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa*, beginning with "The worlds of the three-footed manifestation," as cited in the *Bhagavat-sandarbha* (81): and its status as a *taṭastha-lakṣaṇa* (an incidental definition) is due to its well-known nature as a *jīva* (individual soul), since it does not enter into the category of the Lord (*īśvara*).
The transmigrating being is overcome by *māyā*, which has found an opening through the fault of turning its back on the Supreme.
As it is said in the *Haṃsaguhya-stava*: "The person knows everything, yet he who knows that [Self] does not know the qualities (*guṇas*)."
"I praise the omniscient and infinite one" (BhP 6.4.25);
and in the eleventh book: "Fear arises from attachment to duality" (BhP 11.2.37).
This same pair of categories was also stated by the venerable Vidura:
"O Blessed One, into how many ways do those principles merge?"
Regarding this, the question is raised: "Who would dwell there, and who indeed would lie down there? (BhP 3.7.37).
By this, it is meant that even those who are pure but are averse to the Supreme Lord, though they may possess His powers, [cannot remain there].
From the Supreme Lord, birth occurs as conditioned by an adjunct (upādhi).
And that birth is simply the attainment of an internal state caused by the conceit of being born, which arises from the birth of one's own adjunct.
Regarding this, they say:
"The birth of the two unborn—the primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa)—is not possible; yet through their union, the possessors of life come into being like bubbles in water."
Therefore, in You, the Supreme, who possess manifold names and qualities, all these essences—just as various rivers flow into the ocean or as all flavors dissolve into honey—would find their place.
From the three modes of nature arises the *puruṣa*, and from purity arises the individual soul (*jīva*); yet because both of these are unborn, there is no actual origination.
It is not logical that those embodied beings who possess internal form and are endowed with limiting adjuncts (*sopādhi*) are born as individual souls (*jīva*).

Rather, they are born solely from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as their cause, which is joined with both [material and conscious] powers. Due to the dissolution of the modifications of *prakṛti*, these powers—known as *jīvas*—are pure and have their latent impressions (*vāsanā*) dormant; they are merged within the Supreme Self until the time of creation.

The meaning is that at the proper time, having projected the transformative *prakṛti*, the *satya*s—whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been awakened—depart [from their state] precisely by attaining a conditioned state (*sopādhikāvasthā*).
It is with this very intention that the Blessed One said "one... [and so forth].
The passage beginning with "āsedam" (3.5.23) occurs in the third chapter of the *Skandha*:
"But by the operation of time, Adhokṣaja [entered] into Māyā, which consists of the guṇas..."

"By means of the Puruṣa who has become his own self, the heroic one exerted his vigor"— by this, the placement of the individual soul (jīva), denoted by the word "vīrya," within primordial nature (prakṛti) is stated. Thus, Śrī...

In the Gītā-upaniṣads as well, it is stated in [Gītā 14.3]: "My womb is the Great Brahman; in that I place the seed. And the commentators have explained that by the word "Brahman," primordial nature (prakṛti) is meant.

By the word "embryo" (garbha), it is meant that this very [self] is the living being (jīva); again, this same [self] is mentioned in the third [chapter]: "in a woman whose nature has been disturbed by fate..."
The Supreme Person deposited His seed in His own womb; she gave birth to the Great Principle (mahat-tattva), which was golden-hued.

In this context, [the term] *vīrya* is explained in the *Ṭīkā* as "consciousness-power" (*cic-chakti*); therefore, its nature as power (*śaktitva*) is the position accepted by the *Ṭīkā*. Consequently, the illustration "like a water bubble" refers only to the aspect of its sudden emergence.
Therefore, once again at the time of dissolution, these conditioned individual souls (*jīvas*) with their adjuncts merge into You—

the Supreme Self denoted by the word "Self" in such scriptural passages as "He becomes merged into His own"— who stand as the original prototype (*bimba*), whose nature is the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-cit*), and who consist of the pure power of the individual soul (*jīva-śakti*) characterized solely by consciousness, which stands in the place of rays.

Together with various names and qualities, with diverse designations such as "gods" and so forth, and with various auspicious and inauspicious attributes, they have dissolved and continue to dissolve;
as before, the illustration for this even during the dissolution of the world is like rivers [entering] the ocean.
Thus, as in the cases "all flavors are as if in the honey" and so forth,

even though [the world] has dissolved into that [Supreme Reality] by abandoning its names and forms as gods, humans, and so on, there still exists a distinction of essential nature (svarūpa-bheda) because of the continued existence of their respective portions.
This is the intended meaning.
In this regard, the scriptural passages begin with "the one unborn" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5), and so forth; as it is said:
"Just as rivers flowing toward the ocean... (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.1.13).
"They go there, having abandoned name-and-form;
likewise, the knower, liberated from name-and-form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.8).
Just as, my dear, these honey-makers collect the juices of trees of various forms and bring them to a state of oneness, making them into a single essence. [ChāU 6.9.1]

"Just as those juices do not obtain distinction, thinking, 'I am the juice of such-and-such a tree,' even so, my dear, all these creatures, having merged into Being, do not know: 'We are merging into Being.
// 10.87 // The Śrutis [speak of] the Blessed Lord. [47] [48] Thus, the power of the Supreme Self known as *taṭasthā* has been explained;
now, however, that known as *antarāṅgā*—
It should be understood as before.
Now, that which is called the "external limb" (bahiraṅga) is explained:
this is the Māyā of the Blessed One.
We have described her who brings about creation, maintenance, and dissolution, and who consists of the three letters; what more do you wish to hear?

This power called Māyā, which effects the creation of the universe and so forth as previously described, belongs to the Supreme Self by way of its extrinsic definition (taṭastha-lakṣaṇa), [and it pertains] to the Lord's sovereignty and other attributes that constitute His very nature.
She is she who possesses the three castes;
thus the followers of the Atharvaveda recite:
"White, black, and dark—she is the cow of plenty for all desires of the All-pervading Lord."
Thus it has been said: "For this divine illusion of Mine, consisting of the *guṇas*, is difficult to overcome" (Gītā 7.14). Antarīkṣa is Videha. Of that *māyā*, there are two parts.

In this regard, he explains the mutual distinction between the instrumental aspect called *māyā*, which consists of the quality (*guṇa*), and the material cause aspect called *pradhāna*, which consists of fluidity (*drava*), by means of four verses.
Now I shall fully declare to you Sāṅkhya as previously determined,
by knowing which a person immediately—
"One should abandon the delusion of duality.

And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: For the person who contemplates that all duality arises from the non-dual Supreme Self through *māyā* by way of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, and is again dissolved back into that very same source, [the pairs of opposites—] *dvandva*...
The verse beginning with "atha te" introduces Sāṅkhya in order to state that delusion ceases;
here, the word *prakṛti* is a synonym for *pradhāna*. [50]
When those skilled in discernment [perceive] that there was only one object consisting of pure knowledge, free from conceptual construction;
"In the beginning, in the Kṛta-yuga, in every age. And the commentary says: "The word *atho* signifies completeness;
*jñāna* is the seer."
Therefore, the meaning is that even the entirety of objects, which have the nature of being visible, was merged into Brahman alone as a single reality devoid of conceptual construction (vikalpa).

Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the third *skandha*, the Blessed One states at the outset: "The one Lord is the foremost among selves by his own nature" (*BhP* 3.5.23). That which is designated here as the Blessed One (*bhagavat*) is precisely what is designated here as Brahman.
Just as in the passage beginning with "They speak," a single reality is to be established in both cases;

however, at the end, in the verse beginning with "This method of Sāṅkhya has been declared," by the phrase "by Me" (mayā), [it is shown] even in the form of the Blessed Lord through the vision of the higher and the lower.
The state [of stability] is indeed clear.
To address the expectation of "when," he says:
when, at the beginning, in the Kṛta Yuga, through discernment...
In that age, people become skillful; the meaning is that this was so even in the previous period at the time of dissolution (pralaya). [51] By way of the fruit of that Māyā.
The Great Truth, which is absolute and beyond conceptualization, transcending the sphere of speech and mind, became twofold.
And the commentary [states]: "That" refers to the Great Brahman; "as it becomes" means as it comes within the range of speech and mind; "māyā" is the visible world; "the fruit" is its manifestation;
and "in that form" means in the form of māyā and in the form of creative play (vilāsa).
"It became twofold"—this is the [verse].
Here, "māyā" is the object of perception (*dṛśya*), and "its manifestation" (*tat-prakāśa*) is the fruit; such is the analysis.
Therefore, that visible entity which exists by means of Brahman is *māyā*.
The meaning is that the manifestation and expansion of that Brahman is the fruit.
[52] For one of those two is indeed the object.
That primordial nature (prakṛti) is of a dual nature;
that which is the other state, the knower, is designated as the person (puruṣa).
And the commentary [states]: "Between those two parts which have become twofold, she is of the nature of both, consisting of cause and effect; such is she.
In the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*: "For those others are indeed distinct from the true form of Viṣṇu..."

Regarding the statement, "Pradhāna and Puruṣa, O Brahmin" (ViP 1.2.24), their commentary on this point is as follows: "Beyond Viṣṇu, who is devoid of adjuncts, there are His two forms previously mentioned—namely Pradhāna and Puruṣa; these two are distinct from the other forms produced by Māyā."
11.24 // The Blessed One //52// [53] Furthermore,
he speaks of the distinctions among those two factors— the cause of appropriation— by way of their different modes of operation:
time, destiny, action, the individual soul, and inherent nature.
Substance, field, life-force, self, and transformation—their collection is the flow of the sprouting of seeds; this is His illusory power (māyā).
I take refuge in the negation of that.
And the commentary says: Time is the agitator;
karma is the cause, which, when directed toward its fruit and manifested, is destiny (daiva).
Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is its formation (*saṃskāra*);
the living being (*jīva*) is that which possesses it; substance (*dravya*) is the primary element (*bhūta*).
The subtle [elements] are the field (*kṣetra*); *prakṛti* is the field; *prāṇa* is the thread (*sūtra*);
the self (*ātman*) is the ego (*ahaṅkāra*); [these are] the transformations (*vikāra*).
The sixteenfold aggregate consists of the eleven sense-faculties and the great elements; their collection is the body.
Its continuity is like that of a seed and its growth, where "growth" refers to the sprout.
From the body comes karma in the form of a seed; from that, the body in the form of a sprout; and from that, again in this same way—such is the stream.
You, however, are the ultimate limit of that negation.
"I take refuge; I worship"—thus [is the prayer].
Herein, time, destiny, karma, and inherent nature are the causal factors (*nimitta*), while the others are the material factors (*upādāna*).
The individual soul (*jīva*), possessing both, consists of both aspects. Thus, even within the category of material factors, the aspect of causal power (*nimitta-śakti*) persists.

Just as, in the reality termed "I" (ahaṃ), which is characterized by the limiting adjuncts of the individual soul (jīvopādhi), there exists the state of "I-ness" (ahambhāva); for that is indeed a transformation of ignorance (avidyā), and so forth.
As it is said in the sixth chapter of the third [book]: "And his pride entered the place where his own self was pierced."
"By a portion of his karmas, he enters into what is to be done"— thus [it is said].
Here, "self" (ātman) refers to the ego (ahaṅkāra), and the commentary states that Rudra is the conceit (abhimāna) by means of the activity of the "I-function" (ahaṃ-vṛtti).

And regarding this, the determination of the context— that which is manifested is the substratum, namely the organ of speech and so forth, ending in the third case [as the instrument], and that it is "internal" (*adhyātma*)— has already been made in the *Ṭīkā*. Its nature as a seed-form...
This is said with the intention of expressing merely the state of being a cause.

Thus, here too, the *pradhāna*— designated by the term "field" (*kṣetra*) and constituting the root of all constituent parts of the fundamental *māyā*— is likewise a partial manifestation (*aṃśa-rūpa*).
Thus it has been understood.
By the statement "the living being possesses that," he makes known the state of the pure living being as transcending *māyā*. (10.62) [Jvara addresses the Blessed Lord. (52) [54]

Now he speaks of the first two functions of the constituent part consisting of the causal signs (nimitta-rūpāṃśa): "Know, O Uddhava, that knowledge and ignorance are my two forms for embodied beings."
"The two bodies that cause bondage and liberation were fashioned by me through Māyā at the beginning.
And the commentary states: "The two powers (tanū), which are my Śaktis, are called 'bodies' because bondage and liberation are extended (tanyete) by us two through Māyā."
In the phrase "vinirmite," because it has the nature of the functioning of illusion (*māyā*), the singular form "bandha-mokṣa-karī" is used in the sense of a dual.
[Objection: But if bondage and liberation were its effects, then their beginninglessness and eternality would not be possible.
Regarding that, he says: "In the beginning, [it is] without beginning.
Therefore, the meaning is that as long as I impel ignorance, there is bondage; when I bestow knowledge, then liberation manifests. Thus ends this [section].
In this context, because they function as *māyā*, they are in reality indeed functions of *māyā*; however,
their "being emanated" is stated only because they appear through that [power] which possesses infinite other functions.
The meaning is that it is beginningless (*anādi*).
Likewise, the phrase "it manifests thus" (*tathā sphurati*) is to be construed with the word "liberation" (*mokṣa*);
[this refers to] the soul's (*jīva*) inherent state of being liberated.

Bondage, however, is perceived through mere ignorance; but upon the arising of knowledge, only that [pure reality] shines forth as the "mere" (mātra). Therefore, the sense is that liberation is indeed eternal.
Nor should it be said that [the teaching] beginning with "This is an illusion" (eṣā māyā) is incorrect because its general characteristic— namely, the granting of liberation— is not stated therein;
for by virtue of its being "terminating," liberation in the form of ultimate dissolution is also implied here.

It should be understood that this function called *avidyā* is merely a gateway for the manifestation of the specific power of the essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*), and not [the manifestation] itself. Now, O Lord, there are two functions of the portion known as *avidyā*.
It consists of both the nature of obscuration and the nature of distraction.
Among these, the former, while abiding in the individual soul itself, veils its innate knowledge.
And Uttarā continues to maintain him by concealing his knowledge of that [act] otherwise. // 11.11 //
The Blessed One said:
54. [55] Here, the aspect of the cause (nimittāṃśa) must be discerned in this way: namely, by means of that which consists of the aspect of the cause.

The power known as Māyā is well-known to manifest in three ways, in the form of knowledge, will, and action. Among these, her nature as the knowledge-aspect of the Supreme Lord is as described in the third [chapter]: "She is indeed the vision of this Seer..."
"O fortunate one, that which is called Māyā consists of both the existent and the non-existent; by means of it, the All-pervading Lord fashioned this universe. [BhP 3.5.25] Thus it is said.
In this commentary:
that [nescience] indeed consists of the connection between the seer and the seen;
together with the seen, it is non-existent.
The visible is the self, which is its own essential nature;
it is that whose nature consists of the synthesis of both the existent and the non-existent, because it has the form of the unification of those two.
The nature of that [Self] as being of the form of desire is as stated in that very same work;
it is explained in the commentary on the phrase "the Self" (*ātman*) in the context of its being followed by the desire for the Self (*ātma-icchā*).

Self-will is *māyā*; when its persistence and dissolution occur, its nature as an activity should be understood from the very statement cited in the eleventh [chapter]: "This *māyā* belongs to the Blessed One. This is so if...
The direct knowledge and other attributes of the Supreme Lord are not *māyā*, but rather His own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*).
Nevertheless, that knowledge and so forth do not function for the sake of material effects; rather, [they function for a different purpose].
Since it will be analyzed later that [the self] does not engage in activity through mere attachment even while acting for the sake of devotion,
that which consists of a modification of *māyā* conjoined with a semblance of such engagement—
Other things such as knowledge and so forth are designated by the very same terms "knowledge" and so on;
and that which constitutes such knowledge and so forth is of two kinds.
Because it is established by its own nature, it is grounded solely in the Supreme Lord; and because it is granted by Him, it is also grounded in the individual soul (*jīva*).
Among these, first is the synthesis of the seer and the seen.
The second [form] consists of the desire to create, time, and so forth; the third consists of knowledge, ignorance, the desire for experience, karma, and so forth.
Now follows the definition of *pradhāna*, which is the constituent part of the material cause (*upādāna*):
that which is composed of the three qualities (*tri-guṇa*) and is unmanifest (*avyakta*).
They call Pradhāna, which is eternal and consists of both the existent and the non-existent, the Prakṛti;
it is without distinction, yet possesses distinctions.

That which consists of the three qualities— the aggregate of the three qualities such as *sattva* and so forth— is indeed called the unmanifest (*avyakta*), the primary matter (*pradhāna*), and primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
The reason for its designation as "unmanifest" is its lack of differentiation due to the equilibrium of the three qualities.
Because it possesses the nature of *rūpa*, its specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*) are unmanifest; for this very reason, it is understood to be designated as "unspecified" (*avyākṛta*).

The reason for its designation as "Pradhāna" (the Primary Cause) is that, by being the substratum for its own effects—the specific evolutes such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth—it is superior to them because it possesses those specificities.
The reason for the designation "prakṛti" (primordial nature) is as follows:

it is that whose essence or intrinsic nature (*ātman/svarūpa*) is the cause (*anugata*) that persists through all things— whether existent or non-existent— in their forms as effects and causes, such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest.

Likewise, its nature is such that it remains eternally unmodified during dissolution by virtue of existing as the essence of all constituent parts in the form of the cause alone, and during creation and maintenance by virtue of its fivefold composite parts; thus, both its status as Brahman and its form as the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth are distinguished. Of Brahman—

Because the Great Principle (mahat) and the others are devoid of [independent] qualities, and because they exist in the form of effects relative to the Unmanifest (avyakta); and thus it is said in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"That which is the Unmanifest is the cause."
Pradhāna is declared by the best of sages to be the subtle primordial nature (prakṛti),
eternal, and consisting of both the existent and the non-existent.
That which is inexhaustible, without another support, immeasurable, undecaying, and eternal,
is devoid of sound and touch.
It is not conjoined with form and the other [sensory objects].
That source of the world, consisting of the three qualities,
is without beginning in its origin and dissolution; by that [source], everything existed in the beginning.
"Indeed, [the world] was pervaded following the dissolution," and so forth [ViP 1.2.19–21].

This very *pradhāna*, which is the subtle state of the beginningless universe and is designated by such terms as "unmanifest" (*avyākṛta*) and "unmanifested" (*avyakta*), is also regarded by the Vedāntins as being dependent upon the Supreme Lord.

[The objection is raised: "Since it is dependent on that, it is meaningful," according to such principles as [VS 1.4.3]; however, like the Sāṃkhya, the view that even for some [the pradhāna] is independent and inferential is refuted by such principles as "But that is denied because of its being grasped as presented in the allegory of the body" and "And he shows [it]" [VS 1.4.1].
Furthermore, the word *pradhāna* is heard in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad:
"The Lord of *pradhāna* and the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), the Master of the qualities (*guṇa*), [is] the cause of transmigration..."
It is the cause of bondage, duration, and liberation, and so forth. (3.26)
Śrī Kapiladeva //55// [56] Thus, in these two compositions, the exposition of the three potencies has been made;
therein, that which is produced by the non-difference of names—
Verses for the summary [of the teaching] to eliminate delusion:
Illusion may be internal or it is said to be external;
it is also seen in some cases to reside in primordial matter (*pradhāna*), and it is that which deludes.
In the first triad, there is primordial nature (prakṛti), while the power of consciousness (cit-śakti) is internal;
those two are likewise seen in the pure soul, as well as in the Lord’s knowledge and potency.
The power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti) is said to be the function of both the power of consciousness (cin-śakti) and the power of illusion (māyā-śakti);
yoga-māyā is traditionally held to be equal [to that] in the function of the power of consciousness within illusion.
"The unmanifest (avyakta) is the primary unevolved state (pradhāna), consisting of the three guṇas, which is the primordial nature (prakṛti);
it is not in Māyā, nor in the power of consciousness (cic-chakti). Such [distinctions] should be inferred by the discerning. Now, the world, which is the effect of Māyā, is characterized:
Then, from those [elements] thus permeated and combined, an insentient egg arose, from which the Puruṣa emerged.
That Virāṭ arose;
this is the egg known as Viśeṣa,
consisting of elements increasing tenfold in succession.
Surrounded on the outside by water and the other elements, which are themselves enveloped by the Pradhāna,
therein lies this expanse of worlds.
The form of the Blessed Lord Hari is as follows:
from the Mahat and other principles, which were agitated and permeated by that Lord, an insentient cosmic egg arose; from that egg, this Virāṭ Puruṣa emerged.
Of the Blessed One, the Supreme Person. // 3.26 // Śrī Kapiladeva.
//56// [57] Thus, when it is said that this is the form of the Blessed One, it follows—as in the previous case—that even He is non-material (aprākṛta).
To refute that [objection], he says:
"These two forms of the Blessed One have indeed been described by me to you."
The wise do not grasp either of these two, which are created by *māyā*;
they are merely superimposed upon the Blessed Lord for the sake of meditation as the gross and subtle aspects of the world-soul.

The meaning is that both of those— the Virāṭ and Hiraṇyagarbha (the latter being a synonym for the former), which are the collective bodies described by me to you under the name "subtle"— Vipaścit does not grasp as real entities nor does he worship them; rather, he regards them merely as external seats [of his own self].
Thus it is said in the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa: "This which is seen as a material form is [merely] yours, whose nature is knowledge."
"Those who are not yogis perceive the form of the world through deluded cognition," [ViP 1.4.39].
The meaning is that they know this embodied world to be Your very form solely by means of deluded cognition. And the Śruti says:
"This which they worship here is not [Brahman]"—
the commentary of Śrī Rāmānuja explains that this refers to the world which living beings worship; it is not Brahman.
Therefore, the reason why they do not perceive [the Lord] is that He is created by *māyā*, and not manifested through His own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*).
By this, [it is shown that the perception of the Lord] characterized by four arms and so forth—
The fact that his manifest form transcends *māyā* is also evident.

In this regard, since this world composed of *māyā* has the nature of the Supreme Person (*puruṣa*), the incarnations of Viṣṇu and others who possess the qualities of that Person consist of *sattva* and the other [guṇas].
It should be understood that the portions are forms;
and with reference to them, it is said in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "Viṣṇu, I, and Īśāna [assume] the taking of bodies."
"Since you have caused these [beings] to act, who then would be capable of praising you?"—

for if the word *śarīra* were to denote each respective individual body, then since the distinctions from Viṣṇu and others would not exist prior to that mention, the reference to them would be untenable.
2.10 // Śrī Śuka // 57 // [58] It was stated previously that [the world] is created by *māyā*.
In that context, the word *māyā* does not have the meaning of "ignorance" (*ajñāna*). That—

For in this doctrine, it is held that the entire duality of living beings and so forth is merely imagined through ignorance within Brahman, which is one's own true nature. However, Brahman— which is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), devoid of ego, free from any other attributes, and distinct from everything else— cannot be the locus of ignorance, nor can it be [the object] of ignorance.
Furthermore, while it is not possible for Brahman to be an object or to possess causality,
its possession of inconceivable power is indeed possible because it is a supreme, transcendent reality.
Indeed, this is also observed in the case of the *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling gem) and similar things;

for instance, like a medicine that destroys the three humors (*tridoṣa*), although it possesses mutually contradictory qualities and, while being partless (*niravayava*) and so forth, is nevertheless admitted to have parts (*sāvayava*) and so forth.
