In this regard, there is scriptural authority (*śabda-pramāṇa*) such as that found in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* and other texts: "The ancient Person possesses manifold powers, and the powers of others should be understood to be of the same nature. And so forth.
"He is the Lord of the self, possessing inconceivable thousands of powers," as stated in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam and other texts;
likewise, the Brahma-sūtra says: "In the Self..."
And likewise, regarding the sūtra *vicitrāś ca hi* (VS 2.1.28):

even by means of the impossibility of otherwise accounting for duality (*dvaitānyathānupapatti*), one is not able to postulate ignorance (*ajñāna*) and so forth in Brahman, precisely because such a thing is impossible.
Since the existence of inconceivable power in Brahman is established through reasoning and is also revealed by scripture, the impossibility of duality [otherwise] has long since been dispelled;
therefore, it is indeed inconceivable power itself [that accounts for it].
The cause for the establishment of duality is thus concluded.
Therefore, although the Supreme Self exists as an immutable nature, through its inconceivable power, there occurs transformation and so forth by way of assuming the form of the universe and the like.
It is like the production of all objects from a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) or the movement of iron by a magnet;
this very point was accepted by the venerable Bādarāyaṇa in the statement: "But because of the Veda, [the world] has the Word as its source" (Brahmasūtra 2.1.27).
Therefore, because that [Word] possesses such power, the term *māyā*—which is not like that of ordinary nature—is [used for] the science of sorcery (*indrajāla-vidyā*).
Nor is it logical that [the suffix] expresses the state of being measured;
rather, because one measures— that is, constructs— various things by means of it, it expresses precisely the power to produce various objects.
Therefore, the transformation of the Supreme Self alone is the established doctrine of the scriptures;
this has been explained in the *Bhagavat-sandarbha*. In that regard:
And since transformation is held to occur through the power of inconceivability (*acintyā śakti*) while [the substance] remains untransformed,

it is understood that it transforms only in the form of its powers— namely, those designated as *sanmātra*, *avabhāsamānasvarūpavyūha*, and *rūpadravya*— but not by way of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Just like the *cintāmaṇi* jewel; therefore, because that [the world] has its root in Him, there is no contradiction in the established doctrine that the Supreme Self is the material cause (*upādāna*). This was stated by the Blessed Lord in the eleventh [chapter]:
Prakṛti is its material cause,
the Supreme Puruṣa is its substratum, and Time is the manifestor of that which exists.
"I am indeed that triad of Brahman" (BhP 11.24.19).
For this very reason, in some places it is heard that he has Brahman as his material cause (*upādāna*), while in others he has Pradhāna as his material cause.
In that regard, that power called Māyā is described as being twofold, consisting of the power of transformation (*pariṇāma-śakti*).
The aspect of the efficient cause (*nimitta*) is *māyā*,
while the aspect of the material cause (*upādāna*) is *pradhāna*.
In that regard, the efficient cause is pure power (*śakti*), which consists of its various manifestations (*vyūha*).
The distinction is that it is "with appropriation.
For this very reason, even in the Śruti it is heard that "consciousness and unconsciousness" (vijñānaṃ cāvijñānaṃ ca; Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1), indicating that some portion is insentient.

Furthermore, even in the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the primary authority, in the third book and elsewhere during the primary account of creation, the transformation of *pradhāna* is clearly perceived as being practiced generally for the attainment of other goals and as a limb of knowledge and detachment.

Furthermore, as for the transformation (*vivarta*) that is heard of in the context of praise and so forth, even though it is mentioned as a subordinate factor to knowledge and dispassion (*jñāna-vairāgya*), it does not imply that the world is established otherwise; rather,
it refers to the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of that very world which is already established through the primary transformation of the array of the Supreme Self (*paramātma-yūha*).

Just as in the case of the individual form (*vyaṣṭi-rūpa*), there is another [superimposition] consisting of the false attribution of "self" and "mine" onto the pure Supreme Self (*paramātman*) or onto that which has the nature of being a portion (*aṃśa*) of Him.

In that regard, the cause for such [attribution] toward the Supreme Self is the hearing of scriptural injunctions concerning meditation (*upāsanā*) and so forth; however, toward the individual self (*ātman*), it is that [same hearing].
It must be analyzed whether the cause is the "pervasion" (āveśa) by that [object].
For it is only an object already established elsewhere that can be superimposed elsewhere;
since false things such as sky-flowers cannot be superimposed, there is only a continuous series of prior transformations (vivarta).
Furthermore, because there is no example for an infinite succession of perfected beings (*siddha*),

and moreover, even though a mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of water previously arose from the perception of water, it remains dormant at a time when that [perception] is not occurring; [the same applies to] an object similar to that.
But it remains awake through perception;
without investigating its specific qualities, it superimposes itself as non-different from that [perception] by its own power.
Therefore, water is not false.

Nor is it a mental modification (*vṛtti*) consisting of memory that takes on that form, nor is it a real object such as a mirage that is similar to it; rather, it is merely a superimposition (*āropa*) through non-difference from that [object], which is false because it is not in accordance with reality. And in a dream, it is "mere illusion" (*māyāmātra*) because its true nature is entirely unmanifested.

According to the reasoning [at Vs 3.2.3], when a mental modification takes on the form of an object perceived while awake, the Māyā of the Supreme Self superimposes non-difference between that [mental state] and the object, as previously described.
Therefore, for him, the object does not exist anywhere.
Even falsity [is explained thus]:
it is only the superimposition of such [qualities] upon the pure self or the supreme self that is false, but the universe itself is not false.
Therefore, because the world is born from the Supreme Self, it lacks direct identity with Him; thus, only the ignorant possess various notions regarding that Pure [Self].
Although the world has the Pure [Self] as its very substratum, nevertheless, there is no contact between the world and Him. As it has been said:
"Unattached and yet supporting all," thus it is said in the Gītā [13.14].
Likewise, the scripture teaches that the superimposition occurs in both ways: the notion of "I" and "mine" regarding the body, the home, and so forth, would belong only to those very things.
As in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "That which is seen here as having form," and so forth; or likewise:
"Having regarded you as the Self, and indeed as the Supreme Self."
"The Self, moreover, is sought outside;
oh, what ignorance born of the senses!
(BhP 10.14.27). Thus, having considered You—the Self, the root-form of all, the Supreme—as "other," that is, contrary to that [reality].

Furthermore, for one who, like a follower of Sāṅkhya, considers the Supreme to be merely the other— the individual soul (jīva)— and thus regards the Self as being of that nature, that individual soul must again be sought externally;
by him, through that very [notion].

The meaning is that the notion of the body being the self is produced by illusion (*māyā*) which has acquired a fissure through its cause. Alas, the ignorance of ignorant people is such that knowledge is gradually lost; this is the meaning.
Thus it was said in the *Haṃsa* [Upaniṣad]:

In the Guhyastava: "The body, the vital breath, the senses, the mental faculties, the elements, the subtle constituents, the self, and that which is other than these— the Supreme— they know [all this]."
"A man knows everything, yet he who knows that [Supreme] does not know all; I praise the omniscient and infinite One.
Thus it is said in the dialogue between the illustrious Lord and Uddhava:
The dispute concerning the self,
consisting of "it exists" and "it does not exist," is rooted in the notion of duality;
though it is futile, it does not cease for men, as it is composed of thorough conceptualization.
"For those whose intellects have turned away from Me, [there is no return] from their own world" (BhP 11.22.34).

Furthermore, because *vivarta* (illusory manifestation) is mentioned within the context of knowledge (*jñāna*) and so forth, it is secondary; whereas *pariṇāma* (transformation) is primary because it is mentioned within its own specific context. Thus, regarding both contexts of knowledge and so forth—

And because its status as a recited text establishes its superior authority through the logic of the "part possessing the whole" (*sad-aṃśa-nyāya*), it is understood that the essential purport of the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam* is indeed transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Furthermore, that [purport] is for the sake of knowing the inconceivable sovereignty of the Blessed Lord.

The designation "falsehood," however, like the designation "perishability," serves merely to produce knowledge of the world's worthlessness by inducing its outward-turning from the Supreme Self; it does not mean that the thing itself is non-existent,
nor is it for the sake of knowledge of the identity of the nature of the individual soul and the Lord, because of their difference in attributes.
According to the principle stated as "like a dream and so forth" (Nyāya Sūtra 2.2.29),
and likewise in the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"They dissolved the world."
If it should be argued that [the dissolution occurs] because of that recollection,
it is not certain that dissolution occurs by mere recollection of that. Thus it is said.
In that very context, at the beginning of the discussion on creation, he describes the transformation of the primary cause (pradhāna):
"But by the operation of time, Adhokṣaja [enters] into Māyā, which consists of the qualities (guṇas)."
The heroic one, through the person who had become his very self, exerted his vigor;
from that, the Great Principle (mahat-tattva) came into being.
From the unmanifest, impelled by time,
He who dispels darkness manifests the universe— which resides within the bodies of individual souls— through His conscious self.

From the preceding passage, "The Blessed One alone sat thus" (BhP 3.5.23), it follows that the Lord Adhokṣaja, by means of His own portion— the Puruṣa who is the witness of material nature and the self—
acting as an instrument, [created] through Māyā, whose function is time and which serves as the efficient cause, within the Māyā composed of the modes.

In the unmanifest, he deposited the potency called the individual soul (jīva), according to such scriptural passages as, "Come now, these three deities... and so forth. The principle of the Great (mahat-tattva) is indeed the self of consciousness.
The dispeller of darkness, the destroyer of ignorance that has reached its dissolution; Śrī Maitreya.
[59] Even though he possesses the limbs of knowledge and so forth, he says:
The Lord Nārāyaṇa, the one God, having withdrawn by means of his own power of illusion this previously created world through the movement of time, remains as the Sovereign at the end of the kalpa.
He was alone, without a second, self-supported, and the refuge of all;
when the powers of *sattva* and the other *guṇas* had been brought to equilibrium by Time through His own power, He became the Primal Person, the Lord of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
He dwells as the supreme among the high and the low, designated as Kaivalya;
he is the mass of the bliss of absolute experience, free from all limiting conditions.
O subduer of enemies, by means of his own pure self-experience, he first agitates his own māyā consisting of the three guṇas, and through that, he creates the *sūtra*.
They call that the manifestation of the three qualities (guṇas), creating [the world] with faces on all sides;
that in which this entire universe is woven and by which the person (puruṣa) wanders through transmigratory existence.
Just as a spider, having extended its thread from its heart and from its mouth,
moves about by means of it and then swallows it again, so does Maheśvara. By means of that Māyā, which is under His own control and whose parts are time (*kāla*), there is also the Śruti:
As a spider emits and reabsorbs [its thread],
as herbs arise upon the earth, and as hair and body-hair grow from a living person; so does [the Self].
"Thus, from the Imperishable (akṣara), the universe arises here. [Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.7] // 11.9 // Śrī Dattātreya [spoke thus] to Yadu // 59 // [60] Thus,
from that which has the nature of the subtle conscious and unconscious entities— the pure individual soul (jīva) and unmanifest power (avyakta-śakti)— ...
It has been stated that from the Supreme Self arise the gross forms of sentient and insentient entities, beginning with the internal individual soul (*jīva*) and ending with the earth;
therefore, the causality of the isolated Supreme Self is due to His power (*śakti*).
They consider that the status of being a material cause belongs only to that which possesses both natures;
and they maintain this regarding *prakṛti* at the outset, on account of the initial proposition and the supporting examples.
Thus, in this way, its nature is always pure.
In that regard, because power is not distinct from the possessor of power, it has been stated that [the effect] is not brought forth [from elsewhere].
Likewise, regarding the pre-existent effect (satkārya)—

In accepting this position, the effect is merely a portion of the cause itself, which attains expansion through the manifestation of its own specific attributes residing within it. Thus, the distinctness of the effect from the cause—as established by such scriptural passages as "Modification is a mere verbal handle; the name is clay alone, that is the truth"—is maintained.

However, it follows that the cause is distinct from its effect. Thus, this world is indeed non-different from the Supreme Self, which is characterized by the causal power; yet, he says that the world is certainly different [in its manifestation]— [He says: "The world is indeed non-different from the Supreme Self, which is distinguished by the power of the cause; however, the world is certainly different [in its state of manifestation]. He says:
For this entire universe is like the Blessed One and nothing else, since from him arise the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world; indeed,
you yourself know that to be so, and yet—
"A span's length was shown to you" (BhP 1.5.20).
The meaning is that this entire universe is non-different from the Blessed Lord, just as the Blessed Lord is [non-different from Himself].
Therefore, the other...
And the individual soul (jīva) is called "the bystander" (taṭastha), being like Him, as previously described.
For this very reason, the Śruti says: "All this has that as its Self," and "All this, indeed, is Brahman."
The meaning is that from the Blessed One,
toward you,
only a mere portion, a mere fragment, has been shown. // 1.5 //
Śrī Nārada spoke clearly to Śrī Vyāsa: [60] [61]— he said explicitly:
Thus, my dear son, this Blessed One, the creator of the universe, has been described to you by me in brief; there is nothing other than Hari.
"That which is other than both the existent and the non-existent"—this has been stated in brief, that is, in summary.
To the question "How is it so? Only by means of an external definition," he says:

The existent effect (*sat-kārya*)— the gross, impure reality consisting of the individual soul and the world, comprising both sentient and insentient things— and the non-existent cause (*asat-karaṇa*)— the subtle, pure reality known as the individual soul and primordial matter (*pradhāna*), comprising both conscious and unconscious entities— all this is not other than Hari, because the subtle is of the nature of His power (*śakti*) and the gross is His effect (*kārya*).
The meaning is "because it is of the nature of form.
This very point was stated by Śrī Haṃsadeva: "Understand directly that I alone am [the Self], and nothing other than me" (BhP 11.13.24).

He says "from another" (anyasmāt) to show that even though the world is non-different from it, there is no commingling of its defects with that pure [Brahman]. // 2.7 // Śrī-Brahmā [spoke] to Śrī-Nārada. //61// [62]
Therein, he explains the reasoning for non-difference with five [verses]:
"In the beginning and at the end, it exists for people; externally and internally, as the higher and the lower."
He Himself is knowledge and the object of knowledge, speech and that which is spoken, darkness and light; He who,
as the Supreme Self, exists as the cause at the beginning and the limit at the end of all beings, including their bodies and so forth.

The defining characteristic is that the Reality, which is the cause of all and exists as the present, alone manifests itself externally as the object of enjoyment and internally as the enjoyer; it appears as the higher and the lower, as darkness (tamas) which is non-luminous, and as light which is luminous, and nothing else. The meaning is that anything other than this cannot be established by itself, as it lacks inherent manifestation. [63]
[Objection: But how is it, then, that a collection of objects appears from that [consciousness] as if it were entirely distinct? To this he replies:
For even though an appearance is sublated, it is nevertheless remembered as a real entity.
Because it is difficult to establish, that which is perceived by the senses is likewise conceptualized as an object;
it is sublated from all sides by contradiction with reasoning and is undermined in its independent existence.

Just as a reflected image— such as a ray from the sun and so forth— is cast aside, yet is imagined and conceived by the ignorant as a separate manifestation, as a real entity, and as an independent object because it appears distinct; in the same way,
everything perceived through the senses is variously imagined by the deluded as independent objects, but that is not the case.
The meaning is that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattva*), it is impossible to define [the world] as independent.
He states this very point in two verses: "Of these objects here, such as earth and so forth..."
For it is not something created,
nor is it a composite; it is neither a transformation,
nor is it separate, nor is it inherent— it is unreal.

The shadow of the five elements, beginning with earth— which is the objective basis for the cognition of unity— is not any one of the various transformations involved in the production of the composite body and so forth.
To begin with, it is not their aggregate, as in the case of a forest [which is not distinct from] trees, because when one part is pulled...
Because the drawing forth of the whole would be impossible;
for when one tree is pulled, the entire forest is not thereby pulled along, nor has a composite whole (avayavin) been produced as a modification [of its parts].
By the word "also" (api), transformation (pariṇāma) is also included. Why?

Is it produced and transformed as something separate from its parts, or as that which is conjoined with them? It cannot be the former, because it is not perceived as being absolutely separate [from its parts].
Nor is it pervasive; for does it pervade each individual limb or only partially? In the first case, the cognition of a "body" would arise even in a mere finger.
If, in the second case, one were to accept that [body] also has parts, it would lead to an infinite regress;
therefore, the body and so forth must exist independently.
"It is indeed false.
Having thus stated that the body and so forth cannot be established as independent, he says that their causes, such as the earth and so on, are likewise unestablishable.
And because the elements possess parts,
they could not exist without their constituent parts alone,
for [parts] do not exist in the absence of a whole.
"Even in their final state, they have no constituent parts.
Regarding the term *dhātavaḥ*: the primary elements (*mahābhūtāni*) do not exist without their subtle constituent parts, which are the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
[They] would [be so], because they too possess parts.

If it is argued that, in that case, the part itself must be independent, he says in response: since a whole cannot be established in the manner described, the part also, in the final analysis, is as if unestablished.

It may be so; the meaning is that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of parts characterized as atoms, apart from the fact that the cognition of a whole (*avayavin*) would otherwise be inexplicable.
This has been stated in the fifth [chapter]:
Thus, the etymological derivation of the word *kṣiti* (earth) has been explained in passages such as [BhP 5.12.9].
Therefore, that which is perceived everywhere as the form of the objective support for the cognition of oneness is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). All...

It was rightly stated at the beginning that "the cause is indeed the entity itself," by means of the passage starting with "it exists for people at the beginning and at the end. In the same way, it is also stated in the third [chapter]:
"Thus, without having come together, he [perceives] those inherent powers (sva-śakti) which are existent (satīnām)."
Having observed the course of those who govern the world while it is fast asleep, the Lord [acts].
Then the god of vast strides, bearing the goddess Kālī as his power (śakti),
simultaneously entered the aggregate of the twenty-three principles (tattvas).
"Having entered, the Blessed One, by means of his active form, united that divided group, awakening their dormant karma. (BhP 3.6.1–3).
For this very reason, in the Śruti passage beginning with "He whose body is the earth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.3), of everything...
The well-known status of the individual self is as the body of the Supreme Self, while the Supreme Self is known as the possessor of that body.

Thus, it is established that while the modification of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) exists everywhere in the form of constituent parts, the whole (*avayavin*) is in every case the very reality of the Supreme Self. Consequently, the non-falsity of the world is logically demonstrated. [66]
Now, if the body were everywhere merely the substance of the supreme self (*paramātman*), then,

since the designations such as "Brahmin" and so forth would apply to that very [self], injunctions and prohibitions— which have merit and demerit as their cause— would also apply there; yet those two are not possible.
Therefore, suspecting that it is more logical for the whole (avayavin) to be something entirely distinct [from its parts], he says:
"There may indeed be an error based on similarity."
When there is conceptual construction regarding an object, injunctions and prohibitions exist just as waking and sleeping do within a dream. [BhP 7.15.61]
The meaning is: while there exists doubt or conceptualization regarding the reality that is the Supreme Self— that is, as long as its determination as being such has not occurred—
one remains separate from that [Self], which is the source of the cognition of the identity of all things.
The notion of the body’s unity would be an error based on resemblance;
for when there is a synthesis of preceding and succeeding parts,
there arises a sense of unity and similarity due to their being joined together and situated in one place, as well as through the commonality of their being constituent parts.
The meaning is that because each limb is perceived as a single unit,
this notion "this is the body" is merely an illusion,
just like the notion "this is that forest" with respect to each individual tree.

As it was said by the Blessed One himself: "Just as this lamp is a collection of flames and this water is a collection of streams, so too the notion among men that 'this is the person' is false—a delusion of those whose lives are as fleeting as a cow's. (BhP 11.22.45)

And therefore, since that very conceit of being a Brahmin and so forth exists there, injunctions and prohibitions regarding that [conceit] would occur just as waking and dreaming states occur regarding the objects of a dream; thus he says "jāgrat" (waking). In that manner—that is, by that method—the status of an injunction as an injunction and the status of a prohibition as a prohibition [are established]; such is the meaning. Thus.
"One should neither praise nor condemn the actions of others,
seeing the entire universe as having a single essence through both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*" (BhP 11.28.1).
This and other passages from the twenty-eighth chapter of the eleventh book are to be understood in this way.

In that regard, such questions as "What is auspicious there, or what is inauspicious? and "To what extent does this non-existent duality exist? should be explained solely in accordance with the initial statement: "This is merely an error of similarity."

The meaning is: "of that which is non-substantial, namely duality. Therefore, because it is impossible to define anything independently [of it], the sense of the entire section is that everything is indeed non-different from the Supreme Self.
Śrī Nārada said to Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira:
"Therefore he says:
You are the wind, fire, earth, space, and water—the subtle elements."
The vital breaths, the senses, the heart, consciousness, and grace—
all these are You alone, O Infinite One, both with attributes and without attributes;
there is nothing else that exists apart from You, even as described by mind and speech.

The heart (*hṛdaya*) is the internal sense (*antar-indriya*), consisting of mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*); *cit* is the pure individual soul (*jīva*).
Grace (*anugraha*) is the power to bring [the soul] face-to-face with oneself.
What need is there for much? You alone are all things: possessing qualities when characterized by *māyā*, and devoid of qualities when free from *māyā*. // 7.9 //
Śrī Prahlāda [worships] Śrī Nṛsiṃha. [67] Now, he clarifies His distinctness from the individual souls (jīvas) who are products of His illusory power (māyā-śakti): [68]—
Just as from a firebrand,
or from a spark, or even from smoke produced from itself— though these are regarded as being of the same nature as their source.
Just as fire is distinct from a firebrand, [so He is distinct] from the elements,
the senses, the internal organ, and from that which is called the individual soul (jīva), which is the primary material cause (pradhāna).
Likewise, the Self is the distinct seer, the Blessed One designated as Brahman.
This is the meaning.

From its own source— that is, from its own material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), the firebrand (*ulmuka*) characterized by the clump of wood— as the cause of fire, there arise sparks and smoke; just as the fire is distinct from each of those respective material causes, and just as that [fire] is distinct from the firebrand which is its material cause, so it is with this [Self].
Fire is distinct.
Even from that triad— regarded as its very self—
which is perceived as having the nature of fire due to the presence of a fiery element within the smoke, and likewise from the sparks—

From the individual soul (jīva) designated as the "station" (sthānīya), which corresponds to a firebrand (ulmuka); from primordial matter (pradhāna), which serves as the locus for that [soul] and corresponds to smoke; and from the splendor of the Lord (bhagavat-tejas) conditioned by primordial matter—which is the source of all material causes—the Lord exists as distinct.
That very Self, by means of its own portion through acting as the inner ruler (antaryāmin) of each [individual],
is the Supreme Self; and in some qualified person, manifesting as pure, undifferentiated consciousness, it is designated as Brahman.
"Because the Seer is the witness of their initial, middle, and final states"— thus says the venerable Kapiladeva (3.28).
[69] In that regard, for those whose mind is not fixed upon the Supreme Self,
They say that those who perceive the world as consisting of the Supreme Self grasp only its unreal aspect,
whereas those who know the Supreme Self grasp only its real aspect.
O Bhāgavatas!

Though the mind is inherently unreal, it appears as if real within You; yet the knowers of the Self, having transcended the unreal, perceive this entire universe as the Real by virtue of its being identical with the Self.
For modifications do not abandon gold because they have entered into it as its own nature and are perceived as being of that very essence; likewise,
O You, that mind which dwells upon the unreal is indeed the threefold [mind] within the world, which is the product of the three *guṇas*.
The existent Reality, though residing within you, shines as if it were not present and as if it were not functioning;
for, by the analogy of the taste of soup in a ladle, there is no apprehension of the Supreme Self even though it is immersed within the world. But it is not that...
The meaning is that only the present appears.
For this very reason, it is stated that the unreal aspect consists of the three qualities (triguṇa) and is composed of māyā, and is composed of mind (manomaya).
That which is perceived by the mind, by speech,
by the eyes, by the ears, and so forth,
is perishable.

"Know it to be composed of Māyā and mind. Thus, those who know the Self, for your sake, remain pervading this entire world— from humans down to the lowest beings— as the nature of the conditioned soul (sopādhika-jīva), perceiving it as the Self and as your own form, as the Reality.
The meaning is that their vision is directed toward the existent portion alone and not elsewhere.
In this regard, there is an illustration: "Indeed, it is not the transformation," for they are searching for nothing but the gold itself.
For goldsmiths have no perception of beauty or ugliness in the various forms fashioned from gold;
this is because they grasp only pure gold. The sense is that it is the same for those who know the Self.
Regarding the application of the analogy as well, they state three reasons for its being of that nature: this world, by its own real power...

By you, however, through a specific form of appropriation (*upādāna-rūpa*), you have entered even after the effect has been accomplished; and because of your non-deviation from the causal portion and because of your nature as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), you remain established even during dissolution (*pralaya*) as the very essence of Being, characterized by the power of existence (*sat-śakti*).
In this same way, it should be analyzed even regarding the illustrative example.
Having all of this in mind, it is stated in the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa:
Those of dull intellect perceive this entire world, which is in its true nature pure consciousness,
as being in the nature of external objects.
They wander in the flood of delusion.
But those who possess knowledge and have pure minds perceive the entire world as being of the nature of knowledge.
"Thy form, O Supreme Lord. Thus [end] the Śrutis. (ViP 1.4.40–41) //10.87// Thus, in this manner, transformation and so forth have been established.
And the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) has been refuted;
therefore, unlike those who maintain the doctrine of illusory manifestation, [the world] is not false like a snake in a rope, but rather possesses only perishability, like a jar.
Therefore, even in the absence of falsity (*mithyātva*), because there is deviation across the three periods of time (*trikāla-vyabhicāra*), the world does not possess existence (*sattva*).

For existence is predicated of a real entity (*vastu*) only when it is free from those two defects, namely, through the non-establishment of either illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) or transformation (*pariṇāma*),
as is the case with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) or its power (*śakti*).

In the passage beginning with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," the world denoted by the word "this" [is one], and Brahman, characterized by that power in its subtle state, is the other.
Because the word "existent" (sat) denotes two things that have attained mutual identity,
the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda) proceeds only by relying upon its subtle state.
This being the case, he raises a further objection:
"But if the world has an existent material cause (*sad-upādāna*), how could it not itself be existent while undergoing perishability?
And if it were perishable, then how could it be non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*) like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell?"
It would not fall within the scope of mere transformation (*vivarta*);
having raised this question, they provide the following resolution.
If it is argued that this world has arisen from Being as "Being," is it not then refuted by logic?
For it deviates here and there and is false; nor is it endowed with both [Being and Non-being].
Conceptual construction is accepted for the sake of worldly transaction through a blind tradition.
Your speech, O Bhārati, bewilders those dull-witted by means of its manifold modes of expression.
This entire universe is characterized by *dharma*, for it is established that *dharma* arises from the Existent (*sat*). Indeed, whatever arises from something is seen to be of that very same nature.
Just as earrings and the like produced from gold are of the nature of that [gold], so too [is this];
it has arisen precisely from that, and not like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
Regarding that, they say that the proponent’s own view— that "it is superimposed"— is not established at all;
for [the reason] "because it is destroyed by reasoning" is a contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*), since the mention of the ablative case (*apādāna*) brings about the cognition of a distinction.
Surely we do not seek to establish this [identity];
rather, having merely restated the difference based on the fact that [the effect] arises from that [cause], as in the case of a bracelet and so forth, we negate it.
Anticipating the objection that there would necessarily be non-difference in that case, he refutes the reason by showing its inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) with the words:
"And where does it deviate?"
And in no case whatsoever does the conformity to the properties of the cause deviate;
there is a rule that the property of the effect conforms to the property of the cause in all its aspects.
The meaning is that [it] does not exist;
the intention is that, since qualities such as combustibility are not observed in light and the like when they arise from fire and so forth.
That Brahman has two forms: the manifest and the unmanifest;
these two, consisting of the perishable and the imperishable, abide within all beings.
"That imperishable is the supreme Brahman; all this world is perishable"—this follows immediately after [the verse at ViP 1.22.55].
Just as the radiance of a fire situated in one place spreads far and wide, so too...
"This entire universe is the power (śakti) of the Supreme Brahman"—
this very point has been explained by Śrī-Svāmī himself in the *Śrī-Viṣṇu-Purāṇa* as follows:
having raised the objection, "But how could the perishable form, which is of a different nature from that, belong to the Imperishable Supreme Brahman?"...
He establishes this by means of an illustration with the words "ekadeśa" (in one part):
just as the light or radiance of a localized fire, such as a lamp— which, though it possesses the power of burning, is distinct from it— is the expansion of its illumination, so it is with Brahman.
Since this entire world is an expansion produced by power (*śakti*), let us return to the subject at hand.
[Objection: In that case, if there is deviation (*vyabhicāritva*), let it be just like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
Regarding this, they ask: "And where is it false?
It is false in cases such as mother-of-pearl and the like, where silver and so forth possess only a purely phenomenal existence (*prātītika-mātra-sattā*).
"Otherwise, wherever both [properties]—cognition and the capacity for causal efficiency—are joined or possessed, there it is not false in that way.
Anticipating the objection that "is not causal efficiency also observed in counterfeit copper and the like? they say:

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of differentiation": conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is accepted as an error (*bhrama*) solely for the purpose of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), characterized by buying, selling, and so forth;
it is not, however, for the sake of performing the various well-known, effective causal functions (*arthakriyā*).

Just as one might purchase the fruit of merit and so forth from such acts as giving, yet even after consuming it with the "knowledge" of ginger, it does not produce health but is instead understood to be lethal; so it is here.
Therefore, truth is accepted precisely through the performance of the specific, well-known, and correct purposeful action (*arthakriyā*);
for that [action] is absent in the case of a fake snake and the like, despite the presence of fear and so forth due to a single factor.
But since form (*rūpa*) does indeed exist, it is not the cause of that [error].
Furthermore, it is like a succession of the blind;
and even that worldly transaction characterized by buying and selling is not like that of a real copper coin.
Even among those skilled in conventional usage, it is nevertheless based solely on a blind tradition;
therefore,
since their skill in that regard is unestablished and their usage is merely habitual, it is otherwise than that.

It is not to be inferred; for the point is that in the case of a mere appearance of smoke, there is simply the possibility of its deviation from fire. Thus, having refuted the proponent of the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavādin*) by showing that [the object] truly exists through its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), since it differs from the objects of delusion, the proponent of non-perishing (*anaśvaravādin*) rises up once more to respond.

An objection is raised: "Surely, since the Veda itself—specifically the *Atharvaśira Upaniṣad* (3)—establishes the eternity of the fruit of ritual action through such statements as 'We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal' and 'The merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices is indeed inexhaustible,' it is impossible for that fruit to be perishable. Anticipating this doubt, they say: "It causes delusion."

O Blessed One, Your speech, through its many functions— namely the primary and secondary functions such as indication (gauṇa) and implication (lakṣaṇā)— bewilders those who are dull-witted regarding the hymns (uktha), meaning those whose intellects are sluggish, being overwhelmed by the burden of faith in ritual action.
The meaning is this:
the Veda does not intend for the fruit of action to be impermanent.
However, by way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), it denotes mere excellence;

for other sentences, since they form a single syntactical unit with the injunction, their purport lies in the injunction itself. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a split in the sentence (vākya-bheda). As it is said: "Just as here the world won by action perishes, even so does that which is won in the hereafter."
"The world won by merit perishes" (ChāU 8.1.6); for this principle would contradict other scriptural passages.

Therefore, this notion that the world is merely an illusion belongs only to those dull-witted by their attachment to ritual action; rather, the world is indeed real, yet it is perishable precisely because its nature is subject to transformation.
This has been stated by Bhaṭṭa himself: "Alternatively, since the authority of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas is accepted, both creation and dissolution are also admitted.
Or, having raised such objections as "we do not establish non-difference," [the author proceeds] regarding the three well-known states of existence.
He refutes [the objection] by pointing out their mutual distinctness;
the remainder of the sense is that existence (*sattā*) deviates even in the case of things such as jars, despite their performing causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārin*).
Because another entity lacks the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritā*),
because it would have to come to that other place by itself, and because it would have to disappear at another time;
and where [is there] mother-of-pearl?

Even in the case of silver and the like, at that very time it is false because it lacks the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). "That which is endowed with both" means that [existence] whose conjunction (*yoga*) with both—namely, the existence of jars and the like, and the existence of shell-silver and the like—is simultaneous;
the meaning is that by this [conjunction], existence attains its footing.
The meaning is that this ultimate causal existence is not [static] in that way,
but rather it always and everywhere takes the form of presiding over all purposeful activities and so forth, in accordance with its respective limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

Therefore, although the world is real by virtue of its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), it is nonetheless perishable due to its nature of transformation (*pariṇāma*), just like a jar; it does not have a mere existence consisting of simple appearance, nor does it possess an imperishable existence.
Since their mutual distinctness is thus observed, how could one be the other?
That which ought to come into being is called a "bhāva" (entity). Fearing that it might be like counterfeit copper, they say "transactions" (*vyavahṛtayaḥ*).
It is conceptualized (*vikalpyate*), meaning it is superimposed upon something else.
Thus, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is self-established; that very object, such as copper and so forth, is desired for the sake of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).
This is the meaning: here, whatever transaction you imagine to be accomplished by counterfeit copper, that too is not established by it;
rather, it is established only by genuine copper.
The other object [of cognition] exists in the mind of the speaker, because that very [object] is directly perceived by him;
here, "counterfeit copper" is merely an illustration, for in some cases you [perceive it] even without that.

For instance, when one employs a deceptive tactic such as saying, "A copper vessel was given to me at home," or "It must be given later," the legal transaction is established by that very person even though they are merely recollecting it;
therefore, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritā*) also consists in the form of a legal transaction.
Since it belongs to that very [original] object, it is indeed real;

otherwise, in the absence of a real copper coin, even a hundred blind people would not see [it], according to the maxim that even a succession of counterfeit copper coins cannot constitute a valid transaction.
They say that it would not be established;
[they say] "by way of a blind tradition," because of the defect of a blind tradition, that very same [thing].
The grammatical connection is with the word "vyavahṛtayaḥ" (transactions) and "iṣite" (impelled).
The meaning is that just as a transaction would not be established through a succession of blind men, so too it would not be established through a succession of counterfeit copper coins.

In this very way, the doctrine of consciousness (vijñānavāda) is also refuted; for even in Śaṅkara’s *Śārīraka-bhāṣya*, it is stated that even if [consciousness] were beginningless, such an infinite regress would be unstable according to the logic of a "blind succession" (*andhaparamparānyāya*), thereby destroying all worldly transactional activity (*vyavahāra*).
It has been stated that there is no fulfillment of the intended purpose.
This is what is meant: for example, when asked, "By whom was this gold purchased? someone might say:
"By this blind man"— to the question "How was it familiarized by him?", he replied again: "It was made familiar by that blind man."
And as for how that is so, he says: "by some other blind person"—even through such a succession of the blind, worldly convention (*vyavahāra*) would not be established;
however, in that succession of the blind...

If even a single person possessing vision becomes the initiator of all [conventional] discourse, then it is established at that very moment; for just as in that case, among all [beings], only one who possesses vision is the means of accomplishing conventional usage,
so it is in some instance.
When copper is first [tested] by means of truth, the legal transaction is established only through truth;
and in that case, truth alone is the means of accomplishing the transaction.

Since activity toward that [object] occurs solely through the pursuit of that [perception], just as in the case of one who possesses sight, it follows that it is not a "copper-like" truth; this being established,
[it applies] to one who is skilled in the conventional usage thereof.
Through investigation, reality is understood; yet that very same [reality] would become real even if it were superimposed upon counterfeit copper.

Thus, since its reality consists in its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), it is established that the entire universe, as characterized by that [efficiency], is real and distinct from objects of delusion.
Since the status of the Supreme Self as a whole (avayavin) has been established through conventional usage, that [usage] is indeed logical;
and thus it has been praised by means of such things as delusion (*bhrama*).
"The source of truth" (satyasya yonim), as in BhP 10.2.26; and there is also the Vedic revelation: "That they call Truth. The rest is the same. [71]
Thus, the reality of the world has been accepted, and that [reality] is perishable.
In this regard, its perishability is not absolute; rather, it is merely a state of invisibility due to its persistence in an unmanifest form.
Because of the acceptance of the doctrine that the effect exists [in the cause] (*sat-kāryatā*),
and because of scriptural passages such as, "That which has been, that which is, and that which will be," and so forth; for this very reason.

Just as silverhood does not exist in mother-of-pearl, so too worldhood does not exist in that [Unmanifest] when it is in its unmanifest form. According to the principle stated in [VS 2.1.20], "And like a cloth," the world itself, having attained a subtle state, is the Unmanifest;
thus, although the world is of the same category as the illusory silver in terms of being an object of perception, it possesses an existence distinct from that [illusory silver].

Likewise, because there is an absence of non-transformation (*apariṇatatva*) as in the case of the Self, it does not possess an existence that remains in a single state; for the sake of establishing this point, they said immediately thereafter:
"That which was not here in the beginning, nor will it be after its destruction..."

O You whose single essence shines forth within even that which is inferred, the ignorant perceive You as a mere semblance of life— a false play of the mind— through the paths of conceptual distinctions regarding the various kinds of material wealth; thus they compare You to that which is unreal.

If this universe did not exist (*nāsat*) prior to creation, then it would not have come into being (*na bhaviṣyat*); the absence of the augment *aṭ* is an archaic Vedic usage. It would be like a flower in the sky.
Thus, the Śruti says "it was" (*āsīt*).

Thus they say: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," or "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self," and so forth. Therefore, this world, which exists in its causal state as something subtle through identity with You, becomes the state of effect through its expansion.

Therefore, the meaning is this: it is not established by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) that what was inferred—namely, that "this" [the world] appears within you only in the midst of creation (sṛṣṭi-madhya), and not before or after, due to the cause of its mere destruction at the end, just like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—is false. In that regard:
They call You the "Single Essence" because You are the savoring of the bliss that is the object of no other experience;
for when You are experienced, the manifestation of any other object is impossible— just as [the perception of silver] in mother-of-pearl and the like [ceases upon the realization of the shell].

The meaning is: how could there be the superimposition of objects upon you, who are like base things? Those whose minds rest even once upon you, the Self who is eternal bliss, do not again enter states that rob one of the essence of the person.
This is because we ourselves have stated it thus [in BhP 10.87.35].

Therefore, by means of those very paths— the ways or modes consisting of the various modifications (*vikalpa*) such as jars, earrings, and so forth, which belong to the collection of substances (*draviṇajātīnām*) like clay, iron, and the rest, through the acceptance of transformation while You Yourself remain unfallen from Your own nature by means of inconceivable power— we are compared [to them] by us.
But nowhere [is this seen] by means of bees, cotton, and so forth.
Since this is so, therefore the mental fancies of the ignorant are false; for they perceive that very Brahman—which is of such a nature and is Truth—as this world.
They think thus:
the sense is that such [an effect] cannot arise because it lacks that [cause] as its basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Furthermore, the employment of the word *ita* here is intended to suggest the absence of a false connection (*mithyā-sambandha*).
This is to be understood.
Here, this is the intention of the proponents of the pre-existent effect (*sat-kāryavādins*): that the jar [is already present] within the lump of clay and other such causal materials.
Does it arise as something existent or as something non-existent?
In the first case, it is like grinding what has already been ground;
in the second case, there would be neither action nor agents.
The proof of that [is established]; this is the general direction.

Therefore, it is neither manifest nor absolutely non-existent, but rather exists within the lump of clay itself in an unmanifest state, just as [the jar exists] through the connection with the action of the agent and the production thereof.
It is manifested; likewise, the universe, which resides in You, the supreme cause, is manifested through the connection with the activity produced by Your own inherent power (*svābhāvika-śakti*).
Here, for those who proclaim themselves to be Vedāntins but hold a different [view],...
This is indeed contradicted by reason;
for it is well known there that the mind alone is an effect of the elements, and this is contrary to reason.
Because it is impossible for the mind, ego, and so forth to be imagined by the mind; for if that were the case,
it would follow that there is a doctrine denying the Lord (anīśvara-vāda), which contradicts the Vedas and is censured in the *Pādma Purāṇa*.
"The Śrutis, Smṛtis, and reasonings all declare the Supreme Lord; he who speaks in opposition to that is lower than the lowest.
Thus they say the world is unreal, without foundation, and without a Lord.
"Arising from mutual interaction, what else could it be but caused by desire? (Gītā 16.8).
Those who propound the doctrine of non-divinity (anīśvara-vādin) explain this Śrī Gītā Upaniṣad [in this way]: that it is unreal and illusory.

Because it cannot be defined as either real or unreal, it is unstable and devoid of description; like the notion of a person in a tree trunk, the status of being a Lord (Īśvaratva) is merely imagined through ignorance regarding Brahman. Thus, there is no one at all who possesses the conceit of being a Lord, and so the world is indeed without a Lord (anīśvara), having arisen from mutual dependence and being beginningless.

The meaning is that [this world] has arisen from a succession of ignorance; it is not mutually dependent, yet it exists through the continuity of activity. Therefore, the mind is caused by desire and is born merely from mental construction (*saṅkalpa*), like a dream.
This is what is expressed here by the words "and the engagement," and so forth.
The defect of their ritualistic performance has already been stated;

however, it should be understood that by the verse beginning with "This view" (Gītā 16.9) and so forth, their destiny will also be censured. By these very [verses], it is shown that even the Māyā which is the material cause of Brahman’s sovereignty is imagined through the ignorance of the individual soul (jīva), and by that [Māyā] alone is the creation of the world brought about.
This is the view: as stated in the commentary on that very sūtra beginning with "non-difference from that" (VS 2.1.15)—

name and form, which are as if the very self of the omniscient Lord, imagined through ignorance, indefinable as either real or unreal, and constituting the seed of the manifold world-process, are the *māyā*-power of the omniscient Lord.
It is stated that "prakṛti" is so designated in both Śruti and Smṛti;
however, this contradicts the words of the Blessed Lord, such as: "But knowledge and ignorance are My two bodies" (BhP 11.11.3).
Therefore, this doctrine is known as the "doctrine of illusion" (māyāvāda).
Thus, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa, the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam is listed among the ranks of heretical scriptures (pāṣaṇḍa-śāstra) in relation to the Goddess.
Mahādeva said: "The doctrine of illusion (māyāvāda), an unreal scripture, is called 'concealed Buddhism' (pracchanna-bauddha).
O Goddess, it was by me alone that this was spoken in the Kali age in the form of a Brāhmaṇa."

"But in the great scripture of Vedānta, O Goddess, I myself shall proclaim the non-Vedic doctrine of Māyā for the purpose of destroying the worlds. And it is stated in that very same place that this was by the command of the Blessed Lord himself, for the sake of deluding the Asuras; and by her [it was thus done].
In another place, in the *Pādma* and the *Śaiva*, it is said: "Having appeared in human and other forms through your *kalā* at the beginning of the Dvāpara age and subsequent ages, you shall,
by means of your own scriptures fashioned for that purpose, turn people away from me."
Thus ends the statement of the Blessed Lord; this is the general direction. For this very reason, the words of Yama are spoken in the Śrī-Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa:

Having thoroughly investigated even the vast systems of the world— the words of Śaṅkara, who consumes the poison-bearing grain, and the doctrines of the Ten-Powered One, Pañcaśikha, Akṣapāda, and others—

"Without the word of the Blessed One, there is no accomplishment. Thus, it should not be thought otherwise that only treatises on debate (*vāda-grantha*) are indicated here, and not treatises on mantras (*mantra-grantha*), since even the very syllables of the name are directly indicated.

Therefore, whatever praise may be found in certain places, that too should be understood with the consideration that, having defeated the doctrine of extreme nihilism, the doctrine of belief in the hereafter has been proclaimed even in part.
Therefore, it follows that the independent Lord alone is the creator of all, and not the individual soul;
[this occurs] through his own ignorance and by his own power.

This has also been stated by the venerable Bādarāyaṇa in several places, such as in [Brahma-sūtra 2.4.20]: "But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who makes the tripartition, because of the scriptural instruction," and so forth.

Therefore, in passages such as "He created mind; mind is Prajāpati," the term "mind" refers specifically to the glorious Aniruddha, the presiding deity of the collective mind (samaṣṭi-manas), according to the text:
"May I be many, may I procreate" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3).
Or rather, it should be stated that it is His mere volition:
the Supreme Lord, whose power is real, natural, and inconceivable,
would not create even something as trivial and illusory as Māyā, for He is Himself the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) who presides over all such gems.
Or it is like counterfeit gold and the like.
And thus, there is a scriptural passage authenticated by the Mādhva-bhāṣya:
"Then they said of him, 'He is Satyakarman,' for he indeed created this entire universe as truth. And so it is:
He whose vow is truth, who is devoted to truth, who is the triple truth, the source of truth,
and who is established in truth; he is the truth of truth, whose eye is the truth of cosmic order (*ṛta*).
"I have taken refuge in You, whose very nature is Truth" (BhP 10.2.26).

In this passage, [the Lord's attributes are: having true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpatva*), being the ultimate goal of truth (*satya-pārāyaṇatva*), being real throughout the threefold pastimes of creation and so forth (*sṛṣṭy-ādi-līlā-trayeṣu satyatva*), being the cause of the universe which is itself real (*satyasya viśvasya kāraṇatva*), and existing as the inner controller (*antaryāmitayā*) within the universe that is indeed real (*satya eva viśvasmin*).

The underlying intention and the systematic sequence of these meanings— namely, that truth is stability, that it is the cause of stability, that truthful speech is the instigator of unfailing destiny, and that it possesses the nature of truth— are all consistent.

Otherwise, regarding the triad beginning with "the womb of truth" (*satyasya yonim*), and specifically the phrase "and that which is placed therein is truth," it would be an unjustifiable and painful construction based on the *ardha-jarati-nyāya* (the logic of the half-old woman). Therefore, it is entirely appropriate that the Blessed One made his vow true by making it so. Thus...
If it were praised by Brahmā and others in such a manner, there would be a contradiction of his own nature and a violation of the initial context.
Therefore, it is established that the universe is indeed real. (10.87)
The Śrutis [speak of] the Blessed Lord.

(71) [72] By the statement "That indeed was not this which was in the beginning," even the dissolution into primordial nature (prakṛti-laya) is brought into conformity with the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (sat-kārya-vāda).
However, in the ultimate dissolution characterized by liberation, there is no destruction of earth and the other elements;
for it is illogical that those elements— which consist of the power of the natural Supreme Self— should be destroyed merely by the mental cultivation performed by the individual soul.

Since it is heard that even the portions of earth and other elements residing within the bodies of those who have attained liberation, such as Śrī Parīkṣit and others, remain [in their respective realms], so too will it be for the portions of Hiraṇyagarbha residing in the intellect and other faculties.
Therefore, the complete abandonment of superimposition upon them is called absolute dissolution (*atyantika-laya*). For this very reason,
when a jar is broken, the space within the jar—
"Just as space remains as it was before,
so too, when the body has died, the living soul attains Brahman once again"— thus it is said here.
Likewise—
having thus reflected and having established the self within the partless Self— one [remains unmoved] even while seeing Takṣaka biting one's foot, licking it with his fiery poison.
"You shall not see the body and the universe as separate from yourself" (BhP 12.5.12)—
even here, it is only the conjunction with the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that is negated, and its falsity is not being established.
For instance, there is the section beginning with "the sense-faculties of cognition" (*buddhīndriya*),

etc.; therein, [it is established] that the sense-faculties of cognition and so forth [are not distinct from the self], based on the reasons of being their substratum, being illuminated by them, and being non-different from them.
He states that [the Self] consists of the power whose nature is the Supreme Self:
"Knowledge, having that as its support, shines forth in the form of the intellect, the senses, and their objects."
That which is non-existent, like something having a beginning and an end, due to its being visible and not distinct [from the perceiver],
is indeed knowledge characterized as the Supreme Self, appearing in the form of the internal organs, the external organs, and their objects.
The meaning is that, therefore, the entity consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth is indeed something other than that [Self].
For that cognition is their substratum, having the nature of being the support for them.
The neuter gender is a Vedic archaism;
nevertheless, there would be an absolute distinction between them, as in the case of a king and his servant.
Regarding that, he also states another reason:
"Visibility is its being manifested;
there is non-deviation [of visibility] when that [manifestation] is present, and deviation when it is absent—by means of these two."

Therefore, just as the light of a fire situated in one place spreads out— as in the verse beginning with "tasmāt eka-deśa-sthitasyāgner jyotsnā vistāriṇī" (ViP 1.22.56)— so too [is the case] with the intellect and the other faculties in relation to that [Self].
The intended meaning is that it will be established as consisting of nothing other than its own inherent power (*svābhāvika-śakti*).

For indeed, that silver which is sometimes superposed upon mother-of-pearl and the like— possessing a beginning and an end— is a non-entity (*avastu*), because its nature consists in being based upon that [substratum] and...
Because there is an absence of non-distinction from that which illuminates [it].
The meaning is that the object such as mother-of-pearl is not "not non-different" from the mother-of-pearl and so forth; that is, it is not something other than the mother-of-pearl and so forth.
And consequently, the thesis that "by means of one cognition, all are cognized" would be contradicted; such is the intended meaning.
[72] This should be understood in the same way regarding other theories of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*), even in the case of a single [effect]. [73]
He clarifies, by means of an example, how a single entity can possess the relationship of locus and located through a distinction of its own parts:
"The lamp, the eye, and the form would not be separate from the light."
In this way, the intellect, the sense cavities, and the subtle elements would not exist if [the Lord] were honored as any one of these alone.
Since the lamp is composed of portions of light from the great elements— just as the eye and forms are— it does not follow that the lamp and such things originate from Him alone.

Distinct: thus, intellect and the other faculties would not be distinct from the True Supreme Self. Nevertheless, just as the light of the great elements is not defiled by the defect of a lamp or similar object, so too the Supreme Self is not defiled by the defects of the intellect and the rest.
"In the same way, because this [consciousness] is also one of those [others]," he says "from one of the others" (*anyatamāt*).
Thus, having stated that intellect (*dhī*) and the rest consist of the supreme self’s innate power (*svābhāvika-śakti*),

he nevertheless [distinguishes] from among those which consist of external power (*bahiraṅga-śakti*) [those which consist of] internal power (*antaraṅga-śakti*) and intermediate power (*taṭastha-śakti*).

Having stated that those [mental states] are defective by indicating their impurity through their being one or another distinct from the supreme Self, he now explains the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the pure individual soul (*jīva*) upon those mental modifications (*dhī-vṛtti*), along with its cause.
The waking state, dreaming, and deep sleep are said to belong to the intellect;
all this, O King, is mere illusion.
"Diversity within the inner self":

waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, which consist of the modifications of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*), constitute this diversity—known as Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña—within the inner self, the pure individual soul (*jīva*). This is merely *māyā*, an imposition (*adhyāsa*) produced by *māyā*.
The meaning is that it is produced merely by [the Supreme Self].
Furthermore, he states the meaning that, beyond that, there is absolutely no contact with the world consisting of intellect and so forth, even though it exists within the Supreme Self: [75]...
Just as clouds appear and disappear in the sky,
so too does this universe exist within Brahman.
Because of the arising and dissolution of the whole (avayavin).
Just as in the sky clouds— formed from the transformation of the sky’s own effects, namely air, fire, water, earth, and smoke—
are seen to come into being through the arising of their own respective wholes, and likewise they cease through their dissolution.
It should be understood that although they exist, they are not perceived, and therefore they do not touch [it].
In the same way, this entire universe is to be applied to Brahman.

Therefore, its existence indeed persists in a subtle form, because of the existence of the cause characterized by the power of the universe (*jagac-chakti*). It has been stated precisely thus: "Time is the manifestor of the existent. [75–76]
Thus, in order to state this, he establishes the existence of the cause by means of an illustration:
"For it is said here that the parts of all wholes are real."
"Without the object [of the whole], they would be perceived [as real], just as the threads are the parts of a cloth.
Thus, for all composite entities (*avayavin*) and gross objects, the part (*avayava*) is the cause, and it is real (*satya*). It is real.

It is said to be free from deviation (*vyabhicāra*). He says "without" (*vinā*) because it is observed in the world that [the effect exists] even without the object in its gross form, such as a cloth; thus, the existence of the effect in that [subtle state] is also established through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). [77]
He explains:
"That which might be perceived through both the universal and the particular is an illusion. [BhP 12.4.28]
This is the meaning:
if it is thus asserted that previously the world did not exist even in a subtle form,
but there was only the universal, pure Brahman itself, which, by means of its power acting as the instrumental cause (*nimitta*), [became the world].
To say that [the world] has transformed into the form of the universe in its specific aspects is incorrect;
for whatever is perceived through both the universal and the particular is merely an error, namely the doctrine of illusory manifestation (*vivarta-vāda*).

For in that view, it is held that pure Brahman itself is manifested as the world through its power in the form of ignorance; however, we do not accept that, because the theory of transformation (pariṇāmavāda) presupposes the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in the cause (satkāryatā). This is the meaning. //77// [78]
"Now, let it be understood that even for you, just like those who maintain the theories of *ārambhavāda* or *vivartavāda*, the effect is indeed the *apūrva* (the unseen force); to this he replies:
'Everything [is so] because of mutual dependence.'"
"That which has a beginning and an end is a non-entity" (BhP 12.4.28).
The meaning is that whatever effect possesses a beginning and an end, being unprecedented, is a non-entity incapable of withstanding analytical investigation.
The reason for this is "due to mutual dependence."

As long as the effect has not arisen, the status of being a cause cannot be established for clay, mother-of-pearl, and so forth; and if the status of being a cause is not established, the effect simply does not arise— thus there is the fault of mutual dependence.
Therefore, for the sake of establishing its status as a cause, the potentiality for the effect must necessarily be admitted therein;
and since that potentiality is nothing other than the subtle state of the effect, the existence of the effect is established.
Nevertheless, the point is that since clay and other materials bring about gross form, their status as causes is also established.

Thus, he concludes that the world is indeed composed solely of the power of the inherent nature of the Supreme Self: [79] ...Thus, in this way, he summarizes that the universe is nothing but the manifestation of the single power of the essential nature of the Supreme Self.
Even though a transformation is being perceived, it cannot be defined as even the slightest atom without reference to the inner self (pratyag-ātman).
"If it were equal to consciousness, it would possess a self" (BhP 12.4.29).

Even though the mind is being manifested and is indeed luminous, nevertheless, even the slightest modification cannot be defined as independent, apart from or distinct from the inner self (pratyag-ātman) and the supreme self (paramātman).
This has been stated in the *Tadananyatvavivaraṇa* itself:
"If it were to exist even without that [consciousness], then it would be equal to consciousness; it would be identical in nature to consciousness and would thus be self-luminous."
It would have been eternally in a single state, like the self (ātman) and like the supreme self (paramātman).
Now, if there is no modification (vikāra) apart from the supreme self, then [what follows] regarding the supreme self having limiting adjuncts (sopādhitva)?
The state of being without attributes (nirupādhitva) is not established. Therefore, to the question "Why is that which is with attributes different from that which is without attributes?", he says:
For if one who is ignorant thinks there is multiplicity in reality,
it is like the multiplicity perceived between two apertures.
Like two lights or two winds,
there is indeed no multiplicity in the Supreme Self who is Truth; yet if one perceives multiplicity in Him, [it is due to ignorance].
Therefore, because the ignorant person possesses a manifoldness characterized by being without attributes and being with attributes—

just as between the great ether and the ether within a jar, or like the light pervading both the interior of a house and its courtyard, or like the air outside and the air inside a body— [he perceives duality]. [80]

Since not even the slightest modification, however it may appear, can be defined apart from the inner Self (pratyag-ātman), therefore that [Self] alone is the referent of all words; he states this with an illustration:
"Just as gold is fashioned in many ways."
Thus, by means of words— both worldly and Vedic— the Blessed Lord Adhokṣaja is explained by people through various activities on the paths of worldly conduct.

Just as gold alone is perceived through various actions and specific verbal distinctions in the form of bracelets, earrings, and so forth, by means of those respective words and names; likewise, the Blessed Lord alone is explained by all words, whether worldly or Vedic.
Thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa: "He is the denotation of all names and he is praised by all the Vedas.
Having thus stated that the world consists of the inherent power (*svābhāvika-śakti*) of the Supreme Self, and by means of that, the individual soul (*jīva*)—

Having manifested the capacity of that [ignorance] to be destroyed by knowledge through its agency, he now provides a reasoned argument with an illustration to show the defect of that [ignorance]— which, though consisting of the power of the Supreme Self, takes the form of an adjunct (upādhi) and acts as a veil over the manifestation of the individual soul's (jīva) true nature— in order to instruct on the abandonment of its superimposition for the sake of liberation.
Just as a cloud produced by the sun and seen by the sun dispels the darkness for the eye, which is itself a portion of the sun,
so too am I a quality of Brahman when beheld by Him.
The Self, which is a portion of Brahman, is bound by the self.
Just as the rays of the sun, transformed into the form of clouds, rain down;
so too, an oblation properly offered into the fire reaches the sun.
"From the sun rain is born; from rain, food; and from that, living beings"—according to this statement, the meaning is as follows.
Just as a thick, dense cloud produced by the sun is shown and illuminated by the sun itself,
so too is the darkness in the sky [dispelled] by the eye, which is a portion of the sun.
And on the ground, it takes the form of great darkness;
likewise, I— the ordinary ego,
possessing the qualities of Brahmā and having become an effect produced by the power of the Supreme Self— was gazed upon by that very [Self].

And that which is manifested by the Supreme Self (paramātman) becomes the binder of the self—that is, of the individual soul (jīva), who is an inferior portion of the Supreme Self—because it exists as the external (taṭastha) power of that portion of Brahman; it thus serves to obscure the manifestation of the soul's own true nature (svarūpa). [82]

And that abandonment of superimposition does not occur by itself, but rather through the inquiry into the Supreme Self and by its power alone; to express this, he provides a series of examples as before:
"When the cloud produced from the sun's rays is dissolved..."
Then the eye beholds the sun, which is its own true nature;
for when the ego, which is the limiting adjunct of the self, perishes through the desire for knowledge, then one should remember.

In the illustrative portion [of the example], "just as a dense cloud is torn apart by the power of the sun," it is clear that the tearing apart of that [cloud] is not accomplished by the power of the eye, but rather by the power of the sun; by this,
[it is shown that] in the case of the illustrated subject as well, [the ignorance of the self is destroyed] by that [knowledge] which has arisen through the desire to know the Self, the Supreme Self.

In this context, the view that the destruction of the ego (ahaṅkāra) occurs by fleeing through serenity (*prasāda*)— and thus that the destruction of the ego is to be accomplished by the knowledge of the Person (*puruṣa*)— is refuted.
Therefore, the theory of illusory transformation (*vivarta-vāda*) is not accepted here.
By the qualification "having an adjunct" (sopādhi), it becomes clear that the egoity which constitutes its own nature (svarūpa-bhūta-ahaṅkāra) is indeed something else.

Thus, as in the illustrative example, because of the absence of the veil of dense, pervasive darkness and because of the attainment of fitness through its power, the eye— acting as the agent— is the subject, while its own nature is the object.
The meaning is that he beholds the manifestation of his own essential nature, knows it as existing, and attains the revelation of his own power.

At times, being intent on that vision, he beholds the sun; likewise, in the case of the illustrative example, one should remember [the Lord], for He becomes fit to be recollected by the rememberer who seeks to connect with Him.
And "oneself" is the ellipsis. He concludes:
"When, in this way, by this weapon of discernment..."
Having severed the bondage of the self through the egoism consisting of illusion, one who experiences the immutable Self remains established; O dear one, they call that the ultimate final liberation.
By this previously mentioned weapon of discrimination (*viveka*);
the qualification "consisting of illusion" (*māyāmaya*) is for the purpose of excluding the egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) that constitutes one's true nature (*svarūpa*).

He abides, remaining established in his own true nature. Not only this much, but he remains as one whose experience is of the Infallible—the experience of the Self, the Supreme Self, who is named the Infallible (Acyuta). Thus he abides. 12.4. Śrī-...
Śuka says:
//84// Here, too, there is this position held by some: that the Supreme Lord possesses two powers, namely, that called *svarūpa* (essential nature) and that called *māyā*.

By the former [power], there is the manifestation of the glory of its own essential nature; by the latter, however, there is the display of the creation of the universe and so forth to living beings who are deluded, as if by a magician's trick (indrajāla). Furthermore, such a mode of operation is observed even in some single individual possessed of various types of knowledge. And it is not thus...
As for the Advaitins, their position is undermined;
for in the world as well, a real object is manifested to a real perceiver by a real agent through a real capacity, precisely in that manner.
Let this indeed be called "perceived," since for us,
that which is real is not real apart from the fragrance of Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet.
Whether the world is real or unreal, what is this stubborn insistence regarding it?
In this view, statements such as "this has arisen from that which exists" should generally be understood according to the explanation in the *Ṭīkā*;
for in certain cases, such as in the inferences formulated by him, there is the non-existence of mere difference (*bheda-mātra*).
If that were the case, then in their view, it would follow that even Vaikuṇṭha and other such realms must likewise be [unreal]; however, their intention here is this:
we maintain that whatever object is established through worldly perception and other means of valid cognition is precisely that which [exists].

We establish that [subject] as possessing those properties by means of an example of another established entity. As for that unestablished quality— namely, its being accessible solely through the experience of those learned in the treatises— that indeed cannot be altered even by examples such as the "half of a parārtha" (the subject of an inference for others).
Furthermore, the establishment of the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) consists solely in their being of the nature of consciousness (cid-rūpatā).
Now, by means of his innate power of māyā, the Supreme Lord [manifests] the universe—
It has been stated that the individual soul (jīva) alone performs creation and so forth, and therein becomes deluded.
Regarding this, he dispels doubt through eight verses by means of questions and answers:
Śrī Vidura said: O brāhmaṇa, how is it that the Lord, who is pure consciousness and changeless, [acts]?
"Even the qualities and activities of the one devoid of qualities may be joined with him through his sport (līlayā).
O Brahmin, for the Being who is pure consciousness (cinmātra) by nature, through the power of his own essential nature (svarūpa-śakti)..."
