In Him—the Blessed One who possesses such sovereignty and other attributes residing in Śrī-Vaikuntha and other realms; who is therefore devoid of material qualities (nirguṇa), untouched by the modes of nature, and for that very reason immutable; and in whom there exists an eternally manifest, supreme, and infinite variety of light for those infinite activities which are the playful manifestations of His own essential power (svarūpa-śakti).

Because it is eternally established as the agent of the manifestation of those various activities, and because it does not undergo the attainment of another state, there is no occurrence of modification, unlike the case of an ordinary agent;
and [this applies] to that which is changeless.
How could the primal qualities (guṇas), such as sattva and the rest, be possible; or how could activities such as persistence and so forth, which have attachment to them as their cause, be tenable?
Consequently, both those [qualities] and those [activities] would be in contradiction with the reality that is pure consciousness alone.
[Such actions] are not appropriate;

however, even by means of spontaneous movement, they would not be inappropriate in the state of being the Blessed Lord (bhagavattva). Thus he says, "or even as play. Here, along with immutability and being devoid of qualities (nirguṇatva), there is the state of being the Blessed Lord as pure consciousness (cinmātra-bhagavattva).
The proponent has questioned this while accepting both positions.

Therefore, let his status as the Blessed One belong to that whose nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*); we have no doubt regarding that. However, we ask precisely how the acceptance of other qualities and so forth by him can be logically justified.
This is the meaning of the sentence.

Consequently, since he is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) and the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*), qualities and actions—which are insubstantial—cannot possibly exist in him at all; thus, the question is indeed raised with redoubled force.
He clarifies how they might even be joined through play:
"In play, there is exertion on the part of a child."
Desire arises from the wish to play;
but how can there be desire for anything else in one who is eternally satisfied by himself and ever withdrawn from the external?
It is called "exertion" (udyama) because one sets [the child] in motion by means of exertion.
A child has desire as the cause for engaging in play; however, that [desire] arises from something else—either from another object or from the instigation of another child.

The desire to play arises [in others]; however, for the Blessed One, who is satisfied by his own self and by the majesty of his own essential nature, and who for that very reason is eternally withdrawn from anything else, how could there be a world or living beings from another source?
"Because of the sign, he desired to play.
And it must not be denied that those qualities and those actions do not exist in him. [86]
He says "just so because it is well-known":
"The Blessed One created the universe by means of His own māyā, which consists of the [three] guṇas."

By means of that Māyā— which consists of the *guṇas*, which manifests the three *guṇas*, and which rests upon the Self— he establishes and sustains this [universe]; furthermore, he will again dissolve it.
It will cover over, that is, it will cause to be concealed by way of opposition;
and how is it that the individual soul (jīva) is deluded by māyā? [88]
He states another objection:
"That which [exists] by way of place, time, state, self, or other..."
How could that self, whose nature is unimpaired consciousness, be joined with the unconquered (ajayā)?
That self, the individual soul (jīva), whose consciousness is not impaired by space and other limiting conditions— how could it be joined with the unconquered, namely ignorance (avidyā)?

It would be logical [to say that] its cognition is not lost, as it remains of an unimpeded essential nature—[unlost] due to spatial separation, or due to defects inherent in the location, like the eye;
nor due to time, like lightning; nor due to state, like memory; nor from itself, like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell;
nor from another, like a jar or other objects.
The meaning is: "Precisely because it is the locus of knowledge.
In that very context, he states another contradiction:
"This Blessed One is indeed one alone."
He is present in all fields;
how could there be misfortune or affliction for anyone, arising from their past actions?
This one alone is the Blessed One, the Supreme Self, who dwells within all fields— that is, within the bodies of every individual soul.
Given that this is so, how can there be misfortune for this soul regarding its own true nature?
How could there be no loss of the knowledge of reality and so forth, nor any affliction caused by karma for him?
For it is not logical that, when two things reside in the same water or similar medium, one should have contact with it while the other does not.
The meaning:
since mere consciousness alone (cinmātratva) is not possible in that regard, the venerable Maitreya, accepting only the state of being the Blessed One (bhagavattva), said:
This is the illusory power of the Blessed One,
which does not conflict with the principle of the liberated Lord.
Miserliness or bondage;
that by which the creation of the universe and so forth occurs is this power of the Blessed One called *māyā*, which is His inconceivable essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*).
The meaning is that whatever is contradicted by logic (*naya*) and reasoning (*tarka*), because it transcends reasoning, is likewise "inconceivable" (*acintya*).
Although both [the Buddha and his teaching] are thus inconceivable, nevertheless, of the Blessed One...

The meaning is that, because [the Lord] is manifested by this [power] called *māyā*, He is not touched by the qualities (*guṇas*)— such as *sattva* and so forth— nor by their effects, nor by the pastimes (*līlās*) such as the establishment [of the world], since His own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*) is internal while *māyā* is external.
And this meaning is conveyed through the device of *tantra* (double entendre).
Whatever illusion (*māyā*) is not in contradiction with that Blessed One (*bhagavat*), that is not made an object of opposition; and in this very way, in the ninth chapter of the sixth book,
by the prose passage beginning with "This [nature] of yours is as if difficult to comprehend" (*duravabodha iva tavāyam* [BhP 6.9.34]), his possession of qualities (*saguṇa*)—
Having first raised the objection that agency is contradictory [by the prose passage beginning with] "But then, His Honor...

[BhP 6.9.35], which suggests—on account of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) and falling within the emission of the qualities (*guṇa-visarga*)—the possibility of the Lord's connection with the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) like the individual soul (*jīva*);
[the author then responds] with the prose passage beginning with "For there is no contradiction in both" [BhP 6.9.36].
In that regard, the quality of being inconceivable (*avitarkya*) has been applied specifically to power (*śakti*) in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

Therein, the inconceivability of the power of essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*) is shown by the qualifying attributes such as "the Blessed One" (*bhagavatī*), and the inconceivability of *māyā* is shown by the phrase "my own *māyā*" (*ātma-māyām*).
In that context, the phrase "due to the absence of a dual nature" means that nevertheless, by means of inconceivable power (*acintya-śakti*), His agency and His inclusion within that [nature] exist.
Furthermore, the prose passage beginning with "of those with equal and unequal minds" (BhP 6.9.37) refers likewise to those possessing high and low levels of intellect.
"Thus you flash forth"— this should be understood for the sake of realization.
Regarding the phrase "as if difficult to comprehend" in the preceding prose,
"bodiless" (*aśarīra*) means without bodily movement, and "without refuge" (*aśaraṇa*) means without support such as the earth and so forth.
The meaning is as follows:
in the passage beginning with "atha tatra" and so forth, even though it was composed by oneself, it should be applied because that [self] also possesses the status of being the cause and the agent;
therefore, this applies here as well.
The primacy of the power of essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*) alone has been demonstrated.

For this very reason, in the verse beginning with "that which is perceived without an object" (BhP 2.9.34), the status of *māyā* as a mere appearance is first shown, followed by its state of being untouched by that [essential nature].

Thus it has been shown by the Blessed One; and in the passage beginning with "You are the primordial Person directly," and further by the statement "by the power of consciousness" (BhP 1.7.23), He has likewise made this known, having thereby dispelled the notion of Māyā.
And by the verse, "Māyā fled, feeling ashamed in his presence" (BhP 2.7.47),
it is thus established that in the Blessed One, that—
Having resolved the contradiction, they reconcile even the soul's connection with ignorance through that very *māyā* of His, which has been shown to be inconceivable;
this [māyā] is connected specifically with the word "of the Lord" (*īśvarasya*) by means of the relative pronoun *yad*.
And here, by the force of the sense, it is transformed into the instrumental case;

that [misery] which belongs to the individual soul (jīva)— who, though capable through the knowledge of the Lord's own nature and so forth, is therefore liberated— is [the misery of] wretchedness, each specific instance of which—

Thus, there occurs the manifestation and concealment [of the Self], as well as bondage, which consists of entering the net composed of the qualities (*guṇa*) that perceives that [bondage]. This has been stated: "His sovereignty was lost through attachment to her" (BhP 6.5.15).
Having all this in mind, the Śruti texts also say: "He who, by means of Māyā, [creates] the Unborn," and so forth, beginning with the word *apeta-* [referring to the state of being free from it].

And regarding the word "bhaga" in the root verse [BhP 10.87.38], by the phrase "the Māyā of the Blessed Lord," it follows that the state of being a Blessed Lord (bhagavattva) is illusory (māyika), just as in the expression "the Māyā of Indra," the state of being Indra is so characterized. [91]

The same should be understood for the previous cases as well. Furthermore, although the individual soul (jīva) does not actually possess those various respective states, the perception of them occurs solely through the illusory power (māyā) of the Lord; this is illustrated by an example.
He establishes:
that this man's misconception regarding the self occurs without an external object.
The cutting off of one's own head and so forth is perceived by the observer;
whatever belongs to someone occurs through *māyā* as a cause, even without an external object.

Even though that object does not exist for him at any of the three times, nevertheless, due to the perversion regarding the self— consisting of the conceit of another preceded by the forgetting of the self— there would be such an object as "I alone am the possessor of those qualities."

Of the witnessing individual soul (jīva); the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental. During the state of dreaming, an extremely impossible matter, such as the cutting off of one's own head, occurs by means of the individual soul.
It is perceived; for indeed, no one would see his head severed, nor even the severing of his own head.
Rather, O Blessed One, it is your very māyā that superimposes upon that [perceiver] an object of that form already established elsewhere. [92]

"However, it is merely illusion (māyāmātra) because its true nature is not fully manifested," according to this principle. For this very reason, he establishes by means of another illustration that even for the soul (jīva), which is essentially pure, the assumption of the attributes of the limiting adjuncts occurs solely through its conditioned form.
Just as the trembling and other qualities caused by that [water] are seen in the moon reflected in water,
even though they do not exist [in the moon], yet they appear to the observer.
The quality of both the self and the non-self.

Just as the qualities such as trembling, produced by the limiting condition (upādhi) of water, are perceived only in the moon reflected in the water and not in the moon situated in the sky, even so, although the attributes of the non-self— which has the material nature (prakṛti) as its limiting condition— do not belong to the pure Self, one identifies with them through the absorption of thinking, "I am indeed that very person."

Although this [seeing] belongs only to that seer who exists in an internal state— the reflection-like appearance of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) which has attained identity with the limiting adjunct (upādhi) through illusion (māyā)— nevertheless, the meaning is that he, though pure, perceives it by means of the conceit of non-difference from it.
Thus it was said by the Blessed Lord in the Eleventh [Canto]: "Just as one who sees someone dancing or singing imitates that very performance,"
"Thus, perceiving the qualities of the intellect, even one who is desireless is made to act. Likewise it has been said: "For the pure one beholds the impure agent."

And here, the intended meaning of the prefix *vi-* is precisely that [of non-penetration]; therefore, because the Blessed One possesses an internal, great, and exceedingly powerful inconceivable nature,
there is no creation by the external, powerful, and even inconceivable *māyā* with respect to the individual soul (*jīva*).
But it was established as a tenet that [the world] is created by her.

3.7 // Śrī Śuka // 85–92 // [93] Although the threefold pastimes beginning with creation have been thus presented, a doubt arises once again; therefore, the final conclusion is established according to the maxim of "driving in a pillar" (sthūṇā-nikhanana-nyāya).
Now, as for those various incarnations in the pastime of protection,

and likewise whatever pastimes are heard of therein— such as partiality toward the side of the gods through gestures like smiles and the mudrā of fearlessness that manifest His grace, or the destruction of the demons through acts such as battle— are they not all [pastimes]?
And are they created by the Supreme Lord himself or not?
In the first case, the prima facie argument remains exactly as it was;
moreover, there would be partiality and so forth due to favoritism toward one side.
If it were established that the incarnations and divine sports (līlās) do not constitute His essential nature (svarūpa), there would be a contradiction of consensus;
to this, it is replied:
It is true that for the sake of protecting the universe, the Supreme Lord does nothing Himself; rather, He [acts through] those who have descended along with Him—
the associates of Vaikuṇṭha, as well as those included among the authorized demigods and others, and those who are neutral.
Furthermore, in order to gladden other devotees, He manifests various incarnations and divine sports (līlās) solely by the manifestation of His own essential power (svarūpa-śakti).
As it is said in the Pādma Purāṇa:
Although I am capable of annihilating the Dānavas in even a single moment,
I perform various activities for the sake of the diversion of my devotees.
"By means of sight, meditation, and touch, fish, tortoises, and birds nourish their own offspring; so too do I, O Lotus-born One. Thus it is said in the *Haribhaktisudhodaya*.
"Though my desires are eternally fulfilled, I take various births in order to grant all the desired objects of My devotees; therefore, tell Me what is pleasing to You.
Likewise, there is the speech of the illustrious Queen Kuntī: "For the purpose of prescribing the yoga of devotion, how may we behold [Thee]?"
For it is said, "Indeed, women...
[BhP 1.8.20], and here the commentary states: "To You, who have descended for that purpose, in order to prescribe the yoga of devotion."
And the word of Śrī Brahmā: "Though you are beyond all phenomenal expansion, you mimic the world of manifestation upon the earth."
O Lord, in order to spread the mass of bliss for the people who have taken refuge in You,
the manifestation [of this] has been shown by Śrī Brahmā himself through His own essential power (svarūpa-śakti).

"He shall delight those who have sought refuge by His own power, whatever He shall do," and so forth; the meaning is: "He whose incarnation has taken up qualities"—that is, one in whom qualities such as compassion and the like have been assumed.

Thus, for one who manifests Himself solely for the sake of the bliss of His devotees, the activity of protecting the universe— such as partiality toward the side of the gods— is performed spontaneously by His own nature, even though it is not intentionally pursued.

Just as in the world, some devotees, having gathered together to manifest the radiance of their mutual love for the Lord, take along even certain drummers and others who are unaware of that [devotion], and dancing like madmen in the joy of singing His qualities, they bring misfortune upon everyone.
They destroy even misfortune while increasing auspiciousness;
thus it was said regarding the speech that is faltering and so forth: "One endowed with devotion to me..."
"He purifies the world" (BhP 11.14.24).
It has been stated in this very way:
"The creation and so forth belong to Hari alone."
But depending upon a purpose, he performs [action] solely out of bliss,
just as a mortal performs a dance.
Thus [it is stated in the Nārāyaṇa-saṃhitā]:
"And it should not be said that by their own joy in Him, or by His joy in them, there would be a loss of His self-sufficient satisfaction."

Likewise, if one were to exclude others and delight in them alone, there would also be another form of partiality. In that regard, even though the sages have taken recourse to bodies composed of pure and powerful *sattva* and have thus naturally reached the pinnacle of contentment, this quality [of attachment] is seen to arise from affection for their devotees; therefore, it is merely an attendant attribute of theirs.
However, it is understood that this [statement] is an antidote to that [wrong view],
just as King Parīkṣit’s speech addressed to all the Munis:
"There is no benefit whatsoever here or in the hereafter..."
"Except for the grace of others, there is no self-nature.

Likewise, in the account of Jaḍabharata and elsewhere: "To the lords of the Sindhu who were considering their own true nature, the power of another was taught through supreme compassion," and so forth. (BhP 5.13.24)
In Śrī Nārada’s previous birth— although the sages, who look upon all with equal vision, showed mercy to him as he served them while speaking little—
likewise, in the *Kuntī-stava*:

Homage to Him whose wealth is His devotees who possess nothing, whose conduct consists of the cessation of all qualities, who delights in the Self, who is peaceful, and who is the Lord of absolute liberation.
And the commentary states: "He for whom His devotees—who possess nothing—are the wealth, that is, His entire possession."
Otherwise,
the fault of ingratitude would fall upon the Blessed One, who is faultless; therefore,
such [a consequence] is established even for him.
It follows as a matter of course that through affection for His devotees— whether by removing their suffering or by granting them happiness— His own bliss arises.
Furthermore, even from the essence of His own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*), which is the supreme essence...

That modification of consciousness known as *hlādinī* (the blissful), of which devotion (*bhakti*) is the very essence— a specific modification of that [consciousness]— is synonymous with *rati* (love).
Devotion is that in which both poles— the Lord and the devotee— have surrendered their own selves.
He remains forever;
for this very reason, the Blessed One is called "the one who possesses devotion through his devotees.
Therefore, when the Blessed One is satisfied by that devotion residing in the devotee, there is no loss of satisfaction on His own part; on the contrary—

Although that [devotion] is non-different from Him in its essential nature despite being different as a power (*śakti*), it manifests solely as a mode of differentiation arising in the mind of the devotee, according to the maxim: "In whatever way they approach Me, in that same way do I favor them. Thus, it is said: "His devotion gladdens Me."
And there occurs an extraordinary intensity of the wonder of bliss;
for even in the view that the power (śakti) and its possessor (tadvat) are distinct,
it is agreed that the qualified entity alone constitutes the essential nature (svarūpa).
Intending all this, the illustrious Viṣṇu said to Durvāsas:
"O twice-born one, I am indeed dependent upon my devotees, as if I were not independent."
His heart is seized by the virtuous, and he is dear to his devotees among the faithful.
O Brahmin, I do not desire for myself either eternal prosperity or even my own self, apart from my virtuous devotees.
I am the supreme goal for those [who follow me].
Those who, having abandoned wives, homes, sons, kinsmen, life itself, and this supreme wealth, have come to me for refuge—
How can I bring myself to abandon them?
The saintly persons, who possess equal vision and have fixed their hearts on me,
bring me under their control through devotion.
Just as virtuous women [follow] a virtuous husband.
Through service to Me, you have attained the fourfold goals beginning with *sālokya*;
yet those who are fulfilled by such service do not desire them.
How could anything else not be corrupted by time?
The virtuous are my heart, and I am the heart of the virtuous;
they know nothing other than me.
"I do not desire even the slightest bit from them" (BhP 9.4.63–68).
Here, the triad of wife, home, and wealth are "the means for warding off ingratitude," while "my heart" is for the purpose of avoiding self-satisfaction.
Regarding the fact that devotion is the essence of the hladinī potency within the essential nature of His own power, there are two points: first, "I am dependent upon My devotees," and second,
when He enters even into His devotees in the form of devotion itself, it occurs specifically through service to Me.
It should also be understood as "well-known";
therefore, the previous fault does not apply.
The same applies to the second case as well.

We explain: engagement in bringing joy to others arises in two ways—sometimes for the sake of accomplishing one's own desired goal, and sometimes merely for the sake of accomplishing that [other's] desired goal.
Of these, the first does not apply even here.
It is improper [to claim] that [the desire to act] is merely for one's own sake, because there is no partiality toward anything whatsoever; rather,
in this latter position,
the desire to engage in action arises solely through the experience of another's happiness and suffering, and solely through benevolence toward others.
It does not arise merely from some slight knowledge, because if the mind is untouched by another's suffering, a transformation in the form of compassion is impossible;
just as one whose limb is pierced by a thorn [feels pain].

"According to the maxim: 'A living being does not desire that pain [of another] as much as it desires its own; one who has attained equality with all living beings through their signs is not pierced by a thorn in such a way. Thus it is said.

Consequently, since the Lord— who is eternally of the nature of supreme bliss and free from all taint— is absolutely devoid of both that which is called worldly pleasure and of well-known suffering, just as the eye of a bat is devoid of light or as darkness is devoid of the sun's radiance, there is no experience of those [states] at all.
As for the fact that some, even while wishing to avoid the connection with suffering in the Blessed One, say this:
"The knowledge of the experience of suffering certainly exists in him, and it appears precisely as belonging to another (parakīya), not [as his own]."

But [if one thinks] "as one's own," that too is like "dawn breaking against a wall" (an effort in vain); for what is called the experience of suffering is indeed the touch of suffering within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
And whether that [suffering] arises from oneself or from another makes no difference, because there is no distinction in its connection with suffering;
furthermore, the fault of non-omniscience is demonstrated by the very same analogy of the sun.
On the contrary, it has been avoided and indeed demonstrated as being a virtue;
therefore, let there be whatever slight suffering-knowledge exists in that regard.
But there is no experience of suffering at all,
because he is the crest-jewel of those who possess a mass of supreme compassion and is capable of acting, not acting, or acting otherwise.
Furthermore, the charge of cruelty is avoided by the fact that even though He is manifesting His glory, living beings continue to experience the suffering of saṃsāra;
for whatever happiness belongs to the devotees is itself of the very nature of devotion to Him.
In the same way, their suffering arises precisely through the obstacle to attaining the Blessed One;
and in that regard, an even greater tenderness of heart toward the Blessed One alone is born, and that is indeed devotion (*bhakti*).

In some instances, even for the lordly elephants and others, when they were in ordinary suffering, devotion arose in that very same way through such expressions as, "He alone is my refuge. In other instances, regarding the twin *arjuna* trees and others, [it was shown] by Śrī Nārada and others—

The devotion of devotees is indeed manifest; thus, it is only the experience of the devotion of a devotee characterized by wretchedness (*dainya*) that moves Him with compassion, and not ordinary suffering,
provided that there is a worthy object of compassion.

Since it is improper to postulate [duḥkha] for that which is unfit [to be its locus], the existence of duḥkha is indeed established; for if it were the cause [of suffering], all saṃsāra would be eradicated.
Now, if it is argued that it certainly possesses the status of an indirect cause (paramparā-kāraṇatva), let it be so, for there is no harm whatsoever. Therefore...
It is established that in both cases, for the delighting of the devotees, it is the very experience of devotion to Him that impels the Blessed Lord to act;
this is what has been stated.

If, even after experiencing pleasure or pain oneself, one brings about the attainment of pleasure or the removal of suffering for another by abandoning that very [pleasure or pain] of one's own, only then does an imbalance arise.

But in the case of the Śrī Bhagavatī, because there is an absence of the experience of ordinary pleasure and pain, that [suffering] does not occur, just as it does not in the case of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpa-taru).
Thus it was said by the illustrious Akrūra: "To him, no one is a beloved or a dearest friend."
"He is neither disliked, nor hated, nor merely indifferent;
nevertheless, He favors His devotees just as the celestial tree (kalpavṛkṣa) grants the desires of whoever relies upon it. [BhP 10.38.22]

In this context, it should be understood that He is indeed someone other than a mere devotee; for His state as the Beloved has been declared by the very words of the Lord Himself: "What wise man, other than You—who are dear to Your devotees, whose speech is truth, who are a friend, and who are grateful—would seek refuge in another? (BhP 10.48.26). Śrī...
It has also been said by Mahādeva:
"Indeed, for him there is no one dear, nor anyone not dear, whether one's own kin or a stranger."
Because he is the self of all beings, Hari is dear to all beings.
And this illustrious Citraketu is his dear follower; he is peaceful and looks upon all things with equanimity.
"For indeed, I alone am the beloved of Acyuta.
Thus it was also said by Śrī Prahlāda:
"O wonder! Your activity, O You of immeasurable *yogamāyā*—"

"O You who have sportively emanated the worlds, the expert, the Self of all, the one who looks with equal vision upon all— Your nature is impartial, for You, who are dear to Your devotees, possess the nature of the wish-fulfilling tree. [BhP 8.23.8] Thus it is said.
And the meaning is as follows: that you are dear to your devotees—that too is Your nature, which is equal-visioned and not uneven; it does not become unequal.
In this regard, there is a qualifying epithet containing a reason: "having the nature of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru)."

Therefore, it is truly marvelous that even though you are perceived as having a dissimilar nature, there is no partiality toward you; or rather, since even in other cases— such as with things characterized as wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*) and the like— one must resort to a basis that is indeed common [to all],
the observation of dissimilarity in the form of partiality toward devotees implies that dissimilarity itself is of a uniform nature.
It should be explained in this very way;
likewise, in the previous case as well, it should be construed as "he honors those who honor him," thus applying only the sense of partiality (*vaiṣamya*).
In reality, however, the primary cause for the lack of contradiction [between the Lord and His devotees] is the inconceivable sovereignty (aiśvarya) of the Blessed Goddess herself;
as it is said: "Obeisances, obeisances unto You, the bull among the Sātvatas."
[This is] in the commentary on the fourth verse of the second chapter;
thus, even when an apparent inequality is perceived, he declares that the Lord's sovereignty is inconceivable so that there may be no fault.
Thus it was said by the venerable Bhīṣma: "Indeed, for the Self of all, who is impartial, non-dual, free from egoism,
and faultless, no disparity of intellect is ever produced by that [action]."
"Nevertheless, behold the compassion shown by the Lord toward His exclusive devotees, for as I was about to give up my life, Kṛṣṇa Himself appeared before my eyes.
Thus it is said; and likewise by the Blessed Lord:
I am equal toward all beings;
none is hateful to Me and none is dear,
yet those who worship Me with devotion—
"May I be in them, and they also in me"— thus,
since such partiality toward devotees, even when directed toward those with various faults, is the very essence of the power of His true nature (*svarūpa-śakti*),
He Himself, by His own essential power alone, performs various avataric pastimes solely for the delight of His devotees.
Since it is established that the Lord Himself accomplishes the protection of the universe, the question raised by Vidura does not remain relevant.
In this regard, because the gods and others are composed of material nature (*prākṛta*), [the Lord’s] pastimes with them proceed spontaneously.

The loss of their satisfaction [if one were to accept] the entry of a portion of that [divine essence] into them will be remedied later; likewise, there is no loss of the essential nature of the incarnations (*avatāra*) and so forth as being composed of His own power (*svarūpa-śakti*).
Similarly, [there is no loss of the fact that He is] solely for the delight of His devotees.
Furthermore, because there is an absence of attachment and aversion elsewhere due solely to the spontaneous play of one who has fulfilled their purpose, there is no partiality;

on the contrary, just as those with tongues afflicted by bile find bitterness in sugar, even when restraint is experienced, it results only in benefit characterized by the destruction of their wickedness and so forth. In this regard:
O Lord of the Earth, there is no cause for this birth, whether through karma or otherwise,
for the Supreme Self, the witness of all, who is the master of His own māyā;
yet that which has been manifested by Me is indeed for the sake of the maintenance, creation, and dissolution of beings.
"Grace (anugraha) is intended for the attainment of the Self through the cessation of that [bondage]"—

according to these words of Śrī Śuka found within the Ninth Canto, since qualities such as dharma are impossible for the individual soul (jīva) whose limiting adjuncts (upādhi) have dissolved during the dissolution of the universe (pralaya), grace consists in the provision of dharma and other virtues by means of the creation of the limiting adjuncts and so forth.
And thus, according to his commentary:
"Likewise, O Lord, you have descended into this world with a portion [of yourself],
distinct from others, for the protection of the virtuous and the suppression of the wicked."
"O Lord, we do not know whether some person follows His command or whether one reaps the fruit of their own actions.
Thus, even when informed of the multitude of kings bound by Jarāsandha, You, the Lord, remained for the sake of protecting the virtuous.

If suffering were to befall us even when You have descended [as an incarnation], then we do not understand why anyone else, such as Jarāsandha and others, would transgress Your command; nor do we understand how it is that even a person spoken to by You still encounters the suffering resulting from his own karma.
The sense is that neither of these two positions is tenable. Furthermore, according to his own commentary, although Līlā acts with complete freedom, it is Māyā alone— though difficult to reconcile—
that effects the awakening and coordination of the respective karmas of the gods, Anusūyā, and others at each particular time.

Just as it is observed even in the world that the specific activities of living beings, who are each acting according to their own respective karma, become interconnected through the mutual influence of their auspicious and inauspicious deeds, so too is it with the Supreme Lord; however, in certain instances where this worldly process is unable to keep pace with the swiftness of His divine play (līlā), it is there that the Lord’s direct intervention occurs.
One's independence becomes manifest, as in:
"O Great King, preceded by my command, bring here the son of the Guru, who is bound by his own karma. [BhP 10.45.45]
Thus, according to the instructions of the Blessed One regarding Yama and other sources;
and consequently, because its practice is extremely rare,
there is no occurrence of the undesirable consequences of the loss of what has been done or the acquisition of what has not been done in all cases.

Now, if some [persons] hate even those who are devotees, then, because He is included within the partiality shown toward His devotees, there is no fault for the Blessed One even in hating them Himself;
on the contrary, it is for the sake of the devotees—

By virtue of nourishing that delight which has the [divine] object as its domain, this [state] is indeed a particular manifestation of bliss (*ānanda*) arising from the *hlādinī* function; for by means of that [delight], even the desert-like state of *brahma-kaivalya*— which brings about the attainment of liberation— is surpassed by the great ocean of the nectar of devotion (*bhakti-rasa*), whose diverse richness of intense bliss unfolds at every step.
Because it is the counter-positive (pratiyogin) [of that state], and because otherwise it would be difficult to cure, what is appropriate there is that,
through the suppression of both the power of its own nature and the splendor of the Lord arising from that [state], it attains a status equivalent to absolute non-existence (dhvaṃsābhāva).
According to the principle stated in *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 6.17.28, "even regarding heaven, liberation, and hell, they perceive the same purpose," the Lord—
who acts for the welfare of all— inflicts upon those very lustful ones a specific, severe punishment that is exceedingly difficult for others to endure and which they themselves intensely dislike.

Precisely because its nature is consummate conduct (*paryavasāyi-cāritra*), there occurs the destruction of all the afflictions of *saṃsāra* consisting of various difficult-to-restrain, evil latent tendencies (*durvāsanā*).
Indeed, for those who worship [the Lord] as non-different [from themselves], this is even more arduous—

The goal of human endeavor is that which is to be accomplished. And for those who perceive the ultimate reality, it is no different from hell; yet for those sensualists, it is as intensely desired as excrement is to dung-beetles.
That Supreme Lord grants them a distinguished heaven;
for this very reason, it was said by the wives of the Nāgas: "Even toward the sons of an enemy, one should act as toward one's own sons."
The meaning of "of the gods who are to be protected" is as stated in BhP 10.16.33. Regarding "self-restraint" (*dama*), the sense is that self-restraint is also included therein.
As for the fact that the attainment of the highest state for devotees is heard of in the case of Pūtanā and others, that is merely an imitation of those devotees.
That it is by means of his majesty alone is clearly stated in various places;
for example: "Even Pūtanā was saved along with her clan because of her virtuous appearance," and so forth. [BhP 10.14.35]
Now, if some who are indeed devotees should somehow commit an offense against other devotees,

then by that very offense, they experience the lapping flames of the submarine fire of hatred arising toward both the devotees and the Lord; after a long time, they may somehow again, even while wearing the garb of a devotee, [attain the Lord].
When the fault of that offense, along with its accompaniments such as sensory contact and so forth, has been destroyed, they attain their very own state; however,
they do not attain the absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) of Brahman, because the seed characterized by devotion is imperishable.
Because of their inherent nature, the Blessed One’s anger toward those fools is like that of a mother [toward her children]. Thus,
indeed, the illustrious King said:
O Brahmin, how could the Blessed One himself— who is equal toward all beings, beloved, and a friend—
act for the sake of Indra against the Daityas?
