How did he slay the Daityas as if they were uneven? "Unevenness" is an elliptical expression meaning either "toward an enemy" or "as if toward a friend. [94]
Furthermore, one becomes a partisan of those by whom one's purpose is accomplished;
one slays with hatred those from whom one fears, but that is not the case here— so he says:
For the purpose of this [teaching], which consists of the supreme good, is not directed against the hosts of gods,
nor is there any animosity toward the asuras.
For one who lacks virtue, there is indeed no freedom from agitation;
[the state of] supreme bliss is the ultimate liberation.
Therefore—
Thus, O highly fortunate one, a very great doubt has arisen in us regarding the qualities of Nārāyaṇa.
Therefore,
you ought to dispel this doubt regarding the various qualities, such as favor and restraint.
Here, the venerable Ṛṣi said:
Well asked, O Great King, regarding the wonderful life of Hari,
which is the majesty of the Bhāgavata.
[This is] for the increase of devotion to the Blessed One.
O Great King,
that which you have asked is indeed well-considered.
But the conduct of Hari is wonderful and unprecedented, because it appears as if characterized by inequality even in the absence of inequality, and thus transcends the reach of logical inquiry.
In whatever part of the life-story of Hari there exists an increase in devotion to the Lord,
the greatness of the *Bhāgavata*, and the greatness of the multitude of devotees headed by Prahlāda—
by this it is shown that the Blessed One performs everything solely for the sake of the *Bhāgavata* and not for any other purpose.

Thus, it is indicated that this very meaning will reach its final conclusion. And the commentary is as follows: "I bow to the wondrous Nṛsiṃha, the embodiment of supreme bliss, who tears asunder the opposing side through his partiality for his own devotees. [97]
Therefore, it is sung as the supreme merit by the sages, Nārada and others.
Having bowed to the sage Kṛṣṇa, I shall relate the story of Hari— that story which,
when sung, becomes supremely meritorious. This is what is meant by "that story."
In that case, the connection is established by supplying an ellipsis;
and here, by virtue of being sung by them, it is implied that its sole purpose is the happiness of the devotees. [98]
In each case, he provides an answer to the question that is precisely in accordance with the implied meaning:
"For although the Blessed One is devoid of qualities, unborn, unmanifest, and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti)..."
Having entered into His own illusory energy (*māyā-guṇa*), He has assumed the state of the oppressor and the oppressed.
Since He is beyond *prakṛti*, He is therefore devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*)— that is, free from material qualities— and for that very reason unborn and eternal.

It is established that, for that very reason, the Unmanifest is not manifested by anything else because it is devoid of a material body, senses, and so forth; thus, the meaning is that its body and other attributes are self-luminous.
Consequently, [it is free] from passion, aversion, and so on, which arise from the qualities of *prakṛti*.
The sense is that he is "devoid" [of such qualities].

Even though he is thus constituted, there is a quality residing in his *māyā*—that is, his compassion—which consists of the pure and exalted *sattva* known as the curiosity of divine play (*līlā-kautuka*) toward his own devotees; that [quality]...

Having entered and taken hold [of the body], the Blessed One— who is eternally manifest with the sixfold sovereignty of his qualities— has, even as this is merely an illustration, at times been born, and though manifest within the senses of the world, has come to the state of being both the subduer and the subdued.

Even among the extremely insignificant beings such as gods and asuras, who are incapable of even standing within the range of one's own vision, one may assume a certain splendor characterized by a portion of that [divine power] which has been personally projected in order to provide assistance or to act as an opponent; and through this, one may exercise both the state of being oppressed and the state of being an oppressor.

He has gone. For the sake of the manifold variety of the play of battle, he has at that time transferred a portion of his own splendor—greater even than the splendor manifesting within himself—to those who oppose him, so as to become the one afflicted and suffer defeat;
yet at other times, having certainly transferred [that splendor] from them back to himself, he has attained victory by becoming the afflictor. Such is the meaning. May it be so.
The *Viśvaprakāśa* states that "māyā" refers to both compassion (*kṛpā*) and deceit (*dambha*).

Although other meanings exist here, because [the work] was commenced with the purpose of favoring the devotees (*bhāgavata-anugraha*), and because it will be concluded in that same way, and because of the commonality of the underlying intent, [it refers to] that specific [deceit] consisting of trickery (*chala-maya-māyā*).
Moreover, because it would entail even greater faults were He to act as a creator, He does not depend upon such agency. Therefore,
since there is an absence of attachment and aversion toward anything other than His own spontaneous play— which has the sole purpose of delighting His devotees— there is no partiality here.
This is the intended meaning. For this very reason, it is stated that he undergoes even sublation (*bādhyatā*) together with his state as the sublater (*bādhakatā*).

Likewise, it is suggested that by manifesting his divine play (*līlā*), characterized by the unfolding of the power of his own essential nature (*nijasvarūpaśakti*), his welfare culminates for all beings; thus, his status as a friend (*suhṛttā*) and so forth does not depart from him. [99]

Now, raising such doubts as: "How is it that even this quality called *viśuddha-sattva* is not material (*prākṛta*)? When or where does it transfer that excellence of vigor (*vīryātiśaya*)? Or how is it that the logical fallacies of the loss of what has been done (*kṛtahāni*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) do not arise?", he speaks by means of two verses:
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities of primordial nature (prakṛti), not of the self (ātman);
they do not exist simultaneously, O King.
"Whether it be decline or indeed exaltation,
the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest belong to *prakṛti* alone, and not to the Self;
for that Self is the Supreme Lord."
The meaning is that all those qualities which are eternally manifest do not belong to Him; as it has been said:
"O Lord, sattva and the other qualities do not exist [in You]" (ViP 1.9.44).
[These qualities are] hlādinī, sandhinī, and saṃvit.
And because of the statement, "All things are established in you alone" (ViP 1.12.69),
since there is no [change] in you, the Self, there is consequently neither simultaneous decrease nor increase; rather,
because they are subject to mutual destruction due to their nature as modifications, there is at times a decrease for one thing and at another time [an increase].
The meaning is that at times there is an intensification (ullāsa).

Consequently, this demonstrates the fitness of the gods and others for his assistance, and of the asuras and others for combat against him. Likewise, it shows how, at the time of the intensification of sattva and the other qualities, his divine play (līlā) appears to be dependent upon them.
Repeating that which is understood, he offers a rebuttal:
"But at the time of the victory of sattva, [he conquers] the divine sages; at the time of rajas, the asuras."
During the period favorable to *tamas*, the Blessed One resorts to *yakṣas* and *rakṣases*;
during the time of the victory of *sattva*, He resorts to the gods and the *ṛṣis*. Thus the Blessed One dwells within those respective bodies.

The meaning is that he transmits his own splendor, which has *sattva* as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), by which he makes them companions. In this way, it should be applied accordingly: when *rajas* prevails, [he transmits] that which has *rajas* as its limiting adjunct among the Asuras; when *tamas* prevails, [he transmits] that which has *tamas* as its limiting adjunct among the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas.
And thus, by engaging in combat against those adversaries such as the yakṣas, he defeats the gods and others, demonstrating that he himself is likewise capable; this is the meaning.
In this way, [it describes] the play (*līlā*) which nourishes the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of devotion (*bhakti*).
It has been shown that they enter into a state of mutual sublation for the sake of variety;
and this is also heard in the account of the churning of the Ocean of Milk.
Likewise, Viṣṇu entered the gods in an asura-form, stimulating their strength and heroism, while simultaneously inflaming the hosts of the deities.
"...by the Lord, he assumed the form of the King of Serpents.
Even there, it is understood that such various entries (āveśa) were undertaken by Him solely for the sake of that diversity.
But surely, by being subject to the timing of the awakening of those respective qualities, His spontaneous playfulness (svaira-līlatā) would be lost?

Furthermore, suspecting that the excellence of the connection with the qualities (guṇas) and the status as Vaiṣya and so forth would be quite evident [from that alone], he says "conformable to their time" (tat-kālānuguṇa).
This means that His time alone is conformable to those [qualities], such as sattva and the rest. [This refers to] the Blessed One—
The compound is formed like *caraṇa* (foot).

While He sports according to His own will, Māyā, which is eternally subservient to Him, follows Him accordingly; thus, the world-process, established as an beginningless flow, proceeds through the karma of the world.
The meaning is that Time (kāla), having impelled the aggregate and being set in motion as the specific form of its own function, becomes dependent upon the qualities (guṇas) such as sattva;
this is the dependence of Time upon Māyā’s function.
In the passage beginning with "Time is destiny," it was stated that this is Your own māyā;
or rather, even for them, time is always accompanied by [Your] power, which is characterized by spontaneous activity for the sole purpose of bestowing grace upon devotees.
The meaning is "one who possesses that quality.
The implication is that even from that state, through *māyā*, various things are set in motion precisely in accordance with those activities. As it has been said:
"That which is this time, O friend of the Unmanifest,
they call Your activity, by which the universe acts. Thus,
it follows that in either case, there is no state of dependence on another.
In this very way, the illustrious Lord Kapila also said: "That which is called the twenty-fifth principle is Time;
they call it the power of the Supreme Person."
And regarding the verse, "Some say time, from which fear arises" (BhP 3.26.16),
he has presented therein two views characterized by [the former] being a limb of Māyā and [the latter] being a quality of the Puruṣa.
In this regard, His primary activity is the manifestation of His power solely for the delight of His devotees;
however, effects such as the awakening of their spiritual qualities occur therein spontaneously.
Thus, it becomes such that there is only the appearance of activity therein;
and consequently, since the prior portion is itself [the cause],
it is the play of the power of its own nature (*svarūpa-śakti*), while the subsequent [portion] consists solely of that appearance, being the power of manifestation (*ābhāsa-śakti*).
It is included within *māyā* itself.

It should be understood that the statement beginning with "this which is time" and ending with "the winking of an eye, etc. is made solely with the intention of expressing the non-difference between the two.
Therefore, it should be explained as follows:

just as a servant who follows another servant is called a "subordinate servant" (*anubhṛtya*), so too here, the quality in the form of a manifestation (*ābhāsa*) that follows the quality characterized by power (*prabhāva*) is the "subordinate quality" (*anuguṇa*). And thus:
Their time is also favorable, but it is not a direct quality (*guṇa*) belonging to that [time].
[101] Now, one might ask: "How is it that the light (*tejas*) being infused into those various [elements] is not perceived? To this he replies:
"It appears like light and so forth."
It is not distinguished from the aggregate;
having churned it thoroughly, the sages know the Self abiding within the self.
Although He is pervaded by His own portion of splendor within each of those [elements] and, due to their composite nature and mutual intermingling,
is not distinguished by ordinary people— that is, cannot be discerned— nevertheless, poets who are skilled in discrimination, having ultimately churned through them,
[perceive Him] by negating impossible meanings such as "even His assistance" or "by Him [the elements] fought."
Having discerned it, they know— that is, they realize— the Self, which abides within them and has entered into each respective self, as the Lord; in this regard,
there is an illustrative example containing a reason.
Because that fire appears among perceivers like an object such as light; this is the distinction.
This is the meaning.
Just as this is not the heat of the gem itself because it was not perceived previously,
but rather solar heat has entered into it through contact with sunlight— as is known from the burning of cotton and other materials by a sun-crystal (sūryakānta)— so too [is it here].
Then it appears as something being experienced;
and just as before, it appears to them that this fragrance belongs to the wind, yet it has entered into the earth itself.
"It is the same here as well.
Alternatively, [an objection might be raised]: "In that case, is it not observed that they too play? To this he replies with the word "light" (*jyotiḥ*).
Just as by means of lights such as the eyes, when only form (*rūpa*)—which is their own portion—is being illuminated, [the other] qualities such as smell (*gandha*) and so forth...
It is perceived that the five [senses] manifest as earth alone;
and just as when the sound of a drum is grasped by the space within the ear and other [sensory organs], it is perceived as "this is indeed a drum," so too is that [case].
That [diversity] arises only from the intermingling of its qualities, not from the reality itself. Likewise, poets,
by virtue of abiding within various such aggregates, perceive themselves as the Lord— even though they are indistinguishable from others— [seeing] their own portion residing within the Self.
The meaning is that they know Him as one who sports by means of His very splendors (*tejas*).
Having thus stated that the sole purpose is the delighting of His devotees through His own pastimes such as battle, while the protection of the universe occurs from Him spontaneously;

Extending [the same principle] to the observation of primordial nature (prakṛti) and so forth during both creation and dissolution, he states that there is no distinction among the three [states], in order to dispel all doubts:
"When the Supreme, desiring to emit the cities [of bodies] from Himself..."
By His own māyā, this Lord, desiring to sport in various ways, separately creates the mode of passion (rajas);
and when about to lie down, He impels the mode of darkness (tamas).

When, at that time characterized by His own activity, this Supreme Lord, through His own māyā and out of compassion for His devotees, desires to manifest before Himself the forms of the sādhaka-devotees from previous creations as His own presiding abodes— while they remain merged within those [elements] together with primordial nature (prakṛti)— then [He acts].

When He performs the act of seeing for the purpose of manifestation, then that other power—distinct from His own essential nature and called *jīva* (the individual soul) and *māyā*—is, as before, inflamed by the appearance of His creative influence consisting of activity; it emits *rajas* and causes the unmanifest (*avyakta*), which is the equilibrium of the three qualities (*guṇas*) and its own constituent part, to become agitated or awakened. As it is said:
Or, this very Time (kāla), accompanied by separate māyā, creates [the world] in such a manner; and by the word "asau" (this one), it is Time itself that is denoted.
Furthermore, when He desires to sport within the cities (pūḥ) characterized by those [qualities], which possess a variety of diverse attributes, then He creates sattva.
Furthermore, when he wishes to lie down— that is, when he desires to sleep— having come together with those very [qualities],
then he creates *tamas*. From that...
The sense is that all activities, such as creation and so forth, proceed solely for the sake of the devotee (*bhakta*).
This is exactly as accepted by the commentators (*ṭīkākṛt*) in the third chapter of the eleventh book [of the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*]: "For what purpose did He create Himself... [and so on].
For the sake of attaining the self as the measurer (*mātṛ*):

he who measures himself, measures himself out, and worships the self—that one is *svamātṛ*. Here, "lying down" refers to those preeminent attainments (*siddhi*) of that self, the individual soul (*jīva*).

The descent as a person (puruṣāvatāra) sometimes consists in yoga-sleep within the ocean of dissolution, and sometimes in entering into the Blessed One. Although the Supreme Lord dwells within all living beings as their inner controller (antaryāmin), nevertheless, because He is unattached therein, He is as if not present; however, because He is fully attached to His devotees, it is not so.
"So be it. Furthermore, since he has no desire for attachment to those [objects] and so forth, the aforementioned explanation alone is authoritative.
And thus says the Śrī Bhagavad Upaniṣad:
"All beings abide in Me, yet I do not abide in them."
"And yet the beings do not dwell in Me; behold My divine yoga" (Gītā 9.4–5), and "But those who worship Me with devotion, they are in Me, and I am also in them" (Gītā 9.29).
And it is said in the *Haribhaktisudhodaya*:
"The hearts of devotees are peaceful; endowed with splendor, they are my beloved home. There I dwell, for that alone is the true description of what is called Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus, having explained both creation and dissolution as an incidental digression, he returns once more to the subject of preservation itself.
Explaining the treatise, he concludes with a verse and a half: "O King, the Lord, who makes his promises true, creates time as the substratum for Pradhāna and Puruṣa while they are in motion."
O King, since this very Time is the lord who,
like a host of gods, sharpens the quality of goodness (sattva),
therefore he, the beloved of the gods, [destroys] the asuras who are its adversaries.
The one of vast renown overcomes those characterized by passion and ignorance;
being himself the very manifestation of the performance of ultimate reality through the play of his own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*),
he creates— that is, manifests— time, which is the form of his own activity.

What is He doing? He is moving together with Pradhāna and Puruṣa, for the sake of assisting those devotees who are the agents of their respective relationships and who have entered into the forms of gods and others, as they are being created from portions of His own splendor.

Moving from the very moment of birth through the combination of the unmanifest and the individual soul (jīva), he is therefore the locus of their various states by mere proximity and the cause of their manifestation;
thus [the Lord] addresses him with the vocatives "O Man" and "O God."

Just as for you who perform the primary task by your own desire, even that which is more insignificant accomplishes itself in the same way, so it is here as well— this is what has been taught. Therefore, this effort—
O King, that being whose nature is characterized by *sattva*—predominantly *sattva*—seems to cause the army of the gods, which is like a cloud, to expand;
from that very source, it seems to crush and strike down the enemies of those [gods], the asuras, who are predominantly *rajas* and *tamas*.
Furthermore, those among the gods who are devoted and those among the asuras who are both devoted and hateful, he himself protects them all, as stated previously.
Thus it has been said: since such is the condition of time, which is characterized by those activities, therefore even the Lord (Īśitā) seems to cause growth and seems to measure.
"O King," [he says], referring back to the previous intention.
Now, if the Lord has no purpose [of his own], then why would he not at some time make even the asuras his own allies and fight with the gods?
To this, he says: "He is dear to the gods" (sura-priyaḥ).
He whose dear devotees abide among the gods;
that is, among the gods who are predominantly characterized by *sattva*, for almost all of them.
His following [of the Dharma] is indeed accomplished through following that very [teacher].
For sometimes, when great figures such as Bṛhaspati and others commit an offense, their divinity is obscured by that stain; yet for them and for him, [the Dharma remains] within these [beings].
The intention is that [he says] "there would be no following" because it was stated [earlier] that "at the time of victory, however, [it belongs] to the *sattva*," and so forth.
Now, one might ask: "How is it that they too do not follow them? To this he replies: "consisting of *rajas* and *tamas*. Extremely—
The meaning is that this is because of a lack of appreciation for the two qualities that cause one to turn away from the Blessed One.

Now, one might suspect an inconsistency in the fact that he always performs only the subjugation of the asuras; anticipating this, he says "uruśravāḥ. He is one whose *śravaḥ*—that is, fame or renown—is *uru*, meaning spread everywhere or most extensive, among them.
The sense is that he indeed bestows grace.

Thus, having demonstrated the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), in order to provide an illustration for the proposition that the Supreme Lord performs various acts solely for the purpose of favoring his own devotees, [the author cites] the instances of his compassion toward Prahlāda, Jaya, Vijaya, and others.
He states a specific historical narrative as an illustration:
"In this very context, a historical account was previously cited by the celestial sage."
Out of affection, O King, he spoke to Ajātaśatru, who was questioning him regarding the great sacrifice.
Thus [beginning with BhP 7.1.12], the commentary itself should be consulted. 7.1. Śrī Śuka: 93–104 [105–106].
Thus, since both partiality and cruelty have been refuted,
the principle established in the *Brahma-sūtras*— that God is to be regarded as like the rain-cloud— is also included within this very [argument].
This concludes the explanation of Brahman, Bhagavat, and Paramātman as established by the scriptures.
Thus, the state of being a triple manifestation has been fully elucidated.

In some places, the state of being the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha) beginning with Vāsudeva is observed; and that distinction is not improper, as it is intended by someone to express non-difference [of one aspect] from another.
Thus it is said in the *Mokṣa-* [Dharma-purāṇa]:

In the *Nārāyaṇīya* section of the *Dharma*, it is said: "The division into a single manifestation (*ekavyūha*) is found in some places; it is designated as a double manifestation (*dvivyūha*), reckoned as a triple manifestation (*trivyūha*), and is also seen as a quadruple manifestation (*caturvyūha*)" (Mbh 12.336.53).
And there is scripture: "He becomes one-fold; he becomes two-fold" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2), and so forth.

Now, according to the previous method, since there is no contradiction with the state of having four vyūhas and so on, the fact that there is a state of three vyūhas here is because the first vyūha, the Śrī-Bhagavān himself, possesses primacy, and it is precisely as its proponent that this [text] exists.
Its name is Śrī-Bhāgavatam;
as it has been said: "This Purāṇa named Bhāgavata is equal to Brahman."
For when that [intention] is predominant, the purport is also determined by six kinds of marks:
the opening and the conclusion, repetition, novelty, the fruit, [the explanatory eulogy], and the consistency of the meaning.
Exegetical praise (arthavāda) and logical consistency (upapatti) are the indicators for determining the intended meaning (tātparya).
In the manner thus stated;
for instance, by the unity of the opening and the conclusion:
"From whom [proceeds] the birth and so forth of this [world], through positive and negative concomitance, He is the knower of all objects, the self-sovereign."

We meditate upon that Supreme Truth, whose own splendor eternally dispels all illusion, wherein the threefold creation—of fire, water, and earth—is not false; that by which the primordial poet received the Veda through his heart, and at which even the wise are bewildered, just as there is a mutual transformation of light, water, and clay. [BhP 1.1.1]

To whom and by whom was this incomparable lamp of knowledge revealed in the past? It was revealed in that very form to the sage Nārada; and in that same form, out of compassion, it was revealed to Kṛṣṇa, the lord of yogis, who is identical with that [reality] and is the beloved of the Blessed One.
"Let us meditate upon that which is pure, stainless, free from sorrow, immortal, true, and supreme.
Herein lies the meaning of the former [verse].
This is the meaning of the Brahma-sūtras, according to the statement in the *Garuḍa-purāṇa*: "This is the meaning of the Mahā-..."
Since the Purāṇa constitutes an unartificial commentary on the Brahma-sūtras, it first introduces itself by taking up that very work;
therein, it first explains the sūtra "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (athāto brahma-jijñāsā) through the analogy of fire and water.
By the half-verse beginning with "mṛdām" (of the clays),
[the author] establishes its priority because it comes first in the sequence of application.
Therein, he explains "the desire to know Brahman" by saying, "we meditate upon the Supreme."
Let us meditate upon the Supreme Blessed One;
thus, by means of the practice of yoga with the reins of the mind released, because of its vastness—

That Brahman which is the self of all exists both within and without; yet, like the sun in relation to its own rays and so forth, it remains transcendent over all things by its very nature— this is stated in order to demonstrate its status as the primordial form (mūla-rūpa).
The word *brahman* is explained by means of the word *para*;
and it is intended here that this [word] refers to the Blessed Lord alone, because the Person (*puruṣa*) is a portion of Him, and because the qualityless Brahman is devoid of qualities and so forth.

And it has been stated by the venerable Śrī Rāmānuja’s feet: "The word *brahman* is used everywhere because of its connection with the quality of vastness (*bṛhattva*). And its primary meaning is that in which there is an infinite and unsurpassed degree of vastness, both in its essential nature and in its qualities."
And he is indeed the Lord of All; as it was said by the Pracetasas: "He who is the end of all manifestations is celebrated as Ananta."

Therefore, although it possesses infinite forms that are diverse and enchanting, its nature as the supreme, most wonderful primary form which is the substratum of each of those particular forms is also revealed.
Thus, its embodied nature being established, it is not [limited] by those forms such as Viṣṇu and others, precisely because of that very supremacy.
The state of being the Blessed One (Bhagavat) itself is established, because he alone is shown to be the supreme [reality] behind Brahmā, Śiva, and others.
Here, the explanation of the term "desire to know" (jijñāsā) is "we meditate" (dhīmahi).
Since the desire to know that [Brahman] has its ultimate intent (*tātparya*) in meditation upon it alone, it was said by the Lord himself in the Eleventh [Book]:
"One who is proficient in the Word-Brahman (*śabda-brahman*)."
"If he has learned from others,
his learning is indeed fruitless,
like one who guards a cow that does not yield milk. [BhP 11.11.18] Thus it is said.
Then, by the words "dhīmahi," [the author] accepts as his own the teaching of Śrī Rāmānuja— that the term *jijñāsā* refers exclusively to *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation)—
[this work] named the *Śrībhāgavata*, which is the essence of all the Vedas and other scriptures.
It follows that this text is [composed of] form (rūpa).
The plural number in "dhīmahi" is intended to show that this duty must be performed by everyone existing throughout all times, places, and successions— [an infinite multitude].
Because meditation is prescribed solely upon the Blessed Lord, who is the source (aṃśin) of those persons who are the inner controllers of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
by this [statement], even the theory of illusory manifestation (vivartavāda)— which is the very lifeblood of the doctrine of the single soul (ekajīvavāda)— is refuted.
This is refuted. Furthermore, the root *dhyai* (to meditate) also indicates that the Blessed One possesses a form, because meditation has as its object only that which is embodied;
and when a means to the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*) that is easily accomplished exists, [one would not resort to] that which is difficult to accomplish.
Because [the path] is naturally inferior due to the lack of activity on the part of the person, and because it is determined that only the worshiper of Him is most appropriate;
thus says the Gītā Upaniṣad:
"Those who, having fixed their minds on Me, worship Me, ever disciplined..."
"Endowed with supreme faith, they are considered by Me to be the most disciplined.
But those who worship the Indestructible, the indefinable, the unmanifest, being devoted to the welfare of all beings—they attain Me alone. (Gītā 12.2–4)
"The affliction of those whose minds are attached to the Unmanifest is greater;
for the goal of the Unmanifest is attained with difficulty by embodied beings.
And this very point was explained by Brahmā:
O Lord, those who cast aside devotion— the path to the highest good— and strive only for the attainment of pure knowledge,
find that nothing but their own suffering remains for them.
"Otherwise, it would be like those who thresh coarse husks.
For this very reason, the fact that this object of meditation is the Lord Himself has been established;
and as for Śiva and the others—
Thus, by the optative suffix in the word *dhīmahi*, a prayer devoid of separate mental constructions (*pṛthag-anusandhāna*) is illuminated;

this reveals that the worship of the Blessed One, characterized by meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), is itself the supreme human goal (*parama-puruṣārtha*). From that, the Blessed One’s own nature as such is self-evident.
And consequently, it is precisely this state of possessing a form that is supremely captivating as described above that is perceived;
and thus it is said, "Among the Vedas, I am the Sāmaveda."

And therein, regarding the *Bṛhat-sāman*— whose greatness has been described as "among the *Sāmans*" (Gītā 10.35)— there is the vast abode, the vast earth, the vast intermediate space, the vast heaven, the vast desirable; the desirable for the vast,
and the desirable for the desirable.
Thus, "the desire to know Brahman" has been explained.
Now, he provides the explanation of the words "atha ataḥ" (thereupon, therefore) with the word "satyam" (truth).

Since the word *atha* (then) there signifies immediate succession (*ānantarya*), and the word *ataḥ* (therefore) functions as the cause of what has preceded, therefore [the meaning of] *atha* is: immediately after the correct knowledge of ritual action obtained through the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā* in the section on ritual (*karmakāṇḍa*) which was previously acquired according to the sequence of Vedic study.

The meaning is as follows: "From this" means immediately following that sequence, in the section concerning Brahman (brahma-kāṇḍa) which has been reached, by reason of some statement whose meaning has been studied and partially reflected upon, and which is to be determined through the correct meaning established by the Uttara-mīmāṃsā; such is the sense.

Because the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā serves as the prima facie position (pūrva-pakṣa) for which the conclusion (uttara-pakṣa) is established by the Uttara-mīmāṃsā, and because it must necessarily be relied upon in this [latter system],
and because it acts as an auxiliary in its non-contradictory portions, and because ritual action is a cause for the purification of the mind characterized by tranquility and so forth.
And immediately after that, this very [meaning] is obtained:
these sentences are as follows— "Just as in this world the world won by action perishes, even so in the next world the world won by merit perishes."

Now, those who depart from here having discovered the Self and these [deities] whose desires are true—for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds; he does not return again; and he is fit for infinity. He is stainless, supreme...
"It attains equality":
"Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature;
even at the time of creation they are not born, and at the time of dissolution they do not suffer" (Gītā 14.2).

Both of these points have been elucidated in Rāmānuja’s Śārīraka: it is heard in scripture that action (karman), which is known through the prior portion of the Mīmāṃsā, yields results that are limited and impermanent, whereas the knowledge of Brahman, which is determined by the subsequent portion, yields results that are infinite and eternal.
Therefore, it is implied that after the previously discussed knowledge of action (*karma*), Brahman is to be known;
this is what the venerable author of the *Sarvārtha-siddhi* commentary has stated.
Baudhāyana states: "After completing one's duties, one should desire to know Brahman.
This very point is clearly evident in the Purañjana narrative through the etymological explanation of the sounds *pitṛ* and *hūdvā* from the right and left ears respectively.

Thus, immediately after the correct knowledge of the *karma-kāṇḍa*, regarding certain statements contained within the *brahma-kāṇḍa*, one first gains the knowledge that the bliss of heaven and so forth possesses an existence that is subject to deviation— being of the nature of suffering through an investigation into the reality of things— whereas the [bliss] of Brahman is non-deviating.

Since the knowledge of truth (*satyatva*)—precisely as the state of supreme bliss—is itself the cause for the inquiry into Brahman (*brahma-jijñāsā*), this meaning is obtained from the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*);
thus he states the distilled sense of that very point: "truth" (*satyam*). The meaning is: possessing an existence that is non-deviating and which bestows existence upon all things.
By the connection with the word "supreme" (param) and by the word "Brahman" in the scriptural passage, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1),
it follows that for anything else, its existence is dependent upon His will, and thus its existence is subject to deviation.
Thus, the sense here is that we have meditated upon this very [reality] as having a limited and fluctuating existence, but now we shall meditate upon it as possessing an unfluctuating existence.
Then, he clarifies its supremacy with the word "dhāmnā" (by its own splendor).

Here, by the word *dhāma*, either "power" (*prabhāva*) or "light" (*prakāśa*) is expressed; for according to the section on various meanings in the *Amara-kośa* and other lexicons, "dwelling," "body," and "splendor" are among the meanings of *dhāman*. It does not, however, mean the essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Likewise, by the word *kuhaka* (deceiver), that which performs deception is meant here; and that is indeed the sovereign power (*vaibhava*) of *māyā*, because it causes the obscuration and distraction of the true nature of the individual soul (*jīva*).
And therefore, by itself—
[He is] that from whom the deceptive display of *māyā* has been forever and eternally dispelled by His own power (*dhāmnā*), which consists of His own majesty or His own self-luminous nature;
as it is said: "having cast aside *māyā*."
Regarding the phrase "by its own power" (*sva-śaktyā*): since that power is also adventitious (*āgantuka*), the term "by itself" (*svena*) would be redundant.
However, if it were explained as "by its own nature" (*sva-svarūpeṇa*), then the purpose would be fulfilled by the word "by itself" alone. For example:
Even if one were to provide such an interpretation by some means, it results in nothing other than the capacity characterized by the elimination of deception;
and that [capacity] is manifested by the instrumental case ending (*tṛtīyā*) in the sense of being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*).
By this, [it is shown that the Self is] distinct from illusion and its effects.

The definition of one's own nature (*sva-svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*) is also understood as "whatever is an entity, that is its own nature. And this is indeed well-known from the Vedic revelation (*śruti*): "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and bliss" (*satyaṃ jñānam ānandaṃ brahma*), and "Knowledge and bliss are Brahman" (*vijñānam ānandaṃ brahma*). (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.3)
And this very [reality] has been established as the truth that is both revealed by scripture and indicative;
thus, His own essential power (svarūpa-śakti) is directly introduced, and from that, His status as the Blessed Lord (bhagavattva) becomes all the more clearly evident.
Now, he demonstrates the reasoning for the primacy of truthfulness with the words "wherein":
since the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva exists everywhere by virtue of being Brahman, within him abide the three qualities (guṇas), the elements, and the sense organs.

This creation, which consists of deities, belongs to that very Lord; it is not something falsely superimposed upon Him—like silver upon mother-of-pearl and the like—at the beginning of His power, but rather [it exists] in Brahman, who is well-known from the Vedic scripture: "from whom indeed these [beings arise]. Wherein...
Because it exists at all times, the creation of names and forms belongs to the one who performs the tripartition, as taught [in scripture];
and because they share a single agent, it is indeed true.
In this regard, he establishes its non-falsity even by means of an illustration:
The exchange of fire and the other elements means their mutual interchange of portions— that is, their existence within one another by way of their respective parts.
This is not false, but is exactly as [the nature of] the Lord is.
The meaning is that it is thus a transformation. These three deities become one each as the tripartite [fire].
That which is the red form of fire is the form of heat; that which is white is the form of water; and that which is black is the form of earth.
"From the earth comes that food," according to the Śruti (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.4.1).

Thus, since this meaning is rooted in the Śruti, any other meaning based on mere imagination is refuted by its very nature. Furthermore, regarding the specific nature of fire and the other elements which were indicated there in a general sense:
The transition [of meaning] does not enter the hearts of grammarians;
for if that were indeed intended, then one would have stated it simply as "just as *vāra* and so forth [are used] in the sense of *marīcika* and so forth."
Furthermore, in that view, the primary birth of the threefold creation from Brahman does not exist; rather, it is said that birth is merely a superimposition (āropa), and that, moreover,
arises solely from delusion (bhrama).
And error (bhrama) relies upon similarity;
however, similarity, through a difference in time, makes both [the perceived object and the substrate] the locus (adhiṣṭhāna).
For even in the case of silver, the possibility of mistaking mother-of-pearl for it exists.

Nor is there any rule that the locus of an illusion must be of a single nature while that which is imagined through the illusion is of a manifold nature; for instance, when smoke, a mountain, and trees situated at a distance are perceived as a single, undivided entity.
Because the delusion of clouds arises [from that],
so too in the present case, the threefold creation is perceived through direct perception from time immemorial; and Brahman exists,
shining by its own nature as pure consciousness alone.

Therefore, just as for the individual soul (jīva) who is overcome by beginningless ignorance there may be the delusion of the threefold creation within Brahman due to its similarity to the nature of Being, why should there not likewise ever arise the delusion of Brahman within the threefold creation?
And consequently, if there were no determination that Brahman alone is the substratum, there would follow the undesirable consequence of universal destruction;
however, as for its being the superimposer—
Since even for pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which is insentient in nature, [agency] is not possible,
and Brahman is held to be nothing but pure consciousness,
this is the intended meaning once it is established that the explanation is rooted in scripture (*śruti*).
For when something that does not exist in a particular place is seen elsewhere, its superimposition (āropa) upon that very place is established.

Consequently, since it is in fact incompatible with that [place], its existence cannot possibly be produced there by means of its own existence. However, as for the threefold creation, because it has arisen from the Blessed One—who is characterized by those very powers—in a primary sense, [the relationship is direct].
Because it is heard [in scripture] and because it is distinct from that, He exists in that very place which is the self of all;
therefore, He is not superimposed upon it. Nevertheless, superimposition occurs by way of the aforementioned method—beginning with "upon the locus"—because of His inconceivable power.
Even in the absence of being smeared with it, [the mirror] is of that very nature of Śiva;
and thus, according to the analogy "just as the moonlight of a fire situated in one place spreads abroad," its existence constitutes the existence of that [reflection].

Therefore, the Blessed One’s nature is primarily reality, and the threefold creation is not unreal. Thus says the Śruti: "The Reality of reality" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6), and likewise, "The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed reality; their reality is [the Self]. This refers to the gross and subtle elements denoted by the word *prāṇa*.

It reveals the Blessed One as the ultimate truth, which is the fundamental cause of those things apprehended as true from the perspective of conventional usage. Then, manifesting that very [Blessed One] through its extrinsic definition (*tāṭastha-lakṣaṇa*), it first [proceeds] with clarity of meaning.

And with the desire to make known that this *Saṃhitā* is indeed a commentary on the *Brahma-sūtras*, he first restates the very first sūtra immediately following it: "From which [proceeds] the birth and so forth of this [world].
Birth and so forth refer to creation—
The dissolution of this universe's persistence; [this is] a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that which possesses non-cognition of its qualities."

From that [source], which is endowed with numerous agents and enjoyers ranging from Brahmā down to a blade of grass; which is the locus of specific actions, results, causes, times, and places; and whose nature consists of a manifold and variegated arrangement inconceivable even by the mind—[it arises] from that which, through its own inconceivable power, exists as both the material cause and the form of the agent and so forth.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "We meditate upon that Supreme One whose [nature] begins with birth.
In this regard, the subject matter and the scriptural passage begin with: "Bhūgu, the son of Vāruṇi, approached his father Varuṇa and said, 'Sir, teach me Brahman.'"
"That from which these beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they enter when they depart—desire to know that; that is Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1).
"It created fire," and so forth (Chāndogya Upaniṣad).
6.2.3) And: "Birth and so forth are the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) here, not a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*);
therefore, that [birth] does not exist in the meditation upon it."
They enter;
however, the object of meditation (dhyeya) is indeed pure.
Furthermore, regarding the specific qualification mentioned previously here—
By virtue of being the cause of such distinguished universal birth and so forth, His omnipotence, the state of having true resolve,
omniscience, and lordship over all are indicated;
He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose—
From such scriptural passages as, "His austerity consists of knowledge; he is the controller of all" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.9,
2.2.7), his nature as being entirely opposed to all that is to be discarded and as possessing infinite auspicious qualities such as knowledge is indicated by his transcendence.
This is because of scriptural passages such as, "For him, neither effect nor cause exists. Furthermore,

in the view of those who claim that the object of inquiry is a featureless reality (*nirviśeṣa-vastu*), the sūtra "From which [arises] the birth and so forth of this [world]" would be irrelevant to the inquiry into Brahman.

This is because of the etymological derivation [of the word *brahman*] as "the unsurpassed, vast, and nourishing," and also because of the statement that "that Brahman is the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe.
This same principle applies to the subsequent sūtras as well.
Furthermore, the scriptural citations quoted in the Sūtras do not constitute valid authority for that [position]; nor does reasoning [apply],
because reasoning has as its object a thing that possesses a probans inseparable from the property to be proven, and thus it cannot concern that which is devoid of distinctions.
Furthermore,

in your own speculative position— that Brahman is that from which the delusion of the world's birth and so forth arises regarding the ultimate reality— there is no establishment of a featureless (nirviśeṣa) entity.
Since ignorance is the root of delusion and Brahman is the witness of that ignorance,
its status as a witness is said to consist solely in its nature as pure luminosity.

Luminosity, moreover, is that which distinguishes [consciousness] from the insentient by virtue of its nature of bringing about the capacity for practical activity (vyavahāra-yogyatā) regarding both itself and others;
such being the case, it possesses self-specificity, for in the absence of that, luminosity itself would not exist.
It would be a mere emptiness. Furthermore, since what is intended to be expressed regarding them would be established by the phrase "of fire, water, and earth" alone,
the statement "from which the birth, etc., of this [world proceeds]" would be redundant.
Therefore, once that specific distinction is established, that distinction consists precisely of power (*śakti*).
And power is shown to be threefold: internal (*antarāṅga*), external (*bahiraṅga*), and situated therein (*tadasthā*).

In that regard, since the world’s birth and so forth consist of transformation, it was introduced as being called *māyā*, which is the external instrumental cause (*bahiraṅga*) acting as the direct cause;
and we [the authors] maintain that it is "external" by means of the word *dhīmahi*.

Now, even though his birth and so forth proceed from the Person (puruṣa) who is distinguished by the power called primordial nature (prakṛti), which serves as the material cause and is a portion of the Blessed Lord, nevertheless, they ultimately terminate in the Blessed Lord alone as their cause.
Just as for one whose birth and so forth occur in a single part of the ocean, those births and so forth belong to the ocean itself. As it has been said:
Prakṛti is its material cause,
the Supreme Puruṣa is its substratum, and Time is the manifestor of that which exists.
"But I am that triad of Brahman.
Furthermore, by the statement "from whom the birth, etc., of this [world] proceed," the very fact of His possessing form (*mūrtatva*) is obtained;
for from Him [proceeds] the world which possesses form, as well as those infinite supreme powers (*para-śakti*) of a similar nature, which are the repositories of His formal power (*mūrta-śakti*).
It is argued that he is of the nature of a treasure-store,
because his supreme compassion is accepted as inherent;
and since he possesses form, his birth from another source would not follow, for that would lead to an infinite regress.
Because he alone is accepted as the beginning,
just like the *avyakta* (the unmanifest) for the Sāṅkhyas;
he is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses.
And because of the scriptural prohibition, "He has no progenitor, nor is there any lord over him" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.9),
that [form] belongs to Him by virtue of His being eternally established, non-material, and natural in nature.
And there is universal renown.
Thus, when his corporeality is established, that embodied one is none other than the Supreme Lord Himself, the direct embodiment of Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, and so forth. And so it is said:
From whom all beings come into existence at the arrival of the first age,
and into whom they go to their dissolution.
Once again, at the end of the eon.
Thus, and so forth, in the *Sahasranāma* and other such texts that establish this very point, it is stated therein: "The glorious one whose form is indefinable.
And likewise in the *Skānda*:
He alone is the Lord Hari, the creator, the protector, and the destroyer;
the creative and other powers attributed to others are said to be like those of a wooden puppet.
"Because [the Lord] possesses activity in one part, but not by His entire self, the whole process beginning with creation belongs only to Viṣṇu as the Supreme.
And in the Mahopaniṣad: "He creates through Brahmā; He dissolves through Rudra," and so forth. Therefore...
Thus it has been explained:
"Hiraṇyagarbha is the supreme cause for the creation and destruction of the universe by the Lord; and he is everything for you, who are formless Time."

That time which is devoid of form is merely the instrumental cause (*nimitta-mātra*) of that power of time (*kāla-śakti*); thus, the genitive case is used in a non-co-referential sense (*vyadhikaraṇa*). Similarly, [in such expressions as] "the first incarnation is the Person (*puruṣa*) of the Supreme," and so forth;
it is by a portion of Him that this [world] exists.
And [the passage beginning with] "birth and destruction" and so forth;

thus, even here, the Blessed One himself, possessing such a form, is the subject introduced. Having thus determined the Supreme by means of an extrinsic definition (*taṭastha-lakṣaṇa*), that very same definition is [established] in the *Brahma-sūtra* as the scripture’s—
This has been established by the two sūtras beginning with "Because [Brahman] is the source" (1.1.2) and "But that [is so], because of the concordance" (1.1.4); therein,
the meaning of the former sūtra is as follows:

To the question, "From where does Brahman derive its status as the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe? he replies: because the scripture (*śāstra*) is its *yoni*, meaning its source of knowledge;
for [it is stated in the scripture], "From which indeed all beings [arose]," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "because it is established by valid cognition" (*pramāṇakatvāt*):
here, as in the case of direct perception, there is no establishment by means of inference (*tarka*).

This is because inference is unstable (*apratiṣṭhāna*) and because [the object] is not within the domain of direct perception and other means of valid cognition due to its being absolutely beyond the senses (*atyantātīndriyatva*).
And this is the intention regarding Brahman as well.
As for the nihilists (vaināśikas), however, they will be refuted by means of reasoning alone in the chapter on "Non-contradiction" (avirodhādhyāya).
In this regard, the non-establishment of reasoning is as follows: God is not the creator because he lacks a purpose, like a liberated soul;
[conversely], the body, the world, and so forth have a living being (*jīva*) as their creator.
Because it is an effect, like a jar; or:
the time under dispute is not devoid of a world, because it is time, like the present time, and so forth.

Thus, since the inference of God based on conformity with perception is refuted by its opposition to other forms of perception, the Supreme Lord, who is the Supreme Person and the Supreme Brahman, is known solely through the authority of the Śāstra.

But the scripture [reveals] the ocean of infinite, unsurpassed, immeasurable, and sublime qualities— such as omniscience and the power of true resolve— which are of a nature entirely distinct from all things perceived by other means of valid cognition, and which are free from all that is to be abandoned.
Since it establishes the very nature of the adversary, there is not even a trace of the defect of being based on a similarity with an object established by another means of valid cognition;
for this very reason, its possession of an inherent, infinite, eternal form is also [established].
That is established.
Now follows the meaning of the subsequent sūtra:
regarding how Brahman has scripture as its means of valid cognition, he says that.
The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of removing a possible doubt.
That Brahman can indeed have that scripture as its means of valid cognition is entirely possible.
Why? Because of concomitance (*samanvaya*).
Concomitance is the demonstration through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); it is because of that.
In this regard, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (Taitt. 2.1.1); "Bliss is Brahman"; and "Brahman is indeed one, without a second.
That is the Truth; that is the Self (*ātman*).
Thus: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone";
"In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone, one only, in the form of a person"; "Nārāyaṇa, indeed, is that person."
"Verily, in the beginning, Nārāyaṇa alone existed. "May I become many; may I procreate.
"From this very Self, space was produced."
Thus: "It created that heat," and "From which indeed these beings are born. Verily, it is the Puruṣa.
"Nārāyaṇa desired; then from Nārāyaṇa the Unborn was born, from whom all progeny and all beings [proceed];
Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman, the Reality, Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Truth, the Satya, the Supreme Brahman, the Piṅgala Puruṣa," and so forth.
Now follows the negative argument (*vyatireka*):
"How could the existent be born from the non-existent?
For who indeed could breathe, who could live, if [the existent were not]?
"This bliss would not exist as space," and so forth, beginning with: "In the beginning, indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed— neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara."
And since he thus becomes endowed with the very nature of supreme bliss, the goal of human existence is accomplished through that very attainment; therefore, it is not devoid of purpose either.
Thus, the meaning of these two sūtras being established, he explains this [sūtra]:
"In regard to objects, through positive concomitance and otherwise.
This means that while there exist various kinds of objects, namely the meanings of Vedic sentences, [one understands them] through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), by way of agreement in presence.
The meaning is that since its birth and so forth are perceived from one [cause], and likewise from another by way of exclusion (*vyatireka*), it is therefore perceived from that very source;
for this reason, there is the connection with scripture (*śruti*) regarding that.
Furthermore, by demonstrating its nature as supreme bliss through the method of negative concomitance (vyatireka), its status as the supreme human goal (parama-puruṣārtha) is implied;
and its established form, as previously set forth, is supported by scriptural authority such as the passage beginning, "In the beginning, indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed."
Then, he explains [the sūtra] "Because of seeing, it is not without sound" with the words "the Omniscient One.
Here, the meaning of the sūtra is as follows: this is recorded in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second—Brahman. It thought (aikṣata)."
"May I be many, may I procreate"— thus [it is said],
"He created fire," and so forth.
Here, the Pradhāna mentioned by the opponent also presents itself as the cause of the world;
and [the author] says "because of seeing" (īkṣateḥ) to show that it is not so. In that [which possesses seeing]...
The meaning is that verbal testimony alone is not the means of valid cognition; rather, the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is non-verbal and inferential.
It is not that which is to be established here [in this scripture]. Anticipating the objection as to why it is non-verbal, he says: "Because of [the act of] seeing" (*īkṣateḥ*).

That [subject] is not what is to be established here. Anticipating the objection, "Why is it not expressed by words?", he says: "Because of seeing" (īkṣateḥ). This is because of the hearing of the verbal root *īkṣati*, which denotes a specific activity related to that which is denoted by the word "Being" (*sat*).
The statement "It thought" (tad aikṣata) implies that such thinking is not possible for the insentient *pradhāna*; furthermore, creation elsewhere is preceded by thought alone, as in:
"He thought, 'Let me create the worlds,' and he created these worlds."
First, "inspection" (*īkṣaṇa*) here, by its very nature of investigating that place and the objects to be created, encompasses omniscience itself;
this is what is meant by the term "omniscient" (*abhijña*).
Now, one might object that since it has been stated that [Brahman] is "only to be brought" (tadānīya) and "without a second," the means for its seeing cannot possibly exist;
to this, he says: "Self-ruling" (svarāṭ). This means that it shines forth in such a manner by its own very nature.

"Neither his activity nor his instrument is perceived," and so forth; and from such scriptural passages as "His knowledge, power, and action are innate," it follows that even His possession of a form, like His act of seeing, is purely innate.
Because that which was breathed forth will be shown later on,
and because that is exactly as stated,
[the author] explains another meaning of the phrase "because the scripture is its source" with the word "tena" (by that).
Regarding how that distinct entity is the creator of the birth and so forth of the world, and how it is neither the *pradhāna* taught by others nor any other [cause], he says:

The source, that is, the cause, of the scripture characterized as the Veda is [the Lord], because it has that very nature. Or rather, as it is said: "Verily, this Rigveda is the breath of this great Being."
The Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvāngirasa, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, the sciences, the Upaniṣads, the verses,
the aphorisms, the sub-aphorisms, and the commentaries— such is the Veda;
for the scripture is indeed all this.
It is heard in scripture that Brahman alone is the cause of that [universe], which consists of various and infinite cognitions that are beyond the scope of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Thus, it is primarily omniscient; and without such omniscience, the creation of all things—

Since the origin of anything else is not possible, it has been stated that Brahman, defined by the aforementioned characteristics, alone is the cause of the world, and neither the *pradhāna* nor another *jīva*.
He explains this very point further: "By him, [the Self], was Brahman revealed in the heart... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.4).
Regarding the term "Ādikavaye" (to the first poet): [the Lord spoke] the Veda to Brahmā, the first poet, through the heart— that is, solely by means of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
But not by means of a sentence.
Therefore, he manifested [it].
Here, by the word *brahman*, which denotes that which is vast, its nature as consisting of all knowledge is made known.

By the word "hṛdi," his status as the inner controller (antaryāmin) and his nature as consisting of all powers are made known; by the phrase "the first poet" (ādikavi), his status as the source of the scriptures (śāstrayonitva) is indicated, because he is the fundamental cause of even that [poetry] through his instruction.
And there is a scriptural passage on this point:
"He who in the beginning fashioned Brahmā and who indeed delivered the Vedas to him."
"I indeed seek refuge in that God, the light of self-consciousness"— thus says the seeker of liberation.
He states that even liberated souls do not possess that causal nature, for they say, "They are deluded."
In that Brahman known as the Veda, even the wise ones such as Śeṣa and others [are absorbed];
and by this, the Veda consisting of sighs manifested through the pastime of reclining [is indicated].
And he who possesses the various faces and eyes of Brahmā and others, whose primary forms are Padmanābha and so forth, is declared to be none other than the illustrious Blessed One (Śrī Bhagavān);
this has been explained.
By the passage beginning with "By whom Sarasvatī was impelled in the past" (BhP 2.4.22) and so forth;
this then follows immediately after the sūtra "But that [Brahman is the cause], because of the harmony [of all texts]" (BS 1.1.4).
He says "But that" (tat tu) to show that the reason for the scripture being the source [of Brahman] is indeed seen.
Here, "concordance" (samanvaya) means a correct, all-encompassing connection or derivation.

Since it is determined that the status of being the source of the scriptures is fully understood through the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas, the sense is that there is no knowledge at all regarding the individual soul (*jīva*), for the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is indeed insentient.
He does not know the universe.
This is because of the Vedic revelation that "He knows that.
To make known, by way of negative concomitance, this perfect knowledge of His which He possesses, [the text] states that all living beings whatsoever lack that perfect knowledge of His.
"They are deluded" means that even the wise,
such as Śeṣa and others, are deluded regarding this very Word-Brahman (śabda-brahman);
this has been explained by the Blessed One himself:
"What does she enjoin? What does she declare? And what does she explain by way of restatement?"—in this world, no one other than myself knows her heart.
By this [verse], the Blessed Lord himself is directly expressed.
Now, the alternative meaning of the phrase "not based on the Word" (*nāśabdam*) has already been indicated in the very passage where it says "the Knower" (*abhijña*).
Here is the meaning of the Sūtra: [Objection]—But surely, according to such scriptural passages as "soundless, touchless, formless, immutable," how can that [Brahman] have the Word as its source?
For in that context, the word "Brahman" is not lacking its primary sense.
Why?
Because of the act of seeing (*īkṣati*). In the passage, "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" [it says] "May I be many."
Because of hearing the verbal root *īkṣ* (to see) in the sense of sound; this very point he states: "May I be many," and so forth—namely, the one who possesses supernormal knowledge (*abhijña*).
He is skilled in the investigation of the nature of sound;
and that collection of powers such as sound and so forth is not his primordial nature, because it exists even prior to the agitation of primordial matter (*prakṛti*).
Therefore, he says "Svarāṭ" (Self-ruling) to show that [the Lord] is indeed his own essential nature.
Here, as before, such a state of possessing identical attributes and even corporeality is established. As they have said:
The authors of the Sūtras [state] "because they teach those properties at the end" (Vs 1.1.10).
Therefore, it should be understood that "not being based on the Word" (*aśabdatva*) and so forth refers precisely to the absence of the original Word (*prākṛta-śabda*) and the like.
Herein, the meaning of all four chapters of the Uttara-mīmāṃsā has been shown;
among them, the first chapter, on Concordance (*samanvaya*), is indicated by the words "from the connection" and "and from the other."
"Truth is supreme" refers to the chapter on fruits (*phalādhyāya*).

Likewise, the meaning of the *gāyatrī* is also clear. In that context, "from which the birth, etc., of this [world arise]" is the meaning of the *praṇava*, because it denotes the possession of the power for creation and so forth. Thus it is.
Thus it is stated in the Agni Purāṇa, in the exposition of the Gāyatrī: "That light is the Blessed Viṣṇu, the cause of the birth and other states of the universe.
In this context, the phrase "the threefold creation is false" constitutes the meaning of the three Vyāhṛtis.
Because in both cases, the three worlds are intended to be non-different from that;
"Svarāṭ" refers to the illuminator of the sun.
"O Thou whose speech is supreme splendor!

By that [Veda] which is in the heart, may there be an invocation for the impelling of the activity of the intellect. This indicates a prayer: "May He, out of compassion, impel the functions of our intellect toward His own meditation."
This is the state of being. Thus it has been stated that the commencement is with the Gāyatrī.
And that splendor is within there, because of the teaching of its attributes, and so forth; that which is embodied is the beginningless [reality] of that.
"The object of meditation should indeed be conceived as having form.
In this regard, there are the following statements from the *Agnipurāṇa* concerning the sequence:
"Having thus performed the ritual of the twilight prayers (*sandhyā-vidhi*), one should mutter the *gāyatrī* and meditate upon it."
The Gāyatrī verses, the Uktha hymns, the Śāstra recitations, as well as the splendor and the vital breaths.
Therefore, she is remembered as Gāyatrī and Sāvitrī because she originates from Savitṛ; she is the illuminator, and because her nature is speech, she is Sarasvatī.

That light is the supreme Brahman; it is remembered as *bhargas* because it is splendor (*tejas*). It is said that *bhargas* comes from the root *bhrāj* (to shine), as frequently stated in the Vedic texts (*chandas*).
It is most excellent among all splendors, indeed the supreme among the supreme;
for it is always to be chosen by those who desire both worldly creation and liberation.
Because the root *vṛ* has the meaning of "choosing," [He is] that which is devoid of waking, dreaming, and so forth;
eternally pure, awakened, one, eternal, the radiant power (*bharga*), and the Supreme Lord.
We meditate upon Brahman as the supreme light for the sake of liberation;
that light is the Blessed Viṣṇu, the cause of the birth and other states of the universe.
Some recited Śiva, and some recited the form of Śakti;
some [recited] Sūrya, and some [recited] Agni—the deities of the Agnihotrin priests.
For Viṣṇu, in the form of fire and so forth, is indeed proclaimed as Brahman at the beginning of the Vedas;
that state of the divine Viṣṇu is remembered as his own abode.
Or, from the root *dadhāti* (to hold), "dhīmahi" means we should hold [it] with our minds;
and that *bhargas* of ours belongs to the intellects (*dhiyaḥ*) of all living beings.
Viṣṇu, assuming the forms of the sun and fire, impels and urges the intellects of all experiencers toward all actions, whether their ripening is seen or unseen.
Impelled by the Lord, one may go either to heaven or even into a pit;
this entire world, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), is pervaded by Hari as the Lord.
The Goddess sports with heaven and the other realms; he who is the Haṃsa is the Lord, the Puruṣa.
This Puruṣa is to be beheld through meditation within the solar orb.
Truth is the eternally auspicious Brahman, the supreme state of Viṣṇu;
it is the fourth, most excellent state of the radiant God.
"That person who is in the sun, he is I, the unsurpassed one,
who always sets in motion the auspicious deeds and so forth of people"— and so on. Wherein, taking the Gāyatrī as the subject, the detailed exposition of Dharma is described.
That which is exultant in the slaughter of the demon Vṛtra is called Bhāgavata.
And so forth.
